title: pressure-the-truth-about-the-d-day
html:
It’s 4.15am, Monday, 5th June, 1944, and having had his latest meeting with the respective British and American weather teams, Group Captain James Stagg is back to face the Supreme Commander and the Commanders-in-Chief.  Once again they are in the library of Southwick House, just a few miles north of Portsmouth on the south coast of England.  It’s a room full of largely forlorn and empty bookshelves, but now the requisitioned mansion’s Mess Room.  General Sir Bernard Montgomery, commanding all the Allied land forces for D-Day, is here, looking spry in corduroy trousers and high-neck grey pullover.  They all sit informally on armchairs as Stagg begins his forecast.  If anything, he tells them, there are grounds for greater optimism. Once again, the detailed grilling followed, then he is dismissed.

Back inside the library, it is now decision time. The forecast Stagg has given gives some cause for hope but there’s no getting away from it: the weather has turned, they’ve been dealt a lousy hand and no matter the talk of windows of high pressure, the next thirty-six hours are going to offer only awful conditions in which to launch the largest amphibious operation in the history of the world.  The stakes are simply immense. Monty, General Walter Bedell-Smith and Admrial Sir Bertram Ramsay are for going.  So too is Air Chief Marshal Sir Arthur Tedder, the Deputy Supreme Allied Command.  Air Chief Marshal Sir Trafford Leigh-Mallory – brother of George Mallory of Everest fame and commanding Allied air forces - has major doubts.  Ultimately, though, the decision rested with the Supreme Allied Commander, General Dwight D. Eisenhower. It’s his job, and his alone.

The burden is his.

There’s a new film out about this critical moment in history. Pressure, it’s brilliantly simple but appropriate title, was originally written for the stage by the actor, David Haig, but now is in cinemas with immense fanfare and starring a shaven-headed Brendan Fraser as Eisenhower. Andrew Scott as Stagg and Damian Lewis as Montgomery.  There are sound reasons for keeping a cast tight on the stage, but less so in a movie, so it’s disappointing that there’s no Tedder, for example, responsible for one of the sharpest comments of all in the weather discussions that preceded D-Day.  Nor is there any sign of Bedell-Smith, who was far more of an advisor and influence to Eisenhower than Kay Summersby.  But I get it – this is a movie.  It might based on real events, but this is a drama.  It’s fiction.

So, what was the reality?  Well, weather forecasting in the summer of 1944 was a very imprecise science.  There were no satellites, so crucial to modern forecasting. Weather stations were dotted all over the United Kingdom and there were even such stations on the west coast of Ireland that could be drawn upon by the Allied meteorologists despite Ireland’s neutrality.  Beyond the British Isles, though, the density of sources diminished woefully: a few weather ships and that was it, which was a big problem because the prevailing weather patterns came from across the Atlantc – in other words, where weather stations were their patchiest.  Admittedly, each one was equipped with barometers, anemometers, wind vanes, temperature sensors and thermometers and the meteorologists aboard were read cloud heights, bases, sea swell as well as wind speeds, but the Atlantic was a big place, the variables were massive and ultimately, predicting weather became increasingly hard with every passing day.

There were also different schools of thought about how best to forecast.  One of the senior American weatherman was Dr Irving Krick, attached to US Strategic Air Forces, who was a fervent believer in using historic patterns and weather cycles to supplement what could be learned from weather stations.  This was known as analogue forecasting.  Krick does play a big part in the film and in real life, was considered something of smug self-promoter within American meteorological circles. On the other hand, he had the backing of General Hap Arnold, the commander of the US Army Air Forces and now led the US team based at Widewings, the American Weather HQ.  The British Air Ministry meteorological team, on the other hand, were led by Dr Sverre Petterssen, a Norwegian, and Charles Douglas, who took a more strictly scientific approach.  There was also the Admiralty’s weather team offering forecasts as well and their collected predictions were forwarded to Group Captain James Stagg, a geophysicist by trade, but now Chief Meteorologist to Eisenhower, and Colonel Donald Yates, who was Stagg’s deputy.  It was Stagg, a thin-faced thirty-nine year-old Scot, who had the unenviable task of drawing the various weather forecasts together and drawing some kind of conclusion.

The trouble began brewing on a glorious sunny Thursday, 1 June, when at an evening weather conference the Air Ministry team of Petterssen and Douglas painted a gloomy outlook for D-Day, which had been set as Monday 5 June.  Krick and the Widewings team, in contrast, were far more optimistic.   By the following day, the Air Ministry were even more pessimistic, and Stagg felt compelled to relay this to Eisenhower and his commanders.  By the evening Petterssen was predicting ten-tenths cloud and a risk of a Force 5 gale on the Monday.  This was really not good.  Not good at all.

Reports from the weather stations were arriving every few hours and the charts updated by hand.  By the evening of Saturday 3 June, even Krick and the team at Widewings were agreeing with Petterssen’s view, as were the Admiralty’s weather men.  For Stagg, it was time to confront the commanders of the invasion once more, which he did in the library at Southwick House at 9.30pm.

‘Gentlemen,’ said Stagg, ‘the fears which I hoped you realised we had yesterday, Friday morning…are confirmed.’ A low front was sweeping in bringing low cloud, gales and rain.  ‘Those details apply for Sunday to Tuesday and at first on Wednesday.’

Questions were asked: Leigh-Mallory wanted to know what cloud cover they could expect over the French coast.  Ten-tenths, he was told.  Admiral Ramsay wanted to know whether the Force 5 winds were likely to last on Monday and Tuesday.  Yes.  And Wednesday?  Not settling immediately but getting brighter.  For a moment no-one spoke.  A gloom had descended over the room.  As Stagg and Yates left, he heard Eisenhower say to the others, ‘Are we prepared to take a gamble on this?’ Their discussions continued until around 11pm, when Stagg was told to return for another briefing at 4.15am the next morning, Sunday, 4 June.

‘Pleasant dreams, Stagg,’ said Tedder as he passed him.

The hours passed quickly, with no dream-time for Stagg or any of the weather teams.  Krick and the Widewings team now felt certain a ridge of high pressure from the Azores would keep the worst of the cloud away from the Normandy coast.  Petterssen strongly disagreed.   On the other hand, following a cold front - such as the one due to be passing through - would come a few hours of lighter winds and clearer weather regardless of how the Azores high behaved.  If the front passed across the Cotentin peninsular around midnight then, in theory, there would be an opportunity for the US airborne drop to still go ahead almost on schedule and for the British one a few hours later.  The bombers would most likely have the visibility they needed.

Stagg, though, felt he should side with Petterssen, who felt there would still be too much cloud cover to make the airborne drops and bombing feasible; instinctively, Stagg trusted Petterssen more than Krick, even if, deep down – if he was honest - it was for cultural reasons rather than anything else.  It has to be stressed there were huge reasons for sticking with 5 June and heeding Krick’s advice: the invasion force was already at sea and ready. Even a brief delay would be enormously problematic, both from the security and for the morale of the men now at sea.  At any rate, back in the library he advised the assembled commanders there was no real change; the forecast still looked bad.

Once again, Stagg was thanked and asked to leave while the commanders discussed the matter.   Monty was for pressing on regardless, but Tedder disagreed and opted for postponement.  Ike had always been worried that they would be attacking initially on D-Day with a force of significantly smaller numbers than that available to the enemy and pointed out they had always felt such an operation was possible only because of air power.  If they were unable to bring that to bear, however, then he too felt they should postpone.  ‘Are there any dissenting voices?’ he asked. There were none.  Forces S and J were already on their way and now had to be recalled.  Really, it was a terrible decision to have to make: the entire amphibious invasion force was already loaded onto their ships, where they would have to stay, cramped, uncomfortable, with morale and spirits draining with every passing hour. And what if the weather didn’t improve?  What then?

Outside, Stagg looked up at the still, almost cloudless sky and felt the enormity of the decision resting on their shoulders.  He headed back to the SHAEF command post and to his tent to try and get some rest.  Eisenhower also headed to his caravan, where he was surrounded by Westerns, newspapers and a plentiful supply of cigarettes.  He’d begun chain smoking these past few days.

4.30pm, Southwick House, Sunday, 4 June.  Stagg called a conference with all his weather teams.  All agreed there was a small ridge of high pressure that looked like it might follow in behind the current low, which, if it remained on track should last until Tuesday morning, 6 June.  The weather from Wednesday to Friday still looked unsettled.  It was, however, quite a big ‘if.’  This small ridge of high pressure was being reported from the very few weather ships out the Atlantic; there was a pattern, definitely, but whether it would stay on course and develop into the clearer skies they hoped for really was far from certain.

I discussed this in great detail with Dr Simon Keeling, a leading meteorologist in the UK and someone who specialises in aviation forecasting.  We looked at the original D-Day maps, available for anyone to look at in the Met Office archives in Exeter.  Simon pointed out to me that the weather briefing had been incorrect for the Dams Raid, for example, in May 1943, which had led to some of the Lancasters veering off course and paying the price as a result.  But he also talked me through the weather forecasting for D-Day. He was at pains to point out that the predicted ridge of high pressure forecast to sweep in during the early hours and morning of 6 June 1944, was based on very little indeed.  ‘They were lucky,’ he told me.  ‘It’s there all right, but it’s small and could easily have been swept off into the North Sea and missed the Channel and Normandy coast altogether.’

So, the danger at this time – the early hours of 4 June 1944 - was that in clutching at this potential lifeline they were now resting upon it too much hope and dismissing the risk that such a ridge could easily be pinched, squeezed out, pushed off course.  Then there wouldn't be any high coming in at all.  The low cloud would continue along with the wind and rain. What Krick was recommending was sticking with 5 June and was fairly confident fine weather would follow in the early hours of the morning, albeit for a limited time. Even Stagg agreed. ‘The fair interval from early hours Monday to Tuesday is confirmed,’ noted Stagg in his diary after the next meeting with his teams at 7.30pm that night.’  On the other hand, the small high forecast for the morning of Tuesday, 6 June, was still off the west coast of Ireland with only limited weather stations tracking its progress. During the early hours of Sunday, 4th June, there remained a distinct possibility this small ridge of high pressure could still be pushed north over central England rather than over the Channel. The die, though, had been cast.  The 24-hour postponement had already been made.

At 9pm, Stagg once more spoke to the assembled D-Day commanders and reported the improved picture.  After being thoroughly grilled he left them to their discussions.  Monty was emphatically for going.  So too was Bedell-Smith.  ‘It’s a helluva gamble,’ said Ike’s Chief of Staff, ‘but it’s the best possible gamble.’

‘The question,’ said Eisenhowwer, ‘is just how long can you hang this operation on the end of a limb and let it hang there?’  Because of tides and moons, the next opportunity would be 19th  June.  That was two weeks.  A fortnight in which the Germans further strengthened their defences, and two weeks in which there was a huge dip in morale of the invasion force, and potential security leaks.  It was unthinkable.  They had to go.

Around twenty minutes later, Eisenhower emerged from the library.

‘Stagg, we’ve put it on again,’ he told him.  ‘For heaven’s sake hold the weather to what you have forecast for us.  Don’t you bring any more bad news.’ He smiled then stepped back inside.  Shortly after that, it was agreed they would reconvene once again at 4.15am, Monday, 5th June, for the final irreversible decision.

Stagg returned to his tent around 10.30pm and tried to get some rest but sleep eluded him.  Outside, the rain was slashing down against the canvas, the wind testing the guy ropes to the full.  ‘Lay and thought of what it all meant,’ he noted, ‘and hoped and hoped that our story would come through.’  His choice of words could not have been more apt.

At 3am, he us up again and meeting his weather teams.  By this time the front had already passed through – the skies were largely clear and the winds had dropped; if it was clear in Portsmouth, it was clear in the Cotentin Peninsular too and probably rapidly clearing across the rest of Normandy as well, so had they stuck to the original D-Day, it would hardly have been the disaster that had been feared: the air forces would have had clear views, the weather on the coast would have been better for the actual landings themselves, and only the British airborne drop would have had to have been postponed by a couple of hours; that would not have been a good, and who knows, might have altered the chances of successfully taking Pegasus and Horsa bridges intact and of blowing the bridges further east across the Dives. Alternatively, it might have made the task easier thanks to lesser winds and so resulting in a tighter drop.

Who knows? It’s fascinating to consider and had they gone on 5th June, Krick might have been the hero and Stagg now largely forgotten.  No matter: the decision had already been made.  It was too late to have any feelings of regret over the 24-hour postponement. The decision had been made.  How the weather was going to behave the following night was what now mattered.

And so, just after 4.15am Stagg, along with Eisenhower, his Chief of Staff, his Deputy Supreme Commander and his service chiefs were all assembled in the library. All eyes were on Eisenhower, waiting for his decision.

The Supreme Commander sat in his chair, rubbed his face in his hands, then looked up.  ‘OK,’ he said, ‘Let’s go.’

title: are-we-the-bad-guys
html:
In a brilliant sketch by David Mitchell and Robert Webb, the two comedians, dressed in SS uniforms, question why they’ve got skulls as part of their insignia. ‘Hans,’ asks Mitchell’s character, ‘are we the bad guys?’ Perhaps those soon to be wearing the new US Space Force uniforms will be asking themselves the same question.  In an AI-generated picture, revealed to the world last week, a square-jawed figure stands upright and erect, legs slightly apart, hands behind his back, chin jutting.  He’s the epitome of old-fashioned Caucasian - Aryan? - manhood.  His uniform, meanwhile, reveals a crisp and decidedly 19th-century military tunic, leather belt and silver buckle around his waist, with a stiff, high, collar with military tabs, wings on his chest, tight trousers and rounded off with shiny leather boots extending up just below the knee.

This proposed uniform for US Space Force, the newest wing of the United States’ military and which the President created back in 2019, during his first term, would be considered an April Fool’s trick were it not September and were these images not released at the behest of Trump.  To say this is a ludicrous design is a massive understatement.  He’s claiming it was inspired by the movie, Starship Troopers, which in itself is risible - after all, what serious politician would want their armed forces to be inspired by a lightweight science-fiction movie?  For everyone else, however, this new look is less Starship Troopers and more as though it was lifted straight from the militia of a Bond villain - an image that was, of course, quite deliberately inspired by Nazi uniforms.  It’s even a kind of field grey, for goodness sake.

The uniforms of the Nazis have become so iconic it’s easy just to accept them at face value with their grey and black and plenty of leather.  In fact, they were, for the most part, immensely impractical, pointlessly expensive and over-designed and not really fit for the task allotted them.  Few have bothered to question such a unique look, though, because the uniforms of the Nazi regime just look how they look: distinctive, striking and, of course, sinister or fabulous, depending on your leaning.

During the Blitzkrieg years of German victories, Hitler’s armies gained a reputation for tactical and operational brilliance, augmented by superb training and the best, most modern weaponry.  There were, however, a number of curious paradoxes to the German Army. It may have had innovative sub-machine guns and other finely engineered weaponry, for example, but despite the impression of vast military might, there was also something rather old school about the German Army in other areas. Certain forward-thinking officers, such as General Heinz Guderian, may have spent time writing treatises on the future of armoured warfare, but for the most part the Army was still dominated by a traditional Prussian military aristocracy that cited an inheritance which stretched back to Frederick the Great and the Seven Years’ War in the middle of the eighteenth century. Men like von Clausewitz, von Moltke, von Schlieffen, von Hindenburg, von Ludendorff were all household names in Germany – and at the start of the war, the Army was commanded by yet another Prussian aristo, Field Marshal Walter von Brauchitsch. Even in Nazi Germany, it was hard to climb to the top of the pole without a ‘von’ before your name.

It still had a rather nineteenth-century look to it too. The Pickelhaube, the old pointed helmet, had gone, but the large amounts of leather, the high jackboots, the baggy-thigh breeches and the traditional high-collared tunics all harked back to an earlier era when looking the part – looking militaristic – was very much the brief. They looked smart, they looked efficient. They looked like they meant business, which was precisely the effect they were supposed to achieve. This more traditional military look was eagerly adopted by the Nazis, not least because a powerful military tradition was what set the German character apart; Germany had been forged in 1871 with the Prussian states at its heart, and they, during the 1860s, had drawn upon militarism as being at the very core of their existence.

There is no question that the German nation which emerged from the collection of kingdoms, duchies and principalities less than seventy years earlier was a militaristic society, but the idea that the Prussian – and later German – military was manifestly superior to any other in the world was a dubious claim. Prussia – the largest German kingdom prior to unification – had fought only a handful of small wars in the century that separated the end of the Napoleonic Wars and the conflict in 1914. When it had gone to war alongside Austria against Denmark in 1864, it had barely fought since Waterloo fifty years earlier and most certainly did not out-perform Austria militarily. Two years later, Prussia was at war with its former ally, but Austrian mistakes were every bit as important to Prussia’s subsequent victory as any military genius. Four years after that Prussia was at war again, this time against the mighty France, and it was on this stunning success that much of its military swagger, which would be sustained and would grow further within the newly formed Germany, was based.

Interestingly, however, all three wars, and indeed German unification in 1871, were orchestrated not by a military leader but by a political one, namely Otto von Bismarck. Following unification, the military was elevated in society, with veterans venerated and uniforms and military bearing considered the aspiration of every self-respecting young German male. No one was more fond of standing ramrod straight and wearing military garb than the Kaiser, Wilhelm II, who was always to be seen in a variety of uniforms, shiny breastplates and Pickelhaube, but had never actually seen any combat himself or, frankly, been much of a soldier. Also woven into the military heritage was von Clausewitz’s widely read and acclaimed work On War, but this was based on analysis of Napoleon, who was French, and was, in any case, interpreted to suit Nazi ideology. The other iconic figure was the Prussian king, Frederick the Great, who belonged to the eighteenth century, and who, despite continued veneration by a stream of Germans from Admiral Tirpitz through to Hitler, had won just eight of his sixteen battles and even one of those, the Battle of Zorndorf in 1758, might more accurately be considered a stalemate.

None the less, von Clausewitz’s military theories and Frederick’s victories certainly added to the belief in Germany’s military inheritance. Somehow, the Prussians, and then Germany, had created not only a militaristic society in which soldiers were greatly venerated, but also a reputation for military brilliance, which was based on not a huge amount if they were really honest. At the turn of the twentieth century, when Britain had threatened Imperial Germany with economic blockade and the destruction of its Navy if it became involved in the Boer War, the Kaiser backed down and kept out of it. This humiliation – and his obsession with ships – contributed to the vast building programme of capital vessels, and resulted in a giant fleet that ventured out once, at Jutland in 1916, then retreated, and was scuttled at the end of the war. Germany’s great military tradition was thus based on a somewhat spurious reputation and had, in any case, taken a massive blow with the catastrophic defeat of 1918.

The Nazis were emerging at a time when morale within Germany was low, but they cleverly appealed to this suspect military tradition and to German pride in that sense of martial inheritance. By strutting around with straight backs and chests out, wearing snappy brown or black uniforms, and with starkly striking insignia that harked back to ancient Aryan runes, the Nazis were inviting people to come and join an exciting new club. The message was simple: be a National Socialist, and wear a smart-looking uniform and be reinvigorated with a renewed sense of national pride, identity and purpose. Look good, be part of our gang, and you will be more attractive to a young, blonde and beautiful fraulein.

It was hardly an original ruse, but the cut and design of the uniforms were very deliberately intended to look both smart and debonair while also nodding to the military past.  There was even an imperial eagle only in the Nazi world, the head was facing the other way and was underscored by a swastika. Nazi uniforms were as beautifully tailored as an MG34 machine-gun was engineered, and when it came to dressing the rapidly growing Army, these principles were rigorously maintained. The field tunics of the ordinary German soldier were not quite so sartorially elegant as the SS outfits, but they were smart enough and certainly supremely well made. A private was not paid much, but he was given very decent kit. The jacket, the Feldbluse, was lined in soft cotton or rayon, was thigh length with two generously large and pleated pockets on the chest and two on the waist; it was also pleated at the back, while the cuffs had buttons that could be undone and the waist four lots of eyelets through which metal belt clips could be threaded. The buttons were all aluminium, rounded at the edges for easy use and with a dotted pattern, and quite deliberately designed as opposed to simply mass-stamped. The collar of the Feldbluse was well stitched and around the inside was another row of buttons on to which a smart and comfortable collar liner could be attached. It was warm,comfortable and produced with the kind of attention to detail that would make a bespoke tailor smile with pleasure.

In 1939, each soldier was given no fewer than seven uniforms: field, service, watch, parade, report, walking out and sport. The numbers of cloth suppliers and tailors involved with making all these uniforms was immense, but like most German war production there was no adherence to the principles of mass production. Among these firms was the company, Hugo Boss, but at this stage it was a manufacturer, not a designer; despite the urban myth, Hugo Boss did not design any Nazi uniform, SS or otherwise.  Rather, it was just one of hundreds churning out this huge raft of military garb.  There were, for example, no fewer than 323 different companies producing just one particular type of military linen. This was a trend repeated across the board. Most of the soldier’s webbing was made of black leather: the ammunition pouches, holsters, belts, straps and even the case that held the stout short-handle entrenching tool. Boots came up almost to the knee rather than the ankle. Field packs, although made of canvas, came with leather straps and a fur-covered outer flap. One particularly well-engineered piece of personal kit was the gas mask case, a steel cylinder with grooves down the side to give it added strength. It was quite large and even bulky, but the attention to detail on it was impressive, with a spring metal catch and inside, within the lid, a further little compartment in which spare lenses for the mask were stored and held in place by a delicate spring-loaded catch. The intricacy with which these millions of tins were manufactured – each some 25 centimetres tall – was impressive; and they even came with a leather carrying strap. It became an instantly iconic piece of the soldier’s equipment.

Young officers had even more elaborate uniforms. Their field dress was made of the same wool as those of their men, but their service dress was gabardine with silk or rayon lining and with a cuff that doubled back almost halfway to their elbows, which was almost eighteenth century in its design. Officers were given wool greatcoats or full-length leather versions. There were different uniforms for mountain troops, different uniforms for paratroopers, yet more uniforms for the panzer arm, and even more for the Luftwaffe. Pilots like Hajo Herrmann could choose from a staggering array of breeches, woollen trousers, leather trousers, cotton, wool and leather jackets of differing shades of brown and black, some fur lined, others not.

This attention to detail and to producing a sartorially unbeatable armed services was all well and good and had certainly, in the early years of the Nazis at any rate, served a valid purpose. Unlike Britain, however, Germany had few sheep farms and no Dominions on the far side of the world from where it could easily purchase what it lacked at home. In fact, Germany had very few natural resources of its own at all – no oil, very little iron ore, no tungsten, no bauxite, no copper; a coal industry was about all it did have and even that was as nothing compared with Britain’s, for example. And because so much of the economy was now devoted to war production, Germany had little to export in return. It also had very few sheep - just 4.5 million compared with 24.5 million pigs. Curiously, Britain had just 4.5 million pigs, but 24.5 million sheep as well as access to the wool of its dominions, New Zealand and Australia, useful assets when dramatically increasing the number of military uniforms.  Yet rather than watching the pfennigs in areas where costs could easily have been kept down, there was, in 1939, no armed forces that was more expensively turned out than that of The Wehrmacht. The cost of German uniforms, however, was, from the Nazi perspective, a small price to pay to make soldiers believe they were part of a modern and technologically advanced militaristic society.

They were also an acceptable cost providing the Nazis won the war in quick order.  The problems started to arise once the war continued, year after shattering year and the German economy, and with it precious resources, became increasingly stretched.  A new feld blouse was introduced in 1943 but the concessions to economy was the straightening of the pocket flaps and taking out the pleats; otherwise, it was the same.  So, no real economising whatsoever.  The fancy buttons largely remained to the end of the war, as did the totally pointless gas-mask case. What was wrong with a canvas bag in times of hardship?  Admittedly, canvas did gradually start to be introduced but never entirely kicked the German love of leather into the long grass. Canvas, though, is far cheaper, doesn’t rot so easily if it becomes wet and is in every way more practical. The Nazis never really accepted this, despite later introducing a shorter jacket and ankle boots.  Right to the end, the look outweighed pragmatics.

The British and Americans, by contrast, did take a far more pragmatic approach to uniforms, a reflection that they had become warfare states but not militaristic ones.  In fact, the British Army had the most modern uniforms - and practical - uniforms in the world by the start of the Second World War. Hand-in-hand with rearmament in the second half of the thirties had come the recognition that attitudes had to change, that a modern war required modern equipment, and that Britain needed to use its global reach to full effect. Ironically, the impression from German propaganda of a Reich that was creating a modern, mechanized military Moloch had done much to kick-start this new outlook.

With the scent of war in the air, Britain had, in 1938, designed the Battledress, a highly innovative concept and the most modern and practical combat uniform adopted by any European power. Made of hard-wearing khaki wool serge, it consisted of a short jacket that came down to its wearer’s midriff. This was very sensible given the high-waisted trousers of the day; the battle blouse, as the jacket was called, therefore only covered the waistband of the trousers, and in so doing saved a significant amount of fabric on earlier designs and on those worn by almost every other army the world over.  The German feldbluse, for example, came halfway down the thigh with an extra length of at least eighteen inches on the battle blouse - eighteen inches that the British quite sensibly decided was a total waste of wool. The battle blouse was generously cut under the arms, allowing easy movement, and considerable thought had been given to the pockets – two large ones on the inside of the jacket, two large breast pockets, side pockets on the trousers and a further generous pocket on the thigh, big enough for a map or documents. The old knee-high puttees had also gone, relics of a former era, replaced by durable canvas ankle gaiters. This new soldier’s uniform had no frills, wasted no material, and was exceptionally cheap and easy to mass-produce, while at the same time allowing its wearer easy manoeuvrability and warmth.

The US Army took a similar approach.  Ever since the First Wolrd War, the US Army had equipped its men with the standard round-rimmed Tommy helmet, as used by the British. A completely new design came into service in 1941, however, known as the M1. This fitted comfortably over the head and covered much of the back of the neck and ears, but its liner was both more comfortable than the old helmet and a closer fit. New uniforms were entering service as well. The US Army had issued its men with a wool ‘OD’ – olive drab – service coat, which was similar to the field tunics worn by many nationalities; it was, in essence, a tunic with big pockets and brass buttons that came halfway down the thigh. By early 1940, however, General George C. Marshall, the Army Chief of Staff, felt it was time for a new look – one that reflected the largely civilian and modern army he hoped it would become, and one that provided both comfort and easy movement. A number of civilian windbreakers were examined, but none quite hit the mark, so Major-General J. K. Parsons, commanding the 5th Division, was given the task of overseeing the design, trials and eventual procurement of a new field jacket. ‘In deciding upon the garment to be recommended,’ he wrote to the Adjutant-General, ‘the needs of the Infantry soldier were given primary consideration.  It was therefore decided that a suitable jacket to meet his needs must not only be warm and comfortable, but must be light in weight and have the minimum in bulkiness. This was much the same brief given the designers of the British Battledress, but in its consideration of comfort for the ordinary soldier, quite radical.

A design was drawn up and produced. Although it was olive drab in colour, it did look very like a civilian windcheater, with a centre zip-and-button combination, generous under the arms and coming down to just below the waist. General Parsons tested the jacket extensively using 400 of his men as guinea pigs. Any adjustments – such as taking the flaps off the side pockets – were due to the advice of the majority of these soldiers. The Quartermaster General’s office still sent the design to Esquire magazine, who advised further on cloth and, inevitably, the look of the thing, which prompted a rather terse reply from General Parsons. ‘Esquire may be an authority on what a well dressed gentleman should wear,’ he wrote, ‘but a study of its comments and the design of the garment it submitted as a substitute shows plainly that it does not understand the purpose of the garment and is ignorant of the needs of the soldier in the field.’ Someone else from behind a desk then suggested it was too short and in cold weather might cause kidney trouble. ‘All I can say,’ replied Parsons, ‘is most men have kidney trouble when in the presence of the enemy and it is fear not the length of the garment that causes it.’ The new M1941 field jacket, known, perhaps justifiably, as the ‘Parsons Jacket’, was duly adopted. Made of water-resistant cotton and lined with warm but lightweight wool, there was no other military jacket in the world that looked so casual or modern, nor one that had been designed and adopted with such thorough testing by those who would subsequently be wearing it in combat. As the US Army prepared for war, it was demonstrating a highly pragmatic but forward-thinking outlook – and, crucially, one that was not constrained by its military past.

So, what are the lessons here?  Well, it’s fair to say that the uniforms of the different combatant nations in World War II very much reflected the culture and society of those nations they were designed to clothe: militaristic, self-conscious and with a nod to the past in the case of Nazi Germany, but pragmatic and reflecting the emerging civilian conscript armies as far as the United States and Britain were concerned.  I’ll let people draw their own conclusions about Trump’s planned new Space Force designs…

The British and Americans, by contrast, did take a far more pragmatic approach to uniforms, a reflection that they had become warfare states but not militaristic ones.  In fact, the British Army had the most modern uniforms - and practical - uniforms in the world by the start of the Second World War. Hand-in-hand with rearmament in the second half of the thirties had come the recognition that attitudes had to change, that a modern war required modern equipment, and that Britain needed to use its global reach to full effect. Ironically, the impression from German propaganda of a Reich that was creating a modern, mechanized military Moloch had done much to kick-start this new outlook.

With the scent of war in the air, Britain had, in 1938, designed the Battledress, a highly innovative concept and the most modern and practical combat uniform adopted by any European power. Made of hard-wearing khaki wool serge, it consisted of a short jacket that came down to its wearer’s midriff. This was very sensible given the high-waisted trousers of the day; the battle blouse, as the jacket was called, therefore only covered the waistband of the trousers, and in so doing saved a significant amount of fabric on earlier designs and on those worn by almost every other army the world over.  The German feldbluse, for example, came halfway down the thigh with an extra length of at least eighteen inches on the battle blouse - eighteen inches that the British quite sensibly decided was a total waste of wool. The battle blouse was generously cut under the arms, allowing easy movement, and considerable thought had been given to the pockets – two large ones on the inside of the jacket, two large breast pockets, side pockets on the trousers and a further generous pocket on the thigh, big enough for a map or documents. The old knee-high puttees had also gone, relics of a former era, replaced by durable canvas ankle gaiters. This new soldier’s uniform had no frills, wasted no material, and was exceptionally cheap and easy to mass-produce, while at the same time allowing its wearer easy manoeuvrability and warmth.

The US Army took a similar approach.  Ever since the First Wolrd War, the US Army had equipped its men with the standard round-rimmed Tommy helmet, as used by the British. A completely new design came into service in 1941, however, known as the M1. This fitted comfortably over the head and covered much of the back of the neck and ears, but its liner was both more comfortable than the old helmet and a closer fit. It was ‘cleared for procurement’ on 7 May 1941 and it was recommended that ‘the item be given priority as essential.’ It would take time for the changeover to be completed, but in keeping with the rapid rearmament programmes now under way, a variety of civilian firms were involved in its manufacture, including, for example, the McCord Radiator Company of Detroit, who within a year would be producing no fewer than 400,000 M1 helmets per month.

New uniforms were entering service as well. The US Army had issued its men with a wool ‘OD’ – olive drab – service coat, which was similar to the field tunics worn by many nationalities; it was, in essence, a tunic with big pockets and brass buttons that came halfway down the thigh. By early 1940, however, General George C. Marshall, the Army Chief of Staff, felt it was time for a new look – one that reflected the largely civilian and modern army he hoped it would become, and one that provided both comfort and easy movement. A number of civilian windbreakers were examined, but none quite hit the mark, so Major-General J. K. Parsons, commanding the 5th Division, was given the task of overseeing the design, trials and eventual procurement of a new field jacket. ‘In deciding upon the garment to be recommended,’ he wrote to the Adjutant-General, ‘the needs of the Infantry soldier were given primary consideration.  It was therefore decided that a suitable jacket to meet his needs must not only be warm and comfortable, but must be light in weight and have the minimum in bulkiness. This was much the same brief given the designers of the British Battledress, but in its consideration of comfort for the ordinary soldier, quite radical.

A design was drawn up and produced. Although it was olive drab in colour, it did look very like a civilian windcheater, with a centre zip-and-button combination, generous under the arms and coming down to just below the waist. General Parsons tested the jacket extensively using 400 of his men as guinea pigs. Any adjustments – such as taking the flaps off the side pockets – were due to the advice of the majority of these soldiers. The Quartermaster General’s office still sent the design to Esquire magazine, who advised further on cloth and, inevitably, the look of the thing, which prompted a rather terse reply from General Parsons. ‘Esquire may be an authority on what a well dressed gentleman should wear,’ he wrote, ‘but a study of its comments and the design of the garment it submitted as a substitute shows plainly that it does not understand the purpose of the garment and is ignorant of the needs of the soldier in the field.’ Someone else from behind a desk then suggested it was too short and in cold weather might cause kidney trouble. ‘All I can say,’ replied Parsons, ‘is most men have kidney trouble when in the presence of the enemy and it is fear not the length of the garment that causes it.’ The new M1941 field jacket, known, perhaps justifiably, as the ‘Parsons Jacket’, was duly adopted. Made of water-resistant cotton and lined with warm but lightweight wool, there was no other military jacket in the world that looked so casual or modern, nor one that had been designed and adopted with such thorough testing by those who would subsequently be wearing it in combat. As the US Army prepared for war, it was demonstrating a highly pragmatic but forward-thinking outlook – and, crucially, one that was not constrained by its military past.

So, what are the lessons here?  Well, it’s fair to say that the uniforms of the different combatant nations in World War II very much reflected the culture and society of those nations they were designed to clothe: militaristic, self-conscious and with a nod to the past in the case of Nazi Germany, but pragmatic and reflecting the emerging civilian conscript armies as far as the United States and Britain were concerned.  I’ll let people draw their own conclusions about Trump’s planned new Space Force designs…

title: The Mad Story of the Eagle’s Nest
html:
There’s a photograph taken at the Kehlsteinhaus - or Eagle’s Nest as it is otherwise known - that has always got to me just a little.  It’s taken on the southern terrace, a walkway that runs around the east side and southern face of the building.  The terrace is perhaps one-and-a-half yards wide, with a low granite wall on the outer side with a gently rolled and smooth top.  Walking towards the camera - and the photographer is taking the shot at no more than knee height - is Martin Boorman, Hitler’s personal secretary at the time and Nazi Reichsleiter.  Boorman, not quite forty then - and I think this must have been taken in the summer of 1939 - looks fleshy, more like a Mafia boss than the fair-haired Teutonic ideal. He’s wearing a grey sports jacket and grey breeches; it’s urbane country chic with a touch of militarism.

But Boorman is not even the main subject in the picture, which is clearly just a snapshot.  In the foreground, leaning forward and staring at an unknown figure next to him, is the master of propaganda himself, Josef Goebbels, wearing an entirely civilian ivory double-breasted suit and round, tortoiseshell shades.  His shoes, which can also just be seen, are also ivory coloured. It’s a sharp look, make no mistake.  The man he’s talking to is making notes on a paper pad.  A secretary? Or a journalist? There are two others in the picture, a third sitting next to Goebbels almost entirely out of sight, and a further outsized Nazi at the far end of the walkway, one foot on the wall, a leather-cased pistol at his side.  This is a snapshot of the Nazis taking it easy in their mountain-top retreat.  It’s a strange blend of casualness and informality - an everyday scene - and something altogether more sinister: powerful men, lording it up, protected by outsized thugs.

Until the fire that ravaged this extraordinary building, it was possible for any one of the half a million annual visitors to walk along this very same route, sit where Goebbels is sitting and pause for some deep reflection on the awfulness of the Nazis and the passage of time.  Whether anyone will ever be able to do this again is hard to say.  I suspect it would be hard to justify public spending on one of the last completely surviving structures built by the Nazis and especially one so inextricably linked to Adolf Hitler himself.  On the other hand, half a million visitors is a big contribution to the local economy.  So, who knows.

I first visited there some twenty years ago and have filmed TV documentaries there numerous times and even visited the area on a family summer’s holiday.  The Kehlstein is a stunning mountain, looking down over the Obersalzburg and below that, the remarkably picturesque town of Berchtesgaden. It’s only a stone’s throw from Salzburg. I once took a taxi from the airport to Berchtesgaden and the young driver admitted he’d only recently watched The Sound of Music. ‘You know the bit at the end where they’re escaping into the mountains? Well, they’re going the wrong way. They were heading straight into the jaws of the Nazis!’

In fact, they’re heading towards the Untersberg - a particularly striking ridge of mountains. These, as well as the mass of quaint villages, mountain pastures and lakes such a the breaktakingly beautiful Königsee, make this corner of Bavaria an absolute gem. If anyone gets a chance to visit in May, do take the plunge.  The countryside here is richly green and fecund, birdsong is loud, cuckoos coo gently on the breeze and everywhere looks as pretty as a picture. It’s a fairytale land right out the Brothers Grimm, Wagner operas and cute biscuit tin art.  Houses are wooden and look exactly as one would imagine.  People do sport lederhosen and the women in the bars wear Dirndl, the traditional dress.  Writing on buildings is reassuringly gothic in its script.  It is, without question, one of the most beautiful places to which I’ve ever been.

Hitler thought so too.  Although from Linz in Austria, Hitler had migrated to Munich before the First World War and returned to the city when it was all over, found his voice first while working lecturing former soldiers on the dangers of Bolshevism and then in the beer halls where he discovered he could more than hold a room with his rabble-rousing rhetoric.  After joining the Deutsche Arbeiterpartei - DAP - in September 1919, he quickly became the charismatic mouthpiece of what, in February 1920, became the Nationalsozialistische Deutsche Arbeiterpartei - which in turn was swiftly became abbreviated as the Nazis.  By July 1921, Hitler had become its undisputed leader.

A man who had enormous influence on this young political firebrand was Dietrich Eckart, a völkisch poet and playwright, as well as a journalist and one of the founders of the DAP.  Eckart also became the publisher of the Nazi’s own newspaper, the Völkischer Beobachter.  Charismatic, clever and talented, he had made his name adapting Ibsen’s play, Peer Gynt, into a new version in which Peer Gynt becomes a hero not an anti-hero, and the symbol of Germanic superiority, challenging the trolls of the world, which, in his warped world-view, meant the Jews. Eckart told the impressionable Hitler that Germany needed a great messiah and that the ends would justify the means to create a German world that was racially purer, and which would only heal itself after a brutal war of annihilation in which it emerged victorious.

There’s no doubt that while Eckart was impressed by Hitler’s oratory skills and charisma, Hitler was equally in thrall to Eckart’s philosophising and intellectualism, even if his theories were born of increasingly rabid anti-Semitism and a distinctly skewed racism.  It was Eckart who also extolled the spiritual and physical benefits of living and hiking in the countryside and who lured the impressionable Hitler to Berchtesgaden for the first time.  Eckhart, twenty-one years Hitler’s superior, rapidly became a father-like figure and mentor, guiding him towards his destiny as the saviour and messiah of a new reborn Germany.  Eckart was also a drunk, eventually lost influence with Hitler and died aged only 55 in December 1923.

In fact, it was in the early summer of 1922 that Hitler first made his way to Berchtesgaden.  At the time, Eckart was lying low there, fearing political arrest. Using the alias, ‘Wolf’, Hitler checked into the Pension Moritz on the Obsersalzberg, overlooking Berchtesgaden. It was while there, taking long walks with Eckart in the mountains, that Hitler fell in love with the landscape. ‘For me,’ he said later, ‘the Obersalzburg had become a magnificent place.’ This awakening was in May, that most lovely of months there.

And it was the following May, of 1923, that he once again returned to Berchtesgaden, or more specifically to the Penion Moritz.  From Berchtesgaden, the road wound its way up the hill to the south until reaching a small collection of villas and guesthouses.  From the Pension Moritz, Hitler could look out over the Untersberg, on the other side of the valley, a jagged set of peaks where legend had it that the German emperor, Frederick Barbarossa, lay still asleep inside the mountains, awaiting his resurrection.  Whenever Barbarossa finally left the mountain, so the myth went, the last great battle of mankind would be fought.

Hitler loved these stories, as did Dietrich Eckart, again his companion for a walking and talking holiday in these glorious mountains that May of 1923. The core members of the DAP and then the Nazis were all imbued with a love of völkisch myths and tales of ancient knights and chivalry.  Themes from the Arthurian legends were blended with older tales but all led them back to the same ideology: that there was a need for Germany to return to its purer origins - time of Aryan and Teutonic pure breeds.  There was no room in their Germany for Slavs, incursors from the east, nor Jews, who corrupted hearts, race and society.

Later that year, in November 1923, came the failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich, for which Hitler was lucky to spend just nine months of a five-year sentence.  When he was released, with the first part of his memoir-cum-mission statement, Mein Kampf, largely written, he returned to Munich and continued to cement his increasingly iron-grip on the Nazi party.  With it came a growing acceptance in higher society.  Among those drawn to Hitler’s mesmeric ability to sway the masses was Ernst ‘Putzi’ Hanfstaengl, a giant German-American, Harvard-educated and wealthy businessman.  Hitler became a regular guest at Hanfstaengl’s house, where his lack of table manners and petty bourgeoise awkwardness were willingly overlooked. Hanfstaengl was completely obsessed with how Hitler could transform any crowd of any number with his electrifying rhetoric. When Hitler appalled guests by adding sugar to vintage wine, Hanfstaengl admitted, ‘he could have peppered it for each naive act increased my belief in his homespun sincerity.’

It was the Hanfstaengls who introduced Hitler to Frau Elsa Bruckmann, a society figure who similarly favoured pan-Germanism and was an anti-Semite. Frau Bruckmann was also friends with the Becksteins, the piano manufacturers, and it was through this new circle that Hitler was first invited the Bayreuth Wagner Festival in July 1925.  He was transfixed and Wagner’s operas became one of his great obsessions.  Wagner, also an anti-Semite and similarly entranced by völkisch myths, based many of his operas around heroic but tragic ancient knights, from Parsifal - Sir Percival - to Tristan and Isolde.  His stirring, romantic music set to tales of mythical fantasy in a world of castles, forests and mountains dovetailed perfectly with Hitler’s growing love of the Alpine countryside around Berchtesgaden, where he’d spent much of that summer writing the second part of Mein Kampf.

Once again, Hitler had stayed at the Pension Moritz, although he had also retreated to write what became known as the ‘Kampfhäusl’, a small wooden mountain hut on the slopes just above the Obersalzburg.  While there, Hitler developed a consistent daily routine, rising fairly late, writing and dictating his book, then walking on a track around the mountains to a lovely Alpine meadow lying beneath the towering and almost sheer cliffs of the Hoher Göll. At the end of the meadow stood an inn and tea house, the Scharitzkehlalm.  Hitler, who had a very sweet tooth, used to pause there, take a hot chocolate and eat a plate of windbeutal, a local pastry filled with wild berries and cream.  Then he’d toddle back to the Pension Moritz.

By this time, Hitler had come to think of Berchtesgaden and the Obersalzberg as his special place where he knew he would always want to return.  In 1926, however, the simpatico owners of the Pension Moritz had moved away and Hitler took a dislike to the new owner.  That summer he stayed mainly in the Deutsches Haus in Berchtesgaden, but still spent much time walking around the mountains surrounding the town.

Hitler became increasingly keen to find a place of his own and in 1928 learned that a chalet close to the Pension Moritz at Obersalzberg, known as the Haus Wachenfeld, had become available to rent. The owner, Frau Winter, had been recently widowed, was a party member, and now willingly offered the place to Hitler at a very reasonable 100 marks a month.  Hitler contacted his half-sister, Angela Raubal, and asked her to keep house for him, even though they’d never been close.  Not only did she agree, she brought her daughter,  Geli, an attractive and spirited twenty year-old.  Hitler was particularly fond of his niece, who tragically would be found dead in his flat in Munich three years later.

Hitler now had a home on the Obersalzberg and by 1933 he had not only become Chancellor of Germany but was also by this time very rich indeed, largely thanks to the royalties of his runaway bestseller, Mein Kampf.  Whether Frau Winter wanted to hang on to the Haus Wachenfled is not clear but when Hitler offered to buy the chalet she could hardly refuse.

Almost immediately, Hitler decided to transform it into something altogether more grandiose. The architect, Alois Degano, was hired to dramatically enlarge and repurpose it complete with a new name: the Berghof - the Mountain Court.  Overseeing the entire project was none other than Martin Bormann, then personal secretary to the party deputy, Rudolf Hess, and a highly efficient lawyer and today now rapidly making himself indispensable to Hitler, transformed now into the one and only Führer - the Leader of all Germany.

While Degano oversaw the remodelling of the house, Bormann brought in Gerdy Troost, a celebrated interior designer, and widow to Hitler’s favourite architect, Paul Troost.  Already a member of the Nazi Party and acolyte of the Führer, her task was to transform the interiors.  There was now a grand entrance hall, a panelled dining room, a library filled with books on art, history, music and architecture.  Outside was a large terrace, bedecked with sun loungers and with stunning views across the valley to the Untersberg.  The house even had its own telephone switchboard and projector booth for film screenings and a giant window that could be lowered to give an open-air panorama of the mountains.

Hitler loved it there.  A non-smoker himself, he allowed smoking only on the outdoor terrace, keeping the interior of the house fresh and fragrant.  He also a vegetarian, food mostly produced in neighbouring kitchen gardens.  Inevitably, most other leading Nazis gravitated to the Obersalzberg too.  Hermann Göring, Commander-in-Chief of the Luftwaffe, President of Prussia and the man responsible for transforming the German economy, built a larger house of his own on the hill a short distance from the Berghof.  Hitler’s immediate neighbour was Martin Bormann.  A little way further down the road to Berchtesgaden, Hitler’s new favourite architect, the young Albert Speer, also bought a chalet.  With the Führer spending ever-more time there, security provisions needed to be created, all overseen by Martin Bormann, who requisitioned the entire Obersalzberg and which was swiftly fenced off, becoming the Führer-Sperrgebiet - the Leader’s Restrcited Area.  Gate houses were erected, the Türken Gasthaus, sandwiched between the Berghof and Bormann’s house, became a new base for the Reichssicherheitsdienst, the RSD, or Reich Security Service, while a vast kaserne - barracks - for SS troops was built across a meadow above the Berghof.  With all these incomers, huge coal stores were built, roads improved, while the Pension Moritz was improved and enlarged into the Platterhof and where the Führer’s guests could stay.  The Berghof, however, remained isolated on its perch, its fabulous views unimpeded.  By 1937, Obersalzberg had become Nazis-on-the-Hill.

It was in the summer of that year that Martin Bormann hatched a plan to create a mountain-top retreat: a stone villa, built high atop the Kehlstein, a 6,000-foot high knoll at the end of the even more towering Hoher Göll, and which could be used for parties, meetings and diplomatic gatherings.  After all, who would be able to doubt the mastery of the Reich when standing there, in this improbably built villa, with 360-degree views across the Alps?

No mountain-top construction is straightforward and although it was not built as a birthday present for the Führer, Hitler’s 50th in April 1939 was considered a worthy date by which to have the project completed.  First of all, however, men, machines and materials had to reach this improbable building site, so Bormann oversaw the construction of what was then the highest asphalted road in Europe.  It proved impossible to extend this to the very top of the Kehlstein so instead a 124 metre-long tunnel was blasted into the side of the mountain, into which a large saloon could be driven.  At the far end was a circular ante-chamber and then an ornate elevator was constructed that took guests the final stretch right into the heart of the house above.  Everything about it was designed to impress, right down to the elevator itself, which was mirrored with polished brass and had leather couches on which guests could perch.

The main building contained a large octaganol hall with a pink marble fireplace donated by Benito Mussolini, as well as dining room, anterooms and a glorious covered terrace overlooking the Königsee.  It had underfloor heating and all the mod cons available at the time.  It was, without question, stunning, and an extraordinary feat of both engineering and design.  Bormann loved it, so too did most of the leading Nazis and especially so too did Eva Braun, Hitler’s naïf and companion.  Hitler, though, who didn’t like heights, was less enamoured. He visited it when it was nearing completion in September 1938 and then again on 18 October, when he showed it to André Francois-Poncet, the departing French ambassador.  It was Francois-Poncet who referred to it first as the ‘Eagle’s Nest.’  It was more formally named the ‘Kehlsteinhaus.’ 

Hitler headed up there again on his fiftieth birthday, 20 April 1939, to officially inaugurate it, although whether he subsequently ever went up there again is not certain; if he did, it was only once or twice.  In addition to his fear of heights, he didn’t trust the gaudy elevator.  In all, it cost well on for £300 million in today’s money, all paid from Nazi Party funds. In the years that followed, it was used primarily as a place for Eva Braun and her younger friends to sunbathe and party.  Her sister, Gretl, was married to SS Gruppenführer Hermann Fegelein there.

Hitler continued to return to the Obsersalzburg as much as he could although much less so once the war began.  He did, however, spend a protracted period there in the first half of 1944, which prompted the British to plan a daring assassination attempt, Operation FOXLEY.  Intelligence reached them that Hitler would daily take a walk across the open meadows below the Berghof to another of his new edifices, a small folly known as the Teehaus on the edge of a jutting hill overlooking the valley below known as the Mooslanhnerkopf.  Hitler didn’t like his SS bodyguards being too close so it was thought that if a sniper could reach the edge of the woods next the meadow, the would-be assassin might easily get a clear shot.

Hitler, though, left the Obersalzberg on 14 July, before FOXLEY could be put into action.  Less than a week later came the infamous Stauffenberg assassination attempt at his Wolf’s Lair headquarters in East Prussia. Although vast tunnel and bunker complexes had been built underneath the Obersalzberg, Hitler remained at the Wolf’s Lair and then in Berlin until he decided to blow his brains out on the afternoon of 30 April 1945.

By that time, his beloved Berghof had been largely destroyed a few days earlier.  The RAF’s 617 ‘Dambuster’ Squadron had come over on 25 April, plastering the entire area.  The Berghof was struck twice, causing massive damage while retreating SS troops then razed the building when they left on 4 May.  Only a few hours later, advance troops led by Lieutenant Sherman W. Pratt of the 7th Infantry Regiment, part of the US 3rd Infantry Division, reached the Obersalzberg.  It was a stunning May afternoon when the lead jeeps drove past the abandoned checkpoint.  ‘We rounded a bend,’ noted Pratt, ‘and there before us in a broad opening lay the ruins of what had once been Hitler’s house and the SS barracks.’

Of the Nazis who had once populated this most lovely of spots, there was no sign.  Instead, French troops of Général Leclerc’s 2e Division Blindée as well as the US 101st Airborne were all converging on this incredibly symbolic corner of the Reich. French troops reached Berchtesgaden at around 8pm on 4 May, the 101st the following morning.  French and Americans alike then swarmed over the entire area, the Kehlsteinhaus included, trophy hunting. Mussolini’s marble fireplace still bears the etchings of graffiti from May 1945 and chips where troops used bayonets to hack off souvenir chunks.

The ruins of the Berghof, along with Bormann’s and Göring’s houses, the kaserne, Platterhof and other structures, including the Teehaus, were all blown up and destroyed in 1951 and 1952 by Bavarian authorities with the agreement of the Americans, who still maintained a military base in Berchtesgaden.  Some fifty buildings in all were largely eradicated, part of the plan to wipe the Nazis from the face of the earth.

One building that survived intact was the Scharitzkehlalm, which after the war was handed back to the original owners.  The requisition note, signed by Martin Bormann, remains framed on the wall. It’s possible to walk the same route as Hitler did daily and also drink hot chocolate and eat windbeutal - which is utterly delicious, by the way, but definitely needs the stout walk in the mountains to work it off again.  One can also still pour over the ruins of the Berghof, which was destroyed but not entirely eradicated. The retaining wall remains, one can still see bits of the terrace poking out through the roots of beech trees that have been planted since and scattered around still are remains of the vast camouflage netting that was placed over the house after Hitler left in July 1944.  The ruins of Bormann’s house can also be fairly easily picked over while on the site of Göring’s house there is now the amazingly luxurious Kempinski Hotel.  It’s quite the thing to sit out on their terrace, eating a sumptuous Alpine breakfast, knowing that Nazi monster had had a huge pad here, overlooking the Berghof.  Needless to say, there’s no mention of who lived there before anywhere to be found in the hotel.  Mostly likely, the thin, polar-neck jumpered staff have never even heard of him.

Other traces of the Nazis-on-the-Hill are not hard to find. There’s a giant unfinished tunnel emerging into the woods next to the meadow over which Hitler used to walk each afternoon.  That’s now a golf course, but the woods next to it - where the would-be assassins would have lurked - it still pitted with bomb craters, while the remains of Bormann’s perimeter wire can still be found.  The coal stores remain too, while down below on the edge of Berchtesgaden there is still the building that housed the Reich Chancellor when Hitler was in town.  Rather astonishingly, above the door is a huge Nazi eagle and circle of laurel; only the swastika has been chipped off.  Inside, there’s a large reception room with lampshades showing SS runes and a grand piano reputedly owned by Eva Braun. Underneath this large L-shaped building, are yet more tunnels and bunkers, leading eventually to an old railway siding into which would glide the Führer train. Frankly, it’s all rather jaw-dropping, largely because it’s so unexpected to find it still there.

And, of course, there was the Kehlsteinhaus, one of the premier tourist attractions of the area, if not all of Bavaria.  One can walk up a mountain trial, or take a special bus that leads up to the entrance of the tunnel.  Visitors then walk the 124 metres to the heart of the Kehlstein and the take the very same elevator Hitler mistrusted so much up into the Eagle’s Nest itself.  One can even reenact the photograph of Bormann and Goebbels on the southern terrace…

And now, after all this time, it’s gone.  I feel quite unsettled by this vandalism, I don’t mind admitting. When I’ve been there in the past, it is, of course, impossible to escape its origins but it is equally impossible not to marvel at the astonishingly beautiful views from up there. Pausing to consider the terrible and warped regime that gave this extraordinary building life is also no bad thing.  It’s important, in my view, to have reminders of despicable men and periods in history - after all, why else keep Auschwitz open?  To eradicate is to sweep them from mind and the danger is then that the lessons will be forgotten - not now, necessarily, but in future.  It was surely right to destroy the Reichs Chancellory in Berlin, to block up the bunkers where Hitler met his end, and right to blow up the Berghof.  But the Kehlstein, this astonishing folly to rival the maddest of follies, seemed to me to be justifiably retained: a beautiful spot but one that also symbolised the warped, cruel and utterly misguided fantasy world of Hitler and the Nazis.  It was all right to stand up there, eat a shit hotdog and slurp a Coke, and at the same time feel nothing but contempt for the deranged ideology and failure of Nazism.

A German friend tells them there a plans to restore it.  She pointed out that a decent proportion of the revenue it has raised over the years has been donated to charitable causes.  And she also pointed out that it is the wood, timbers and furniture laid there at the direction of the Nazis that have gone and that they will be replaced with now untarnished timbers.  It’s a good way to think about it. At any rate, the stone walls are still there and so is that terrace with its curved grantie wall…
