title: The Hanging
html:
A friend of mine recently urged me to read the essays of George Orwell, a collection from the great writer I’d not looked at before. ‘There’s one on a hanging,’ he said. ‘It’s incredibly powerful.’ The conversation had been prompted by Pete Hesgeth’s manic announcement to a journalist that he planned not only to execute the mass murderer, Nidal Hasan, by firing squad, but also to live stream the event.

This being 2026, I ordered it straight away and by the following day, the book was in my hands – a handsome Penguin Modern Classics paperback with a photograph of Orwell writing at a desk, somewhere hot and faintly exotic, cigarette stuck between his lips. ‘A Hanging’ is the third essay, written in 1931, four years after he had returned from Burma, where he’d been an Assistant District Superintendent in the Indian Imperial Police. Although Orwell – or rather, Eric Blair as he really was – had been born in India and had grown up immersed in colonial life, his time in Burma had prompted increasing disillusionment. His first novel, Burmese Days, published in 1943, paints a highly critical portrait of the British Raj. His essay, ‘The Hanging’ and ‘Shooting an Elephant’ reinforce this picture of class and racial prejudice and of men corrupted by local petit power and casual cruelty.

I can see why my friend found the essay so unforgettable. A prisoner is being pulled out of his cell at the local prison and taken to a tatty and rather overgrown yard to be hanged. The officials are impatient to get on with it so they can get on with the rest of the day and not least feeding breakfast to the other inmates. The condemned man is small, overly trussed and guarded by burly Indian warders equipped with rifles and glinting bayonets. Orwell is there as a witness – a grim aspect of his job as a colonial police officer. As they’re walking the forty yards or so to the gallows a stray dog suddenly appears, yapping and wagging its tail, delighted to see this entourage and jumping up happily at the prisoner. The dog is eventually led away and Orwell then notices the condemned man carefully step to one side of a puddle and is struck by how his mind was still alert even in his last minutes. ‘This man was not dying, he was alive just as we were alive,’ wrote Orwell. ‘All the organs of his body were working – bowels digesting food, skin renewing itself, nails growing, tissues forming – all toiling away in solemn foolery.’ Yet in a few minutes’ time, this would be over. ‘He and we were a party of men walking together,’ wrote Orwell, ‘seeing, hearing, feeling, understanding the same world; and in two minutes, with a sudden snap, one of us would be good – one mind less, one world less.’

The execution is quick and seemingly painless – the man dispatched with perfunctory efficiency although there was much discussion after that this is not always so. One time, Orwell is told, a doctor had to pull on the condemned man’s feet to finish him off. They all laugh at this then get on with the rest of their day. Christa Pike was far from the only botched execution in history.

It’s a haunting piece and reading it reminded me in turn of a letter that I came across a few years ago when I was researching the Italian campaign, and which I have since looked up again. I’ve got this letter on file, digitised, but it’s on slightly faded paper, typed and signed by General Sir Harold Alexander, and dates to 18 February 1944. It addresses the problems of desertion in his armies. ‘It is not, of course, a new problem,’ he wrote, ‘but periods of severe fighting, such as the present, bring it to the fore.’ Alexander was the Commander-in-Chief of 15th Army Group in Italy, comprising the British Eighth and US Fifth Armies. Italy was peculiar in that despite these nominally different national armies, there were more than twenty different countries represented in the troops fighting across both. No American commander in the Second World War commanded as many different international troops as General Mark W. Clark, the Fifth Army commander, for example.

And Alexander was writing to his immediate superior, General Hery Maitland-Wilson, the new Supreme Allied Commander in the Mediterranean, asking for his help. The Italian campaign was already playing very much second-fiddle to Allied plans for the cross-Channel invasion of Normandy, planned for June that year, but also, in the bigger picture, to shipping and supply demands in the Pacific. Even in Italy itself, priority for shipping lay with the development of the Fifteenth Air Force, now operating from southern Italy. It meant Alexander’s armies were badly under-supplied, which in turn led to his troops being expected to do more with less. Compounding this challenge was the weather, which was dreadful that winter, and the terrain, which was mountainous, riddled with rivers and meant a terrible burden on the infantry, especially. The Allied way of war was to use machines, firepower and air power as far as possible to do as much of the hard yards of fighting and so keep those in the firing line to a minimum. In Italy, though, those hard yards – slogging through mud and up mountains – fell on the shoulders of the PBI: the poor bloody infantry. No wonder desertions were massively on the rise.

As Alexander pointed out, the problem was that the normal sentences carried out by Courts Martial were rarely sufficiently severe. ‘A sentence of penal servitude is ineffective,’ he wrote, ‘because the man knows that it is likely to be suspended after he has served a short term, secondly because he counts on a general amnesty at the end of the war.’ Alexander was asking for a return to capital punishment. The news would be passed on to all ranks and would, he suggested, act as an effective deterrent. The current sentences issued for desertion were, he believed, unfair on commanding officers and company commanders, who shouldered a heavy enough strain without the additional uncertainty around the behaviour of some of their men. ‘It is unfair to the men who stay to fight,’ he added, ‘without the aid of their disloyal comrade.’

Alexander is one of my greatest heroes: a superb commander of truly vast experience, a brilliant artist, the speaker of seven languages and utterly charming, modest and instinctively kind, generous and blessed with a wonderful sense of humour. The subject of the letter troubled me because it seemed to sit so starkly at odds with the man I thought I knew. Alexander was suggesting that if brought back, the death penalty would rarely, if ever, be used, but as it happened, his request came to nothing. The matter had been swiftly referred back to General Sir Ronald Adam, with whom Alexander had served in France in 1940 and who was by then Adjutant-General. ‘One cannot see any prospect of this being re-introduced,’ he noted. ‘It should be noted, however, that the crime of self-inflicted wound is almost unknown now and would certainly reappear if the death penalty were re-introduced for desertion.’ Adam also questioned whether reintroducing capital punishment would be the deterrent Alexander believed it would prove.

Instead, it was made clear there would be no end-of-war amnesty and those deserting could also be re-posted to Burma and the Far East and would be the last to be demobilised once the war was finally over. And that was that. No-one in the British Army was going to be shot at dawn any more for running away.

In fact, capital punishment for desertion in the British Armed Forces ended on 19 April, 1930, after a campaign in Parliament by Ernest Thurtle MP, a former captain in the previous war and actually, the last person to be shot by firing squad was Private Ernest Jackson on 7 November, 1918, while the last British servicemen executed was Theodore Schurch in 1946, hanged for working for German and Italian itelligence after being captured at Tobruk.

The United States, on the other hand, did still have capital punishment for desertion throughout World War II, but only ever exercised it once, at the end of January 1945. Eddie Slovik had deserted before an attack had been due to be made by his division, the 28th Infantry, during the bitter and brutal fighting in the Hürtgen Forest, in October 1944. The attack was expected to be costly and so it proved and Slovik had fled when many equally terrified comrades had stuck it out and paid the ultimate price. He was caught, tried and sentenced and although he appealed for clemency, it came at a time when desertions were on the rise and it was felt an example needed to be made. Slovik was to be that example and was shot by firing squad at 10.04am on 31 January 1945. It was not, however, a public event, nor was that of the prisoner Orwell described in ‘The Hanging.’

Which leads me back to the current case of Nidal Hasan. I’ve always been against capital punishment. I just don’t believe anyone has the right to take the life of another. An eye for eye and tit-for-tat is not, in my experience, a healthy approach. Having a high moral bar is, however. I believe in basic Christian values and while we in the West are now increasingly secular – I’m not a church-goer - and our countries places of mixed religions, the Ten Commandants and the preaching of the New Testament seem to me to be a pretty good coda for living one’s life. Pete Hesgeth’s worryingly over-excited rant, sleeves rolled up, showing the ink on his arm, appeared less connected to the Christian values he repeatedly avows to believe it and more the words of a somewhat unhinged man harking back to the days of the medieval Inquisition. Power corrupts, as JRR Tolkein so brilliantly demonstrated. It is as though Hesgeth is now wearing the One Ring.

This is not to say that crimes should be left unpunished but there are two points here worth considering in the case of Nidal Hasan. The first is that there is a fate worse than death. It was why so many risked their lives resisting tyranny in the Second World War, for example. Jean Moulin knew that living in France under the oppression and cruelty of the Nazis was not a life worth living. He preferred to fight back, to put himself at immense risk, knowing he would almost certainly lose his life; rather that than exist in a world where his freedoms were curtailed. It’s also why so many in Ukraine are still fighting, as underdogs, against Russia. They voted to be apart from Russia and do not want to fall under its yoke, its oppression, its secret police and its fundamental cruelty any more. Ukrainian freedom is worth fighting for. It’s worth dying for.

Nidal Hasan is a different case. He murdered thirteen, injured thirty-two more and ruined the lives of many more besides by his cruel actions. But Hasan was a radicalised Muslim and was fully aware that his actions would lead to his own death. He wanted to become a martyr. For him, just as for Jean Moulin, there is a fate worse than death, but in his case it is to be utterly forgotten and to be left to rot in jail for the rest of his life. The whole point of his insane action was to have these murders broadcast around the world, to have millions discussing both them and him and radical Islam. His salvation, in his mind, would come from giving up his own life for God.

It’s why Hegseth’s announcement is so spectacularly ill-judged. There is no better way for to fulfil Hasan’s wishes than to broadcast his execution to the world. And let’s face it, if this gruesome spectacle really does go ahead, it will almost certainly be one of the most-watched moments in television history. And how does that make us feel? That nagging, awful realisation that there’s a cruel, wild core deep inside many of us that will be titillated by watching another man gunned down at the say-so of powerful men certainly sits ery badly with me, no matter his ghastly crimes.

Hegseth’s inadequacies – his intellectual shortcomings, his power-corrupted mind and his slavish determination to constantly win the approval of his master – have made him blind to the fundamental stupidity of his decision. Morally, it’s grotesque and abhorrent to publicly execute anyone, feeds only the hungry mob, and reflects terribly on both government and society. It’s why public executions stopped in Britain in 1868 and in the US in 1936. Only despotic regimes like Iran and Afghanistan and terrorist groups such as ISIS carry out public executions in today’s world. The idea that the USA will be joining these lunatics is an abomination.

Pragmatically, however, it makes no sense at all. Punishments should fit the crime. Let Hasan remain in prison, all his freedoms deprived, for the rest of his life. Never mention his name again. Consign him to obscurity. Hope he spends year after long year alone with the consequences of his terrible deeds.

Capital punishment is terrible and we in the West should not condone it. ‘When I saw the prisoner step aside to avoid the puddle,’ wrote Orwell in his essay, ‘I saw the mystery, the unspeakable wrongness of cutting a life short when it is in full tide.’ I urge everyone to read this stark but brilliant essay.
excerpt: Why Pete Hesgeth’s Decision Is So Very Flawed
author: James Holland

title: Are We the Bad Guys?
html:
In a brilliant sketch by David Mitchell and Robert Webb, the two comedians, dressed in SS uniforms, question why they’ve got skulls as part of their insignia. ‘Hans,’ asks Mitchell’s character, ‘are we the bad guys?’ Perhaps those soon to be wearing the new US Space Force uniforms will be asking themselves the same question.  In an AI-generated picture, revealed to the world last week, a square-jawed figure stands upright and erect, legs slightly apart, hands behind his back, chin jutting.  He’s the epitome of old-fashioned Caucasian - Aryan? - manhood.  His uniform, meanwhile, reveals a crisp and decidedly 19th-century military tunic, leather belt and silver buckle around his waist, with a stiff, high, collar with military tabs, wings on his chest, tight trousers and rounded off with shiny leather boots extending up just below the knee.

This proposed uniform for US Space Force, the newest wing of the United States’ military and which the President created back in 2019, during his first term, would be considered an April Fool’s trick were it not September and were these images not released at the behest of Trump.  To say this is a ludicrous design is a massive understatement.  He’s claiming it was inspired by the movie, Starship Troopers, which in itself is risible - after all, what serious politician would want their armed forces to be inspired by a lightweight science-fiction movie?  For everyone else, however, this new look is less Starship Troopers and more as though it was lifted straight from the militia of a Bond villain - an image that was, of course, quite deliberately inspired by Nazi uniforms.  It’s even a kind of field grey, for goodness sake.

The uniforms of the Nazis have become so iconic it’s easy just to accept them at face value with their grey and black and plenty of leather.  In fact, they were, for the most part, immensely impractical, pointlessly expensive and over-designed and not really fit for the task allotted them.  Few have bothered to question such a unique look, though, because the uniforms of the Nazi regime just look how they look: distinctive, striking and, of course, sinister or fabulous, depending on your leaning.

During the Blitzkrieg years of German victories, Hitler’s armies gained a reputation for tactical and operational brilliance, augmented by superb training and the best, most modern weaponry.  There were, however, a number of curious paradoxes to the German Army. It may have had innovative sub-machine guns and other finely engineered weaponry, for example, but despite the impression of vast military might, there was also something rather old school about the German Army in other areas. Certain forward-thinking officers, such as General Heinz Guderian, may have spent time writing treatises on the future of armoured warfare, but for the most part the Army was still dominated by a traditional Prussian military aristocracy that cited an inheritance which stretched back to Frederick the Great and the Seven Years’ War in the middle of the eighteenth century. Men like von Clausewitz, von Moltke, von Schlieffen, von Hindenburg, von Ludendorff were all household names in Germany – and at the start of the war, the Army was commanded by yet another Prussian aristo, Field Marshal Walter von Brauchitsch. Even in Nazi Germany, it was hard to climb to the top of the pole without a ‘von’ before your name.

It still had a rather nineteenth-century look to it too. The Pickelhaube, the old pointed helmet, had gone, but the large amounts of leather, the high jackboots, the baggy-thigh breeches and the traditional high-collared tunics all harked back to an earlier era when looking the part – looking militaristic – was very much the brief. They looked smart, they looked efficient. They looked like they meant business, which was precisely the effect they were supposed to achieve. This more traditional military look was eagerly adopted by the Nazis, not least because a powerful military tradition was what set the German character apart; Germany had been forged in 1871 with the Prussian states at its heart, and they, during the 1860s, had drawn upon militarism as being at the very core of their existence.

There is no question that the German nation which emerged from the collection of kingdoms, duchies and principalities less than seventy years earlier was a militaristic society, but the idea that the Prussian – and later German – military was manifestly superior to any other in the world was a dubious claim. Prussia – the largest German kingdom prior to unification – had fought only a handful of small wars in the century that separated the end of the Napoleonic Wars and the conflict in 1914. When it had gone to war alongside Austria against Denmark in 1864, it had barely fought since Waterloo fifty years earlier and most certainly did not out-perform Austria militarily. Two years later, Prussia was at war with its former ally, but Austrian mistakes were every bit as important to Prussia’s subsequent victory as any military genius. Four years after that Prussia was at war again, this time against the mighty France, and it was on this stunning success that much of its military swagger, which would be sustained and would grow further within the newly formed Germany, was based.

Interestingly, however, all three wars, and indeed German unification in 1871, were orchestrated not by a military leader but by a political one, namely Otto von Bismarck. Following unification, the military was elevated in society, with veterans venerated and uniforms and military bearing considered the aspiration of every self-respecting young German male. No one was more fond of standing ramrod straight and wearing military garb than the Kaiser, Wilhelm II, who was always to be seen in a variety of uniforms, shiny breastplates and Pickelhaube, but had never actually seen any combat himself or, frankly, been much of a soldier. Also woven into the military heritage was von Clausewitz’s widely read and acclaimed work On War, but this was based on analysis of Napoleon, who was French, and was, in any case, interpreted to suit Nazi ideology. The other iconic figure was the Prussian king, Frederick the Great, who belonged to the eighteenth century, and who, despite continued veneration by a stream of Germans from Admiral Tirpitz through to Hitler, had won just eight of his sixteen battles and even one of those, the Battle of Zorndorf in 1758, might more accurately be considered a stalemate.

None the less, von Clausewitz’s military theories and Frederick’s victories certainly added to the belief in Germany’s military inheritance. Somehow, the Prussians, and then Germany, had created not only a militaristic society in which soldiers were greatly venerated, but also a reputation for military brilliance, which was based on not a huge amount if they were really honest. At the turn of the twentieth century, when Britain had threatened Imperial Germany with economic blockade and the destruction of its Navy if it became involved in the Boer War, the Kaiser backed down and kept out of it. This humiliation – and his obsession with ships – contributed to the vast building programme of capital vessels, and resulted in a giant fleet that ventured out once, at Jutland in 1916, then retreated, and was scuttled at the end of the war. Germany’s great military tradition was thus based on a somewhat spurious reputation and had, in any case, taken a massive blow with the catastrophic defeat of 1918.

The Nazis were emerging at a time when morale within Germany was low, but they cleverly appealed to this suspect military tradition and to German pride in that sense of martial inheritance. By strutting around with straight backs and chests out, wearing snappy brown or black uniforms, and with starkly striking insignia that harked back to ancient Aryan runes, the Nazis were inviting people to come and join an exciting new club. The message was simple: be a National Socialist, and wear a smart-looking uniform and be reinvigorated with a renewed sense of national pride, identity and purpose. Look good, be part of our gang, and you will be more attractive to a young, blonde and beautiful fraulein.

It was hardly an original ruse, but the cut and design of the uniforms were very deliberately intended to look both smart and debonair while also nodding to the military past.  There was even an imperial eagle only in the Nazi world, the head was facing the other way and was underscored by a swastika. Nazi uniforms were as beautifully tailored as an MG34 machine-gun was engineered, and when it came to dressing the rapidly growing Army, these principles were rigorously maintained. The field tunics of the ordinary German soldier were not quite so sartorially elegant as the SS outfits, but they were smart enough and certainly supremely well made. A private was not paid much, but he was given very decent kit. The jacket, the Feldbluse, was lined in soft cotton or rayon, was thigh length with two generously large and pleated pockets on the chest and two on the waist; it was also pleated at the back, while the cuffs had buttons that could be undone and the waist four lots of eyelets through which metal belt clips could be threaded. The buttons were all aluminium, rounded at the edges for easy use and with a dotted pattern, and quite deliberately designed as opposed to simply mass-stamped. The collar of the Feldbluse was well stitched and around the inside was another row of buttons on to which a smart and comfortable collar liner could be attached. It was warm,comfortable and produced with the kind of attention to detail that would make a bespoke tailor smile with pleasure.

In 1939, each soldier was given no fewer than seven uniforms: field, service, watch, parade, report, walking out and sport. The numbers of cloth suppliers and tailors involved with making all these uniforms was immense, but like most German war production there was no adherence to the principles of mass production. Among these firms was the company, Hugo Boss, but at this stage it was a manufacturer, not a designer; despite the urban myth, Hugo Boss did not design any Nazi uniform, SS or otherwise.  Rather, it was just one of hundreds churning out this huge raft of military garb.  There were, for example, no fewer than 323 different companies producing just one particular type of military linen. This was a trend repeated across the board. Most of the soldier’s webbing was made of black leather: the ammunition pouches, holsters, belts, straps and even the case that held the stout short-handle entrenching tool. Boots came up almost to the knee rather than the ankle. Field packs, although made of canvas, came with leather straps and a fur-covered outer flap. One particularly well-engineered piece of personal kit was the gas mask case, a steel cylinder with grooves down the side to give it added strength. It was quite large and even bulky, but the attention to detail on it was impressive, with a spring metal catch and inside, within the lid, a further little compartment in which spare lenses for the mask were stored and held in place by a delicate spring-loaded catch. The intricacy with which these millions of tins were manufactured – each some 25 centimetres tall – was impressive; and they even came with a leather carrying strap. It became an instantly iconic piece of the soldier’s equipment.

Young officers had even more elaborate uniforms. Their field dress was made of the same wool as those of their men, but their service dress was gabardine with silk or rayon lining and with a cuff that doubled back almost halfway to their elbows, which was almost eighteenth century in its design. Officers were given wool greatcoats or full-length leather versions. There were different uniforms for mountain troops, different uniforms for paratroopers, yet more uniforms for the panzer arm, and even more for the Luftwaffe. Pilots like Hajo Herrmann could choose from a staggering array of breeches, woollen trousers, leather trousers, cotton, wool and leather jackets of differing shades of brown and black, some fur lined, others not.

This attention to detail and to producing a sartorially unbeatable armed services was all well and good and had certainly, in the early years of the Nazis at any rate, served a valid purpose. Unlike Britain, however, Germany had few sheep farms and no Dominions on the far side of the world from where it could easily purchase what it lacked at home. In fact, Germany had very few natural resources of its own at all – no oil, very little iron ore, no tungsten, no bauxite, no copper; a coal industry was about all it did have and even that was as nothing compared with Britain’s, for example. And because so much of the economy was now devoted to war production, Germany had little to export in return. It also had very few sheep - just 4.5 million compared with 24.5 million pigs. Curiously, Britain had just 4.5 million pigs, but 24.5 million sheep as well as access to the wool of its dominions, New Zealand and Australia, useful assets when dramatically increasing the number of military uniforms.  Yet rather than watching the pfennigs in areas where costs could easily have been kept down, there was, in 1939, no armed forces that was more expensively turned out than that of The Wehrmacht. The cost of German uniforms, however, was, from the Nazi perspective, a small price to pay to make soldiers believe they were part of a modern and technologically advanced militaristic society.

They were also an acceptable cost providing the Nazis won the war in quick order.  The problems started to arise once the war continued, year after shattering year and the German economy, and with it precious resources, became increasingly stretched.  A new feld blouse was introduced in 1943 but the concessions to economy was the straightening of the pocket flaps and taking out the pleats; otherwise, it was the same.  So, no real economising whatsoever.  The fancy buttons largely remained to the end of the war, as did the totally pointless gas-mask case. What was wrong with a canvas bag in times of hardship?  Admittedly, canvas did gradually start to be introduced but never entirely kicked the German love of leather into the long grass. Canvas, though, is far cheaper, doesn’t rot so easily if it becomes wet and is in every way more practical. The Nazis never really accepted this, despite later introducing a shorter jacket and ankle boots.  Right to the end, the look outweighed pragmatics.

The British and Americans, by contrast, did take a far more pragmatic approach to uniforms, a reflection that they had become warfare states but not militaristic ones.  In fact, the British Army had the most modern uniforms - and practical - uniforms in the world by the start of the Second World War. Hand-in-hand with rearmament in the second half of the thirties had come the recognition that attitudes had to change, that a modern war required modern equipment, and that Britain needed to use its global reach to full effect. Ironically, the impression from German propaganda of a Reich that was creating a modern, mechanized military Moloch had done much to kick-start this new outlook.

With the scent of war in the air, Britain had, in 1938, designed the Battledress, a highly innovative concept and the most modern and practical combat uniform adopted by any European power. Made of hard-wearing khaki wool serge, it consisted of a short jacket that came down to its wearer’s midriff. This was very sensible given the high-waisted trousers of the day; the battle blouse, as the jacket was called, therefore only covered the waistband of the trousers, and in so doing saved a significant amount of fabric on earlier designs and on those worn by almost every other army the world over.  The German feldbluse, for example, came halfway down the thigh with an extra length of at least eighteen inches on the battle blouse - eighteen inches that the British quite sensibly decided was a total waste of wool. The battle blouse was generously cut under the arms, allowing easy movement, and considerable thought had been given to the pockets – two large ones on the inside of the jacket, two large breast pockets, side pockets on the trousers and a further generous pocket on the thigh, big enough for a map or documents. The old knee-high puttees had also gone, relics of a former era, replaced by durable canvas ankle gaiters. This new soldier’s uniform had no frills, wasted no material, and was exceptionally cheap and easy to mass-produce, while at the same time allowing its wearer easy manoeuvrability and warmth.

The US Army took a similar approach.  Ever since the First Wolrd War, the US Army had equipped its men with the standard round-rimmed Tommy helmet, as used by the British. A completely new design came into service in 1941, however, known as the M1. This fitted comfortably over the head and covered much of the back of the neck and ears, but its liner was both more comfortable than the old helmet and a closer fit. It was ‘cleared for procurement’ on 7 May 1941 and it was recommended that ‘the item be given priority as essential.’ It would take time for the changeover to be completed, but in keeping with the rapid rearmament programmes now under way, a variety of civilian firms were involved in its manufacture, including, for example, the McCord Radiator Company of Detroit, who within a year would be producing no fewer than 400,000 M1 helmets per month.

New uniforms were entering service as well. The US Army had issued its men with a wool ‘OD’ – olive drab – service coat, which was similar to the field tunics worn by many nationalities; it was, in essence, a tunic with big pockets and brass buttons that came halfway down the thigh. By early 1940, however, General George C. Marshall, the Army Chief of Staff, felt it was time for a new look – one that reflected the largely civilian and modern army he hoped it would become, and one that provided both comfort and easy movement. A number of civilian windbreakers were examined, but none quite hit the mark, so Major-General J. K. Parsons, commanding the 5th Division, was given the task of overseeing the design, trials and eventual procurement of a new field jacket. ‘In deciding upon the garment to be recommended,’ he wrote to the Adjutant-General, ‘the needs of the Infantry soldier were given primary consideration.  It was therefore decided that a suitable jacket to meet his needs must not only be warm and comfortable, but must be light in weight and have the minimum in bulkiness. This was much the same brief given the designers of the British Battledress, but in its consideration of comfort for the ordinary soldier, quite radical.

A design was drawn up and produced. Although it was olive drab in colour, it did look very like a civilian windcheater, with a centre zip-and-button combination, generous under the arms and coming down to just below the waist. General Parsons tested the jacket extensively using 400 of his men as guinea pigs. Any adjustments – such as taking the flaps off the side pockets – were due to the advice of the majority of these soldiers. The Quartermaster General’s office still sent the design to Esquire magazine, who advised further on cloth and, inevitably, the look of the thing, which prompted a rather terse reply from General Parsons. ‘Esquire may be an authority on what a well dressed gentleman should wear,’ he wrote, ‘but a study of its comments and the design of the garment it submitted as a substitute shows plainly that it does not understand the purpose of the garment and is ignorant of the needs of the soldier in the field.’ Someone else from behind a desk then suggested it was too short and in cold weather might cause kidney trouble. ‘All I can say,’ replied Parsons, ‘is most men have kidney trouble when in the presence of the enemy and it is fear not the length of the garment that causes it.’ The new M1941 field jacket, known, perhaps justifiably, as the ‘Parsons Jacket’, was duly adopted. Made of water-resistant cotton and lined with warm but lightweight wool, there was no other military jacket in the world that looked so casual or modern, nor one that had been designed and adopted with such thorough testing by those who would subsequently be wearing it in combat. As the US Army prepared for war, it was demonstrating a highly pragmatic but forward-thinking outlook – and, crucially, one that was not constrained by its military past.

So, what are the lessons here?  Well, it’s fair to say that the uniforms of the different combatant nations in World War II very much reflected the culture and society of those nations they were designed to clothe: militaristic, self-conscious and with a nod to the past in the case of Nazi Germany, but pragmatic and reflecting the emerging civilian conscript armies as far as the United States and Britain were concerned.  I’ll let people draw their own conclusions about Trump’s planned new Space Force designs…

title: Pressure: The Truth About the D-Day Weather
html:
It’s 4.15am, Monday, 5th June, 1944, and having had his latest meeting with the respective British and American weather teams, Group Captain James Stagg is back to face the Supreme Commander and the Commanders-in-Chief.  Once again they are in the library of Southwick House, just a few miles north of Portsmouth on the south coast of England.  It’s a room full of largely forlorn and empty bookshelves, but now the requisitioned mansion’s Mess Room.  General Sir Bernard Montgomery, commanding all the Allied land forces for D-Day, is here, looking spry in corduroy trousers and high-neck grey pullover.  They all sit informally on armchairs as Stagg begins his forecast.  If anything, he tells them, there are grounds for greater optimism. Once again, the detailed grilling followed, then he is dismissed.

Back inside the library, it is now decision time. The forecast Stagg has given gives some cause for hope but there’s no getting away from it: the weather has turned, they’ve been dealt a lousy hand and no matter the talk of windows of high pressure, the next thirty-six hours are going to offer only awful conditions in which to launch the largest amphibious operation in the history of the world.  The stakes are simply immense. Monty, General Walter Bedell-Smith and Admrial Sir Bertram Ramsay are for going.  So too is Air Chief Marshal Sir Arthur Tedder, the Deputy Supreme Allied Command.  Air Chief Marshal Sir Trafford Leigh-Mallory – brother of George Mallory of Everest fame and commanding Allied air forces - has major doubts.  Ultimately, though, the decision rested with the Supreme Allied Commander, General Dwight D. Eisenhower. It’s his job, and his alone.

The burden is his.

There’s a new film out about this critical moment in history. Pressure, it’s brilliantly simple but appropriate title, was originally written for the stage by the actor, David Haig, but now is in cinemas with immense fanfare and starring a shaven-headed Brendan Fraser as Eisenhower. Andrew Scott as Stagg and Damian Lewis as Montgomery.  There are sound reasons for keeping a cast tight on the stage, but less so in a movie, so it’s disappointing that there’s no Tedder, for example, responsible for one of the sharpest comments of all in the weather discussions that preceded D-Day.  Nor is there any sign of Bedell-Smith, who was far more of an advisor and influence to Eisenhower than Kay Summersby.  But I get it – this is a movie.  It might based on real events, but this is a drama.  It’s fiction.

So, what was the reality?  Well, weather forecasting in the summer of 1944 was a very imprecise science.  There were no satellites, so crucial to modern forecasting. Weather stations were dotted all over the United Kingdom and there were even such stations on the west coast of Ireland that could be drawn upon by the Allied meteorologists despite Ireland’s neutrality.  Beyond the British Isles, though, the density of sources diminished woefully: a few weather ships and that was it, which was a big problem because the prevailing weather patterns came from across the Atlantc – in other words, where weather stations were their patchiest.  Admittedly, each one was equipped with barometers, anemometers, wind vanes, temperature sensors and thermometers and the meteorologists aboard were read cloud heights, bases, sea swell as well as wind speeds, but the Atlantic was a big place, the variables were massive and ultimately, predicting weather became increasingly hard with every passing day.

There were also different schools of thought about how best to forecast.  One of the senior American weatherman was Dr Irving Krick, attached to US Strategic Air Forces, who was a fervent believer in using historic patterns and weather cycles to supplement what could be learned from weather stations.  This was known as analogue forecasting.  Krick does play a big part in the film and in real life, was considered something of smug self-promoter within American meteorological circles. On the other hand, he had the backing of General Hap Arnold, the commander of the US Army Air Forces and now led the US team based at Widewings, the American Weather HQ.  The British Air Ministry meteorological team, on the other hand, were led by Dr Sverre Petterssen, a Norwegian, and Charles Douglas, who took a more strictly scientific approach.  There was also the Admiralty’s weather team offering forecasts as well and their collected predictions were forwarded to Group Captain James Stagg, a geophysicist by trade, but now Chief Meteorologist to Eisenhower, and Colonel Donald Yates, who was Stagg’s deputy.  It was Stagg, a thin-faced thirty-nine year-old Scot, who had the unenviable task of drawing the various weather forecasts together and drawing some kind of conclusion.

The trouble began brewing on a glorious sunny Thursday, 1 June, when at an evening weather conference the Air Ministry team of Petterssen and Douglas painted a gloomy outlook for D-Day, which had been set as Monday 5 June.  Krick and the Widewings team, in contrast, were far more optimistic.   By the following day, the Air Ministry were even more pessimistic, and Stagg felt compelled to relay this to Eisenhower and his commanders.  By the evening Petterssen was predicting ten-tenths cloud and a risk of a Force 5 gale on the Monday.  This was really not good.  Not good at all.

Reports from the weather stations were arriving every few hours and the charts updated by hand.  By the evening of Saturday 3 June, even Krick and the team at Widewings were agreeing with Petterssen’s view, as were the Admiralty’s weather men.  For Stagg, it was time to confront the commanders of the invasion once more, which he did in the library at Southwick House at 9.30pm.

‘Gentlemen,’ said Stagg, ‘the fears which I hoped you realised we had yesterday, Friday morning…are confirmed.’ A low front was sweeping in bringing low cloud, gales and rain.  ‘Those details apply for Sunday to Tuesday and at first on Wednesday.’

Questions were asked: Leigh-Mallory wanted to know what cloud cover they could expect over the French coast.  Ten-tenths, he was told.  Admiral Ramsay wanted to know whether the Force 5 winds were likely to last on Monday and Tuesday.  Yes.  And Wednesday?  Not settling immediately but getting brighter.  For a moment no-one spoke.  A gloom had descended over the room.  As Stagg and Yates left, he heard Eisenhower say to the others, ‘Are we prepared to take a gamble on this?’ Their discussions continued until around 11pm, when Stagg was told to return for another briefing at 4.15am the next morning, Sunday, 4 June.

‘Pleasant dreams, Stagg,’ said Tedder as he passed him.

The hours passed quickly, with no dream-time for Stagg or any of the weather teams.  Krick and the Widewings team now felt certain a ridge of high pressure from the Azores would keep the worst of the cloud away from the Normandy coast.  Petterssen strongly disagreed.   On the other hand, following a cold front - such as the one due to be passing through - would come a few hours of lighter winds and clearer weather regardless of how the Azores high behaved.  If the front passed across the Cotentin peninsular around midnight then, in theory, there would be an opportunity for the US airborne drop to still go ahead almost on schedule and for the British one a few hours later.  The bombers would most likely have the visibility they needed.

Stagg, though, felt he should side with Petterssen, who felt there would still be too much cloud cover to make the airborne drops and bombing feasible; instinctively, Stagg trusted Petterssen more than Krick, even if, deep down – if he was honest - it was for cultural reasons rather than anything else.  It has to be stressed there were huge reasons for sticking with 5 June and heeding Krick’s advice: the invasion force was already at sea and ready. Even a brief delay would be enormously problematic, both from the security and for the morale of the men now at sea.  At any rate, back in the library he advised the assembled commanders there was no real change; the forecast still looked bad.

Once again, Stagg was thanked and asked to leave while the commanders discussed the matter.   Monty was for pressing on regardless, but Tedder disagreed and opted for postponement.  Ike had always been worried that they would be attacking initially on D-Day with a force of significantly smaller numbers than that available to the enemy and pointed out they had always felt such an operation was possible only because of air power.  If they were unable to bring that to bear, however, then he too felt they should postpone.  ‘Are there any dissenting voices?’ he asked. There were none.  Forces S and J were already on their way and now had to be recalled.  Really, it was a terrible decision to have to make: the entire amphibious invasion force was already loaded onto their ships, where they would have to stay, cramped, uncomfortable, with morale and spirits draining with every passing hour. And what if the weather didn’t improve?  What then?

Outside, Stagg looked up at the still, almost cloudless sky and felt the enormity of the decision resting on their shoulders.  He headed back to the SHAEF command post and to his tent to try and get some rest.  Eisenhower also headed to his caravan, where he was surrounded by Westerns, newspapers and a plentiful supply of cigarettes.  He’d begun chain smoking these past few days.

4.30pm, Southwick House, Sunday, 4 June.  Stagg called a conference with all his weather teams.  All agreed there was a small ridge of high pressure that looked like it might follow in behind the current low, which, if it remained on track should last until Tuesday morning, 6 June.  The weather from Wednesday to Friday still looked unsettled.  It was, however, quite a big ‘if.’  This small ridge of high pressure was being reported from the very few weather ships out the Atlantic; there was a pattern, definitely, but whether it would stay on course and develop into the clearer skies they hoped for really was far from certain.

I discussed this in great detail with Dr Simon Keeling, a leading meteorologist in the UK and someone who specialises in aviation forecasting.  We looked at the original D-Day maps, available for anyone to look at in the Met Office archives in Exeter.  Simon pointed out to me that the weather briefing had been incorrect for the Dams Raid, for example, in May 1943, which had led to some of the Lancasters veering off course and paying the price as a result.  But he also talked me through the weather forecasting for D-Day. He was at pains to point out that the predicted ridge of high pressure forecast to sweep in during the early hours and morning of 6 June 1944, was based on very little indeed.  ‘They were lucky,’ he told me.  ‘It’s there all right, but it’s small and could easily have been swept off into the North Sea and missed the Channel and Normandy coast altogether.’

So, the danger at this time – the early hours of 4 June 1944 - was that in clutching at this potential lifeline they were now resting upon it too much hope and dismissing the risk that such a ridge could easily be pinched, squeezed out, pushed off course.  Then there wouldn't be any high coming in at all.  The low cloud would continue along with the wind and rain. What Krick was recommending was sticking with 5 June and was fairly confident fine weather would follow in the early hours of the morning, albeit for a limited time. Even Stagg agreed. ‘The fair interval from early hours Monday to Tuesday is confirmed,’ noted Stagg in his diary after the next meeting with his teams at 7.30pm that night.’  On the other hand, the small high forecast for the morning of Tuesday, 6 June, was still off the west coast of Ireland with only limited weather stations tracking its progress. During the early hours of Sunday, 4th June, there remained a distinct possibility this small ridge of high pressure could still be pushed north over central England rather than over the Channel. The die, though, had been cast.  The 24-hour postponement had already been made.

At 9pm, Stagg once more spoke to the assembled D-Day commanders and reported the improved picture.  After being thoroughly grilled he left them to their discussions.  Monty was emphatically for going.  So too was Bedell-Smith.  ‘It’s a helluva gamble,’ said Ike’s Chief of Staff, ‘but it’s the best possible gamble.’

‘The question,’ said Eisenhowwer, ‘is just how long can you hang this operation on the end of a limb and let it hang there?’  Because of tides and moons, the next opportunity would be 19th  June.  That was two weeks.  A fortnight in which the Germans further strengthened their defences, and two weeks in which there was a huge dip in morale of the invasion force, and potential security leaks.  It was unthinkable.  They had to go.

Around twenty minutes later, Eisenhower emerged from the library.

‘Stagg, we’ve put it on again,’ he told him.  ‘For heaven’s sake hold the weather to what you have forecast for us.  Don’t you bring any more bad news.’ He smiled then stepped back inside.  Shortly after that, it was agreed they would reconvene once again at 4.15am, Monday, 5th June, for the final irreversible decision.

Stagg returned to his tent around 10.30pm and tried to get some rest but sleep eluded him.  Outside, the rain was slashing down against the canvas, the wind testing the guy ropes to the full.  ‘Lay and thought of what it all meant,’ he noted, ‘and hoped and hoped that our story would come through.’  His choice of words could not have been more apt.

At 3am, he us up again and meeting his weather teams.  By this time the front had already passed through – the skies were largely clear and the winds had dropped; if it was clear in Portsmouth, it was clear in the Cotentin Peninsular too and probably rapidly clearing across the rest of Normandy as well, so had they stuck to the original D-Day, it would hardly have been the disaster that had been feared: the air forces would have had clear views, the weather on the coast would have been better for the actual landings themselves, and only the British airborne drop would have had to have been postponed by a couple of hours; that would not have been a good, and who knows, might have altered the chances of successfully taking Pegasus and Horsa bridges intact and of blowing the bridges further east across the Dives. Alternatively, it might have made the task easier thanks to lesser winds and so resulting in a tighter drop.

Who knows? It’s fascinating to consider and had they gone on 5th June, Krick might have been the hero and Stagg now largely forgotten.  No matter: the decision had already been made.  It was too late to have any feelings of regret over the 24-hour postponement. The decision had been made.  How the weather was going to behave the following night was what now mattered.

And so, just after 4.15am Stagg, along with Eisenhower, his Chief of Staff, his Deputy Supreme Commander and his service chiefs were all assembled in the library. All eyes were on Eisenhower, waiting for his decision.

The Supreme Commander sat in his chair, rubbed his face in his hands, then looked up.  ‘OK,’ he said, ‘Let’s go.’

title: Resilience
html:
‘The metal trade,’ wrote Oliver Lyttelton just after the Second World War, ‘is truly international, for no country is self-supporting in all the non-ferrous metals. Thus the United States have no tin, the United Kingdom – if classified apart from the Commonwealth – has no significant resources of any of them. All the great industrial countries have to import some of their needs from their colonies or from overseas. Metals must be exchanged across all the international frontiers.’

Lyttelton – who by that time had become Lord Chandos – was a fascinating fellow. Having survived four years of the First World War fighting with the Grenadier Guards and winning a Distinguished Service Order and Military Cross in the process, he had made it home and gone on to forge a highly successful business career. By 1939, he was chairman of the British Metal Corporation, who were, in essence, metal merchants, and under his leadership had become the biggest metal company in the UK. They had further consolidated their position by striking a number of affiliations with Continental partners, which had enabled Lyttelton to become a director of the German metals firms Metallgesellschaft and Norddeutsche Raffinerie, a position he held even during the Nazis’ time in power. This had given him an invaluable picture of the German metal trade and the importance of non-ferrous metals in any future war. He had learned, for example, that back in 1914, just a few months into the war, the directors of Metallgesellschaft had been approached by the German General Staff because they were already running out of copper and needed help in finding more. Copper, tin, lead and zinc were all needed – copper and zinc especially – in times of war.

Subscribe

The British, with their global fleets and world trade, had always been wedded to the idea that war was really a battle of supplies, and frankly, they weren’t wrong. All manner of raw materials were needed to fight a war, and not one country in the world had an abundance of all, not even America and the USSR, despite their vast size and geographical range. Among those raw materials were metals, and in Britain few people understood the myriad and truly international world of metals better than Oliver Lyttelton.

It was with this in mind that in the spring of 1939 Lyttelton had begun a plan to buy up as much of these all-important metals as possible. As he was well aware, many of the leading mining companies around the world would be worrying about the uncertainty war might bring – would they still be able to ship their metals? Would existing buyers continue to purchase them? He had already been approached by the Ministry of Supply to become the Controller of Non-Ferrous Metals should it come to war, and so back in March, with the Germans walking into Czechoslovakia, he had approached Noranda in Canada, Broken Hill in Australia and others, and begun negotiating. What he was proposing was assured purchases, no matter whether they had the shipping or not, in return for guaranteed quantities at a low price.

Much to his immense frustration, he was unable to galvanize the Ministry of Supply into buying these metals right away, even though he knew Germany had been stockpiling copper, so although Lyttelton had personally secured small stocks of nickel, it was not until the outbreak of war that he was finally made Controller of Non-Ferrous Metals and given carte blanche to start purchasing. He hoped it would not already be too late. Lyttelton, like most others in Britain, was expecting a German offensive almost immediately in September 1939, but was hoping the enemy would delay any action for as long as possible.

In the autumn of 1939, Lyttelton was forty-six and the epitome of the debonair and cultivated Englishman, with his lean features, slicked-back hair and trim moustache. From an aristocratic background, he had been educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, and had an exemplary war record. Indeed, the war had taught him much: the extremes under which the human body and mind can be placed, the awfulness of the slaughter, the importance of never, ever, giving in. He had been temporarily blinded by gas, had been nearly broken, but somehow had kept going so that when peace finally came he was among an elite of his generation who had fought for almost the entire war and was still standing. During the war, he had also got to know and befriended a number of key people, from Winston Churchill and Anthony Eden to soldiers now generals in the Army. In the intervening years, he had travelled widely, learned everything he could about both modern business and the world of metals, and developed an outstanding and international web of contacts, as well as finding time to get married and raise a family. Intelligent, worldly and imbued with a razor-sharp business acumen, he was one of the key civilians from the business world from which Britain would greatly benefit now that war had come.

Oliver Lyttelton was, in fact, a man who understood about resilience: human resilience and national resilience in terms of natural resources.

He would make a useful role model for people in the UK today, because right now, we’re lacking both types of resilience in this country and that’s a problem. Diane Abbott can claim all she likes that Russia doesn’t pose a threat, but how does she know? Has she got some insight into Putin’s mind that no-one else has accessed? She was, of course, entirely wrong when she predicted that Putin wouldn’t invade Ukraine. Putin’s actions - the corruption, the cruelty, the murders, the malevolence, and, of course, the ongoing war with Ukraine, tell me he is not to be trusted and that Britain is a country upon which he would wish harm. The same is true of the Iranian regime, that of North Korea and plenty of other dark forces around the world besides. There are plenty who argue we’re already at war – those daily cyber attacks, the disinformation, the terrorist cells. At the very least, we should all have ours open to what is happening now and how this might dramatically escalate in the future.

And, in any case, why risk it? Wouldn’t it be better for the nation to become more, not less, resilient? And better able to deal with the threats that we now face, whether from malevolent actors on the global stage or so we’re ready when global environmental crises truly come home to roost: global warming, the breakdown of international supply chains, population rises and migration all threaten the supply of food, water, and energy.

Long years of peace and prosperity have made us a little soft. We like our creature comforts - that new car every three years, foreign holidays, cheap food, disposable income for the latest fashions, expensive live events, the morning blueberry açai matcha that costs a fiver, streaming subscriptions so we can watch one twelve-hour TV series commitment after another, and so on. Yes, there are a staggering 14.2 million people below the poverty line in the UK, but a visit to central London or any other major city will show you there are plenty of people gulping down £7.50 pints, eating in restaurants and going to shows. Or try an airport in August. It’s not only the well-to-do indulging. The truth is, we spend roughly the same amount on new cars each year as the government’s defence budget and almost double that on holidays. That’s about £150 billion. So, we’re not that broke in this country.

Let’s take individual resilience first - or moral resilience as it’s more formally termed. Perhaps we all just need to become a little bit hardier. Less dependent on the hand-holding of the state. The trouble is that the threat of litigation at every turn has badly blunted swift progress and limits freedom of action and decision making. On the Underground in London we’re always being told to ‘hold onto the hand rail.’ This riles me because I think, I’m a grown-up, I’ll be the judge of whether I need to hold onto to something while either standing stationary or even running down the escalator. Treat people like infants and they’ll become infantilised. And let’s be clear: TFL don’t care whether I trip and hurt myself. They just want to ensure they’re not sued when I twist my ankle.

Back in 2016 at the Chalke History Festival - a brilliant annual event, by the way - a superbly recreated section of First World War trench was built out of the chalk landscape, part of the 100th anniversary commemorations of the Battle of the Somme. It was historically researched, so the right depth and widths, with a series of different styles of revetments, dug-outs and so on, and built under the guidance of professional engineers and surveyors. Three days before the festival, the local Health & Safety Executive team turned up and shut it down immediately. The risk of it collapsing with people in it, they said, was too great. We suggested getting people to sign a piece of paper acknowledging that they understood the risks, but this was dismissed out of hand. ‘Not worth the piece of paper it’s written on.’ When it was eventually filled in nine months later, after a particularly wet then cold winter, there was not one part of it that had even remotely crumbled. What a shame and what a terrible waste that was.

In the 1930s, there were also plenty of people claiming the younger generation were soft, and as we all know, that generation arguably became the greatest of all, answering the call and fighting to rid the world - or the western world at any rate - of the forces of autocracy and repression. That generation, craving peace in the decade before and claiming they wouldn’t fight if it came to it, then did so and suffered unspeakable privations and hardships in the nearly six years that followed. Many paid the ultimate price. The survivors, though, came home, understanding the value of life, of freedom and that it should never be taken for granted. They strived to create a better world and did so. But they’ve now mostly gone and we’re left with a generation that does not so readily understand the cost of the freedoms we all take for granted today. Oliver Lyttelton, who survived the First World War, absolutely understood the cost of war.

His experiences in the late 1930s, dealing with a government reluctant to invest in resources when it was perceived to be advantageous but not, strictly speaking, essential, also throws up interesting parallels with today. His world was metals, essential in peace and war, but especially so in times of conflict. He also understood the need for private enterprise to do the right thing and not necessarily wait for the government contract. And during the war, Lyttelton was willing to use his knowledge and experience not to fight but to serve the government. Today, we need more people with experience of life, of business, of dealing with people from all nationalities and backgrounds, and perhaps fewer special advisors who have first class degrees from Oxbridge but little broader experience. As Chaucer’s Wife of Bath pointed out, experience not authority was what had helped her make her way through life.

Of course, we still need resilience in sourcing metals, but we also need vital resilience in terms of water, food and energy. We demand cheap food and tolerate totally inhumane farming practices in order to consume vast amounts of cheap chicken, for example, or bacon, eaten mostly on the fly. We don’t need to eat so much meat, most of which is available only thanks to pumping chickens and pigs with unspeakable amounts of growth hormones - and which we in turn ingest. A chicken in Tesco has lived for 33 days. Naturally, a chicken will take 147 days just to get to the point where it can lay an egg.

We can eat much better, and still inexpensively, by cooking it ourselves and also by eating less - we throw away a third of all cooked foods, for example. If we ate better and less, we’d be healthier. We might also sit down and converse with our family and fellows. And if we were healthier, we’d have a healthier welfare bill too, and ease the pressure on the NHS. So simple! What’s not to like?

But instead, we pile on inheritance tax on our farmers, the supermarkets grind them down on prices, and so our ability to produce food becomes that much harder. This in turn piles on pressure for greater yields. These come with increased use of fertilizers, with larger fields, fewer hedgerows and larger machinery, which then compacts the soil. The rule of thumb is that every third mouthful we eat is because of pollination. Yet, pollinating insects are down in number by 23% since 1980 and the UK now has the most depleted natural world of any country in Europe. This is a catastrophe that needs rapidly alerting not just because it’s lovely to see bumble bees and hear nightingales, but because a depleted natural world threatens our own ability to produce food. As a farmer friend of mine pointed out recently, we don’t need food security, we need food self-sufficiency. There’s a big difference, and at present, we’re a long way off achieving that.

The same goes for energy. Currently, around 42% of our energy comes from renewables, roughly the same amount from fossil fuels and just over 16% from nuclear power. The figure for renewables is quite impressive but one of the problems we face is that it can take years for any new wind farm or solar park to come onto the grid. A vast field of solar panels might make sense for a farmer today, but the company investing in such a project will then have to wait 4-5 years before it’s connected and then helping to power homes and businesses. They don’t have such issues in Norway or Japan, but the lack of investment in the national grid by successive governments here in Britain means it’s now old, creaking and on its knees.

Then there’s the thorny issue of fossil fuels. We will always have a very small number of people wanting to protest in illogical places about our use of fossil fuels, and hurl soup over the Mona Lisa or try and bring down literary festivals over that matter, but in this current age we live in, we need to be both practical and realistic rather than ideological. And we need to be honest. Most of the gas we use - and it amounts to 33.3% of our electricity power source - comes from overseas. Why? We have gas and oil or our own, and even the least sulphurous coal just about anywhere in the planet, but we prefer to import it so that our carbon footprint figures look good. This, though, is selling a lie, because our carbon footprint should apply to our reach, not just what happens within these shores. We’re an island nation and dependent on shipping, just as we have always been. Almost exclusively, shipping uses marine diesel - that is, a fossil fuel. Cheap food, cars, gadgets, clothes, most plastic, Sky boxes for those TV seasons we want to stream etc etc etc, come into this country using filthy dirty diesel. An average freighter of, say, 40,000 tons deadweight, will use 35-40 metric tons of fuel oil per day, which is around 9,500 - 11,000 gallons per day. That’s 36,000 - 41,500 litres of dirty diesel. Per day. An ordinary car takes around 50 litres to fill up. And a 40,000 ton ship is at the lower end of an average size freighter. In 2024, British ports handled 429.7 million tons of shipping. Imagine how much marine diesel that used!

Nearly 50% of our gas, meanwhile, enters this country from Norway via pipelines under the North Sea. Why would we pay the Norwegians for this when we can produce this ourselves? Currently, we mine around 30% of gas but why not almost all of it? There are plenty who argue that this won’t dramatically cheapen our electricity costs, but there’s also the small matter of resilience. Pipelines on the seabed are very vulnerable, and because societally we’re not prepared to put up our defence spending, they’re not adequately protected. Nor are the many electricity cables through which 99% of our daily data flows. These also run across the seabed of the worryingly shallow North Sea - cables, which, by the way, the Russians have been busily mapping.

It is ridiculous that it is so difficult to have proper conversations about this. Do so, and you risk becoming labelled a Trumpist or madly right-wing. No sane person would deny we’re facing global warming or that challenges in the global supply chain are looming. So, let’s do something about it. Let’s drill for our own oil and gas, use it up, and while doing that, invest in the national grid and pave the way for more renewable energy around the corner. And yes, let’s follow the South Koreans and start investing a bit more in nuclear energy too. Let’s not put all our eggs in one energy source basket, but spread the load and, in the same breath, become 100% domestic producers. Inevitably, in time, that will reduce the cost of electricity. That, in turn, will make Britain a more attractive proposition for investment. That will create jobs, boost the economy. Make us wealthier. Make us safer.

Societal change is needed. Better defence certainly requires greater investment in our armed forces but it also means resilience too. We will be safer if we are self-sufficient in food and we will be safer if we can produce our own energy. And better able to confront the disruptions to the global supply chain. That’s the point. We can let the very small numbers of protestors protest - we’re a free nation, after all - but for the rest of us it’s time to be realistic and practical. This is no time to be ideological.

None of this is rocket science and none of it needs to be an either/or with other demands on our creaking budget. A pragmatic approach to the challenges already facing us from a dramatically changing and evolving world should be approached as an exciting opportunity to improve our lives, national cohesion and future wealth. The answers are staring us in the face but societally neither the wider public nor the government are prepared to accept that urgent change is what is needed.

In the late 1930s, Oliver Lyttelton understood that it was far better to secure resources that would be vital in a future war before the starting gun of conflict was fired. We collectively need to take a leaf out of his book. We urgently need to move the dial: show greater moral resilience and start planning for resilience in regard to essential resources too. And we need to start this now.

We’re also in a situation where from a working-age population of 43.55 million in the UK, 10 million are getting benefits from the Department of Trade & Pensions. My guess is that 33.55 million people in this count

title: One Man's War: Okinawa '45
html:
This is a longer than usual piece for me, but Bill Pierce’s story is one worth telling properly, I reckon…

April 1, 1945 – April Fool’s Day, Easter Sunday, and, as it happened, D-Day for the invasion of Okinawa. In the deep blue waters around the island were over 1,457 ships and landing craft, crammed with more than half a million men, and including a joint US Army and Marine Corps landing force of around 182,000 troops.

Subscribe

As a beautiful, clear, spring morning broke over the massive invasion fleet, twenty year-old Bill Pierce, aboard the troopship APA General Clymer, was readying himself for his first ever taste of combat action. From Queens Village, New York, Bill was a Marine, and proud of it too. Part of the US 6th Marine Division, he had waited nearly two years for this moment; two years of training, first in the United States, and then, for the past ten months, on the island of Guadalcanal in the Pacific. And he felt ready – if not a little apprehensive – for the task ahead.

One of a five-man 37mm gun crew, Bill was in the Weapons Company of the 29th Marine Regiment, and as such was not to be in the first wave of landings. Even so, he and his comrades were up early, roused from their bunks by the bugler shortly after six in the morning. In the mess hall, the men were given a good breakfast of steak and eggs – what for many could be their last cooked meal. Some were too nervous to eat, but not Bill, who wolfed his down then went up on deck to attend Mass. Coming from a catholic family, Bill had always gone to church every Sunday as a boy. Now, on this day of days, praying to God gave him comfort. Despite the vast armada surrounding him, the sea looked calm, and twinkled in the early morning sunlight as he received Holy Communion.

The service over, Bill went back down to his bunk to put on his kit and to wait for the call to board their landing craft. He and his comrades did not have long to wait. Over the speaker his Weapons Company was called to get ready to board their landing craft. Bill put on his helmet with its distinct Marines’ camouflage, heaved his 60-pound pack onto his back and slung his M1 rifle over his shoulder. No-one spoke much. The jokes and normal banter had dried up. ‘My throat was already dry,’ Bill noted later, ‘and all of us looked at each other with wide eyes.’ Up on deck, there was a mass of activity. Cranes were hoisting up trucks, guns, tanks and jeeps from the lower decks. Bill and his gun crew watched their 37mm appear from the depths of the ship and then swing over the rail and down into the waiting landing craft below. Then it was the turn of the men themselves, who clambered awkwardly down the ropes, rifles clunking and their heavy packs slipping, and then jumped into the boat as it bobbed gently on the surface.

The noise and smell of the diesel engines was overpowering, and although Bill was never seasick, the stench of fumes made him feel nauseous as they circled round and round waiting for the order to head to the shore. It got to the point where no matter what horrors awaited them on the beaches, he just wanted to get off the landing craft and get onto dry land. By mid-morning, however, they were at last heading inland. Bill could not really tell what was going on. Overhead, naval shells whistled through the sky. He and his buddies stood up on the side of the boat, their arms on the railings so they could see where they were heading. The shoreline itself was shrouded in smoke from exploding shells, but along the landing beaches it seemed calmer, with hundreds of landing craft already moored at the water’s edge. None of them had much idea what to expect, however. All Bill knew about Okinawa was what they’d been told in the briefing: that it was an island some sixty miles long, and that because of its relative proximity to mainland Japan itself, would be an important staging post for the ongoing aerial assault of the last of the Axis powers.

Okinawa was, in fact, the largest of Ryuku Islands that made up the long, curling, tail south of Kyushu. The Island lay 320 miles south of mainland Japan, and although home to nearly 450,000 native Okinawans, the Island was also heaving with Japanese Imperial Army troops. Part of Japan’s home territories, it was unthinkable for the Land of the Rising Sun to concede such a jewel. The Americans might have assembled a task force of astonishing fire-power - the largest of the entire war - but they would need it. On every island onto which the Americans had stepped during the Pacific War, the Japanese had shown what tenacious and determined troops they were: Guadalcanal, Saipan, Iwo Jima; these had become bywords for the savagery with which every one of these pinprick islands had to be prised from the Japanese forces that held them. No-one expected Okinawa to be any different, least of all Bill – he’d heard the stories from the combat veterans amongst them; he’d even seen evidence of the fighting during his time on Guadalcanal. US Army and Navy planners reckoned it could take as much as a month to complete operations on Okinawa.

Their landing craft came to a halt some hundred yards from the shore, and the ramp lowered. Bill and his crew heaved their gun off the boat, but it immediately dropped several feet into the water – unbeknown to the coxswain, they had become grounded on a coral bar. Cursing, Bill and his crew hailed a Marine alligator, a kind of tracked beach craft, which came to their rescue. Even so, cursing furiously and soaking wet, they had to heave the gun up the alligator’s ramp themselves.

There seemed to be a fair amount of confusion on the beaches, but there was little sign of the enemy. Small-arms fire was only sporadic and so Bill and his crew were ordered to dig in for the night. ‘No-one was hit, killed, or wounded whatsoever in the area we were in,’ noted Bill. ‘The units assigned to take the airfield at Yontan took it in a matter of hours.’ As dusk began to fall, so the sky was lit up with tracers fired without let-up from the vast naval armada sitting off shore. Shells screamed over, aeroplanes rumbled through the night air, and the men now ashore looked up and watched a fireworks display more spectacular than any 4th July celebration. At the end of Day 1, the invasion was ahead of schedule.

But the attackers were to be cruelly deceived. The Japanese had chosen not to contest the beaches, believing they would have suffered unsustainable casualties defending the beaches against overwhelming American fire-power. As the sea lapped gently against the shore on that warm, spring evening, few could have guessed what lay in store, yet for the next eighty-one days, Okinawa was to witness the biggest single land-air-sea battle of all time, a brutal campaign whose savagery and brutality surpassed anything that had come before in the Pacific War. At sea, naval casualties were higher than at any point in the war, with Japan unleashing almost its entire kamikaze effort against the joint American and British task force around the Islands. On land, the scale of killing was even worse. Okinawa was to witness a blood bath of barbaric savagery, where American and Japanese regarded each other with both contempt and hatred, and in which more than a quarter of a million people were killed. Okinawa was to be the last, and most costly, battle of the Second Word War.
