excerpt: It's possible, even now, and history is there to help...
author: James Holland

title: Rearming the UK: There Is A Solution
html:
One of the many frustrating aspects of the British government’s ongoing unwillingness to commit to any dramatic or meaningful rearmament, despite the very obvious threats the UK faces and the urgent need for the country to defend itself, is the repeated trope, ‘we can’t afford it.’ The notion that major rearmament has to spell financial doom is ridiculous. Big business loves investing in defence but so too do small and medium sized enterprises – SMEs - many of whom are crying out for the kind of boost a major commitment to defence spending would offer.

This is how it works: the government initially borrows money, but at super long-term, low-interest rates, and reinvests this in defence. Yes, this initially means extra debt, but debt is only a problem if the economy is stagnating and there’s no means of reducing it, which is the situation the UK finds itself in at the moment. So, take the loan. This boosts growth, gets factories and businesses running, which in turn provides jobs and then more jobs as the growth impacts on an ever-wider proportion of the employment market. Enterprise and investment are suddenly encouraged. This in turns reduces the welfare burden because it gets people working, while at the same time bringing in more tax – income tax, VAT, corporation tax and so on. So, one very sizeable drain on government money is reduced while the amount flowing back into the treasury increases. And by the way, working and being part of a worthy, unifying national purpose is a terrific panacea for those suffering from low self-esteem and bouts of the blues. Individual self-worth is vital for the greater health of a nation, while, obviously, the converse is also true.

Subscribe

Investment during economic downturns is known as counter-cyclical economics and was first given this term by the great British economist, John Maynard Keynes. He in turn drew his economic theories from the analogue study of history, which showed, conclusively, that there are repeat patterns in the way markets and economies flow. This is because humans haven’t changed very much and our response to the economic ebbs and flows is generally the same: we embrace growth with optimism, hope, and a renewed sense of vigour and drive, and downturns with dissatisfaction, despondency and ennui. Think about it: we all have a spring in the step when there’s cash in the bank account and we gloomily retreat when we’re skint. This doesn’t require either an economics degree or a deep understanding of human psychology. And if anyone wants proof of this theory, just look at history. The past, after all, is there to help and only a fool would ignore it.

There is a reason why the German company, Rheinmetall has had such a growth in its stock value in recent times and ditto Krupp. The German government has done exactly as outlined above, investing over 100 million euros in defence and killing two birds with one stone: making Germany safer and boosting the flagging economy. And it was ever thus. Britain in the 1930s, for example, has traditionally been accused of both appeasing Hitler and failing to rearm. The Prime Minister most certainly did everything he could to avoid sending Britain to war in 1938 but the idea that Britain was not preparing for war at that time is nonsense. Appeasement and rearmament when hand-in-hand, with government and private business working together to play a critical part in the country’s preparations.

The British back then, with their global fleets and world trade, had always been wedded to the idea that war was really a battle of supplies, and so it always is the moment the opportunity for a swift, tactical and overwhelming victory passes. All manner of metals and raw materials were needed to fight a war, and not one country in the world had an abundance of all, not even America and the USSR, despite their vast size and geographical range.

Amongst those raw materials, for example, were metals and not just iron ore, and in Britain, few people in the 1930s understood the myriad and truly international world of metals better than Oliver Lyttelton, a man who was to play a major role in Britain’s war effort but who has been rather forgotten these days. Having survived four years of the last war fighting with the Grenadier Guards and winning a DSO and MC in the process, he had made it home and gone on to forge a highly successful business career. By 1939, he was chairman of the British Metal Corporation, who were, in essence metal merchants, and who under his leadership had become the biggest metal company in the UK. They had further consolidated their position by striking a number of affiliations with continental partners, which had enabled Lyttelton to become a director of the Germany metals firms, Metallgesellschaft and Nordeutsche Raffinerie. This had given him an invaluable picture of the German metal trade, and the importance of non-ferrous metals in any future war. He had learned, for example, that back in 1914, just a few months into the war, the directors of Metallgesellschaft, had been approached by the German General Staff because they were already running out of copper and needed help in finding more. Copper, tin, lead and zinc, were all needed - copper and zinc especially - in times of war, yet Lyttelton understood that the trade in non-ferrous metals was truly international, because no country on the planet was self-sufficient in all.

It was with this in mind, with the tale of the German Staff in 1914 lodged in his mind, that in the spring of 1939 Lyttelton had begun a plan to buy up as much of these all-important metals as possible. As he was well aware, many of the leading mining companies around the world would be worrying about the uncertainty war might bring - would they still be able to ship their metals? Would existing buyers continue to do so? He had already been approached by the Ministry of Supply to become the Controller of Non-Ferrous Metals should it come to war, and so back in March, with the Germans walking into Czechoslovakia, had approached Noranda in Canada, Broken Hill in Australia and others, and begun negotiating. What he was proposing was assured purchases, no matter whether they had the shipping or not, in return for guaranteed quantities at a low price.

Much to his immense frustration, he was unable to galvanise the Ministry of Supply into buying these metals right away, even though he knew Germany had been stockpiling copper – it is not just today that governments could be cumbersome and slow to make decisions. So, although he had personally secured small stocks of nickel, it was not until the outbreak of war that Lyttelton was finally made Controller of Non-Ferrous Metals and given carte blanche to start purchasing. He hoped it would not be already too late. Lyttelton, like most others in Britain, was expecting a German offensive almost immediately; and like others, was hoping the enemy would delay any action for as long as possible.

In the autumn of 1939, Lyttelton was forty-six, and the epitome of the debonair and cultivated Englishman, with his lean features, slicked-back hair and trim moustache. From an aristocratic background, he had been educated at Eton and Trinity College, Cambridge, and had an exemplary war record. Indeed, the war had taught him much: the extremes under which the human body and mind can be placed, the awfulness of the slaughter, the importance of never, ever, giving in. He had been temporarily blinded by gas, had been nearly broken, but somehow had kept going so that when peace finally came, he was amongst an elite of his generation who had fought for almost the entire war and was still standing.

During the war, he had also got to know and befriended a number of key people, from Winston Churchill and Anthony Eden to soldiers now generals in the army. In the intervening years, he had travelled widely, learned everything he could about both modern business and the world of metals and developed an outstanding and international web of contacts, as well as finding time to get married and raise a family. Intelligent, worldly, and imbued with a razor-sharp business acumen, he was one of the key civilians from the business world from which Britain would greatly benefit now that war had come.

And with war declared, and with Lyttelton now Controller of Non-Ferrous Metals, the British Metal Corporation was taken over by the Government and sent to new offices out of London in Rugby in the Midlands. Once installed at Rugby, Lyttelton and his hundred or so staff worked at ‘white heat’ and six weeks later, despite frustrating and unnecessary amounts of red tape from the Treasury, they had secured Britain’s projected requirements. This had been done in precisely the manner Lyttelton had envisaged. The total sum was a staggering £250 million but had come at a fraction of the price per ton for which these metals had been purchased in the previous war.

The pre-war purchase of non-ferrous metals was just one area in which Britain was rapidly preparing for war. Another was air power, which the British viewed as key to future conflict. It also involved far less combatants at the coal-face than the millions of troops dug into trenches that had been such a feature of the previous war. Britain was determined to use ‘steel not flesh’ in any future conflict as far as possible, harnessing technology, science, industry and global reach to reduce the number of young men flung into the firing line. Air power seemed one of the most important means of achieving this.

This in turn meant new, modern aircraft and not least state-of-the-art fighter planes to defend Britain’s skies against the expected hordes of enemy bombers that were bound to appear. The contract for a new, modern fighter had been won by Hawker in 1934 but the Air Ministry had had the foresight to issue a second, entirely unique contract to Supermarine for what became the Spitfire. Supermarine, however, was a small company, bought out by the much larger Vickers Aviation in 1928 but which for the next decade had been left largely to its own devices. Only in 1938, with the urgent need to rapidly increase production of the new Spitfire, did Vickers bring it more tightly under the reorganized Vickers-Armstrongs (Aircraft) Ltd.

Already by 1935, Vickers-Armstrongs, which also made a range of other armaments from tanks to machine-guns to warships, was the third-highest manufacturing employer in the UK, after Unilever and ICI. It also remained an entirely private British engineering conglomerate throughout the war until finally being nationalised in the 1960s; it was consumed by what is now BAE. None the less, the British government had the foresight to work hand-in-glove with British industry and even from the early 1930s when Britain was the largest exporter of armaments in the world. This, of course, provided the UK with a huge advantage when it suddenly needed to dramatically improve its own defences; much of the required infrastructure was already there. Much, but nothing like enough. Anticipating the need for massively increased production, the government initiated the shadow factory programme in 1935, when Neville Chamberlain had been Chancellor of the Exchequer. This, it is worth underlining, was at a time when national debt was 135% of GDP; we’re currently at around 93%.

By early 1939, when conscription was brought back but still months before the outbreak of war, new modern factories were already making arms with increased vigour. Sixteen new ordnance factories had been authorised in March 1939 at a time when the United States had just six in the entire country. A further twenty-nine were given the green light in December. Planned spending on arms for 1939/40 was £580 million, approximately half of all government expenditure at that time. More guns, more aircraft, more ships – more war materiel until the world was rid of Hitler and the Nazis. Nor was anyone much complaining. Despite Chamberlain’s concerns about introducing conscription in peacetime, the Munich crisis and the perfidy of Nazi Germany in breaking promises and invading Czechoslovakia in March 1939, persuaded the wider British public that this was an existential threat that needed combating with grim determination. It also helped that the British press was by now completely on board. The ability of the press to manipulate free-thinking democratic populations should never be underestimated.

The shadow factories had some teething problems not least because, in time-honoured fashion, the government and civil service had a tendency to give contracts to the wrong people and appointed incompetents to run development projects. So, for example, the automobile magnate, Lord Nuffield, was appointed to oversee the creation of a vast new factory at Castle Bromwich in Birmingham in which it was planned that sixty Spitfires would be rolling off the production line each week by April 1940. Nuffield, the founder of Morris Motors, offered his services and expertise to create the most advanced and dynamic aircraft factory in Britain, claiming he could build four times as many aircraft at his new plant than any other in the UK.

Despite reservations about handing over such a vital undertaking to Nuffield, a known anti-Semite with pro-fascist tendencies, he was still given the task in the kind of circumstances familiar with some of the dodgiest contracts issued by the government during the recent pandemic. The decision proved a fiasco. Although work began in 1938, costs ballooned as designs and layout plans kept changing. By May 1940, not one Spitfire had been built at Castle Bromwich. While plenty of other shadow factories were working very efficiently by this time, it took the creation of the Ministry of Aircraft Production and the appointment of Lord Max Beaverbrook, the Canadian press baron, as the first minister that same month of May 1940 to turn things around. Beaverbrook sacked Nuffield and put his own men in charge. By the war’s end, Castle Bromwich had produced half all the Spitfires produced.

Beaverbrook was a fascinating case of how to harness sound business practices to the task of war production, just as, incidentally, also proved the case during the Covid pandemic. Although he knew a lot about newspapers and the press and very little about aircraft, he brought his no-nonsense business acumen to the task of aircraft production at a vital moment. Key to his approach was streamlining with no more faffing about, no quangos, no buck-passing, and no prevarication through reams of red tape and officialdom. Beaverbrook didn’t like committees. In his office he had two notices. One said, ‘Committees take the punch out of war,’ while the second read, ‘Organisation is the enemy of improvisation.’ The buck stopped with him; he liked to be informed and then he made his decision. Scientists, businessmen, industrialists – men he respected and trusted – were all brought in and given loose job titles. ‘They are all captains of industry,’ Beaverbrook explained, ‘and industry is like theology. If you know one faith, you can grasp the meaning of another.’ There was little hierarchy and he used his force of personality and closeness to the new Prime Minister, Winston Churchill, to cut through red tape. Bottlenecks were solved not by sending letters but by making phone calls, or, if that didn’t solve it, sending one of his team to head to the trouble and sorting it out on the spot.

In a matter of weeks, aircraft production had risen exponentially; so too had the processing of damaged aircraft. Supply chains had been quickened, wastage got rid of, and a new sense of fire and purpose put into the workforce, who were expected to work, collectively, 24-7, but were rewarded for doing so. By the end of June 1940, aircraft production had increased to 300 per week, while by the same time 250 aircraft had been repaired and sent back to squadrons. Within a month, Beaverbrook had increased aircraft production by 62%, new engines by 33% and repaired aircraft by a staggering 186%. Germany produced more aircraft in the years 1934-1938, but there was parity in 1939 and by 1940, Britain had eclipsed Germany, a trend that would continue throughout the war. Overall, Britain built 132,500 aircraft during the war, around 50,000 more than Germany. It was an astonishing turn-around but played to an essential truism: that Britain had the means, capacity, workforce and motivation to do what was needed. That potential had simply needed unlocking.

Britain was fighting on alone in Europe following the fall of France and did continue to fight alone alongside its dominion nations and empire right up until the end of 1941, albeit with brief forays on the Allied side from Yugoslavia and Greece. That it was able to do so and continue to play a major and decisive role right to the very end of the war was in no small part down to its preparation before war broke out. The British Government worked in tandem with private businesses, making the most of its global reach, immense shipping assets and a labour force still reeling from the Great Depression of the first part of the decade. As Britain proved in the late 1930s, being in a state of economic stagnation actually helped kick-start meaningful and dynamic rearmament because the labour force – in fact, the entire nation – was primed for the kind of single-minded purpose and possibilities for jobs such expansion offered.

The war production problems facing the British government before and during the war were immense. Before the war, armaments production had to sit alongside civilian production and the rate at which the former superseded the latter was not an easy matter to resolve. There was also, as now, a shortage of skilled labour, which then had to be both recruited and trained. The fall of France in June 1940 meant that Britain no longer had an ally with a large army; so much of Britain’s war production strategy had lain with aircraft but this now had to be amended to factor in the creation of a sizeable army too. Yet, Britain met that challenge and not only saved democracy in the UK but helped defeat its enemies and secure liberty and freedom throughout much of the western world.

The lessons are, I hope, all too obvious. Britain needs to act now. A year ago, during the 80th anniversary commemorations for the end of the Second World War in Europe, I interviewed the Prime Minister along with my great friend and podcast partner, Al Murray. The first thing Sir Keir Starmer told us was that defending the people of Britain was the number one responsibility of the Prime Minister. Yes – absolutely. Since then, very little has happened. Defence spending has not increased, there have been no dramatic defence projects, no rallying cry to motivate the nation nor any sign at all that the long-winded and cumbersome procurement process has been overhauled. The cables that flow from this country into the North Sea and which handle 99% of our daily data, financial and otherwise, remain largely unprotected. It’s not good enough.

Chamberlain and the Conservative government of the second half of the 1930s have been routinely condemned ever since for not reacting to the threat of Nazism and fascism soon and for only slowly waking up to rearmament. Should those cables be cut or we find ourselves on the receiving end of a strike by our enemies how will history judge this government and the ones that preceded it? Very, very badly. The way to ensure our enemies are not emboldened is to have a strong defence ourselves. Deterrence is the best safeguard of peace.

Why are we being so complacent? There is a lack of enterprise at present. A lack of vision. Frankly, a lack of anyone able to sell anything like an enlightened and hopeful vision. People are tired of the Westminster elites because they all say the same thing, no matter which party is in government and all are defined by an apparent inability to sell a dynamic message of hope and inspiration. The current dire state of the UK’s defences are not remotely unsolvable. Rather, there are clear solutions that can and should aid economic growth. Many of the current issues – an unsustainably bloated welfare, lack of defence, appalling youth unemployment, a deep suspicion of a cumbersome and ineffective civil service – especially in the Treasury and MOD - and a general malaise that appears to be playing into the hands of political extremes, can all be solved by a focussed drive towards one primary aim: to make Britain safe from its enemies. If the government won’t instigate this, perhaps private industry will have to lead and humiliate them into action instead.

Subscribe
excerpt: And It Doesn't Have to Plunge Britain into Greater Economic Mire Either
author: James Holland

title: Wake Up, People of Britain!
html:
‘One of the best ways to keep the peace,’ noted the first President of the United States, George Washington, ‘is to be prepared for war.’ What was true of the late eighteenth century remains every bit the case to this day, and certainly so at a time when here in the UK, we’ve become complacent about the peaceful state in which our country exists. As a consequence, we no longer seem sufficiently willing to protect ourselves against our enemies. There are plenty calling for urgent rearmament and massively increased defence spending, but they all seem to be ‘formers’: former senior military commanders, former ministers, a former Secretary-General of NATO, former newspaper editors. Mostly elder statesmen. I can’t think of any influencers on social media, any British George Clooneys putting their political heads above the parapet, any prize-winning novelists or rock legends. The Sun newspaper might call for action, and there have been a fair few columnists doing so, but while the wider public appetite remains mute - and let’s face it, worryingly disinterested - the current government can kick the can of defence spending down the road.

It’s worth pointing out that the best Russian troops are not getting themselves slaughtered in the Donbas in eastern Ukraine but are facing the Baltic states. The 11th Army Corps is based in the Kaliningrad Oblast, formerly East Prussia and Königsberg before 1945, but now an isolated enclave on the Baltic coast with Lithuania in between it and the rest of Russia. The Baltic Fleet is based there, as well as special forces and various missile capabilities. The 6th Combined Arms Army, meanwhile, faces Estonia, as does the 76th Airborne Division, the 1st Tank Army and 44th Army Corps. If you’re Estonia or any of the other Baltic States or Scandinavian countries, this is a very serious and real threat. An alternative view is that Putin has his forces there at China’s behest to create the impression of a possible incursion into the Baltic States and has no intention of any military operation in that theatre. China, the theory goes, is anxious to understand US intentions in the Indo-Pacific and so wants to test America’s commitment to Europe and NATO. As President Trump has made clear, he’s no longer interested in Europe or NATO.

Subscribe

The consensus is that Putin is in no position at the moment to test the water in the Baltic but why would anyone risk betting against it? No-one can seriously doubt that he wants to wrench back the Baltic and even Finland too, given half the chance. Right now, Putin is currently trying to change to law in Russia to give him greater legal freedom to intervene internationally to ‘defend’ Russians, and just as there are ethnic Russians in the Donbas, so there are in the Baltic states and not least Estonia. Why do this if he doesn’t have plans to call upon these new powers? He might, for example, cross the border and capture an Estonian village known to have a majority of ethnic Russian citizens, or, as the Swedes are currently suggesting, perhaps order his troops to storm and take one of the many islands in the Baltic Sea. This would constitute an act of war and trigger Article 5, compelling fellow NATO allies to leap to the defence of the afflicted nation. Trump would almost certainly renege on the Article 5 commitment, which would then leave the rest of NATO jumping to the rescue without their most powerful ally. That would mean war. Shots would be fired, missiles directed and furious negotiations take place before things got really out of hand. Meanwhile, Russian subs could dip into the North Sea and cut a handful of cables in the North Sea - just to make the point that they hold the upper hand.

Russian surveying of our cables is so far the most sinister and serious threat they’ve made to Britain’s sovereignty, notwithstanding the relentless cyber warfare they’ve already been carrying out. Most of us store data on the cloud these days and I suspect the majority assume it is somehow magically stored so that we no longer have to worry about it and without giving it too much further thought. It’s important to understand, however, that this information doesn’t drift through the ether. It’s not in the atmosphere or floating around an actual cloud. Rather, cloud storage depends on immense physical infrastructure and reaches those storage data centres in Nevada or Utah via a massive network of underwater cables. These run through the North Sea and across the Atlantic. Britain has a network of some sixty undersea cables that carry more than 99% of our international data, including daily internet traffic, much of our financial transactions and global communications. On top of that, 77% of our gas - the most common means of household heating in the UK - comes via pipelines across the North Sea from Norway. A large proportion of our electricity is also transmitted along cables running across this all-important seaway.

It is these very cables that the Russians have been relentlessly mapping in recent times. They’re not doing just for kicks. They’re doing it so that one day they can cut them should the opportunity arise. And should they do so, the consequences hardly bear thinking about. In the meantime, as Swedish intelligence has just reported, Russia is dramatically ramping up its cyber operations against European energy supplies.

Meanwhile, around 40% of our food also comes from overseas, and while that means we produce some 40% domestically, most farmers can barely keep their businesses afloat. As a friend and farmer recently pointed out to me, it’s not so much food security we need but food self-sufficiency. We do not have this at present. What’s more, Britain is also still dependent on imported fertilisers, needed for home production. We need to become more resilient across the board – and especially so because we’re different from the rest of Europe, not just because we’re no longer in the European Union, but because we are a collection of islands separated from the continent by the sea.

There has been much talk in recent times of comparisons with the 1930s. The governments of that dark decade have been routinely criticised by historians for the lack of investment in defence while Nazi Germany turned itself into a military superpower, Japan became ever more militarised, and democracies came under attack from autocracies. Neville Chamberlain, Prime Minster at the start of the Second World War, has copped the most flak for appeasing Hitler at Munich in 1938. He was warned that kowtowing to Hitler would not work and nor did it. ‘The maintenance of peace,’ noted Winston Churchill, one of the strongest critics of appeasement and then out of government, ‘depends upon the accumulation of deterrents against the aggressor.’ He was spot on, as was George Washington before him. It’s a sentiment as relevant today as ever.

Despite the vilification Chamberlain has received ever since, more than 90% of the population was opposed to going to war over Czechoslovakia in the autumn of 1938, a percentage in a democracy that was decisive. Nor was the Chamberlain government ignoring defence. It’s important to know that in 1939, Britain had comfortably the world’s largest navy, largest merchant navy and the world’s only fully co-ordinated air defence system. Sure, the army was small, but factories were already working around the clock during the Munich crisis making arms, more ships, upgrading older models, building aircraft and explosives, while more factories were under construction. By the summer of 1940, Britain was out-producing Germany in aircraft at a rate of more than 2:1 and, by late summer, by 3:1. In other words, despite the army’s defeat on the continent in France in May and June 1940, Britain was incredibly well placed to hold out, fight back and later play a significant role in eventual victory.

What do we have now? Excellent special forces and 16 Air Assault, half-decent anti-cyber ops, a growing number of drones and that’s about it. Our navy has become a laughing stock, the RAF is woefully depleted and our army run into the ground and tarnished by expensive procurement projects such as the Ajax that speak of ineptitude and mismanagement. Morale is also poor at present, in part because of the negativity surrounding the state of all three services, but also because of a shortage of equipment and ammunition. The harsh reality is that our armed forces are woefully denuded. Can we defend our cables in the North Sea? No way. Can we sustain a lengthy contribution to a European war? Nope. Can we deter our enemies with a show of military strength? Not remotely.

Currently, there is neither a plan to rescue British farmers - after all, there are not enough of them to make a meaningful difference to voting intentions – despite the urgent need for food self-sufficiency, and no firm plan to increase defence spending. In fact - and I find this hard to comprehend - military chiefs are currently under instruction from their civilian bosses to further cut expenditure. The truth is that the majority of people in Britain simply know little about this precarious situation in which we find ourselves, and don’t care either, because it’s not a threat they are directly experiencing right now because, other, more immediate issues, seem more pressing. We’ve become so used to living in peace, the experience of that earlier world war is slipping from living memory and because the idea of being at war here, on our backdoor, seems fantastical. It won’t happen to us.

But it might.

Meanwhile, politicians continue to dither, faff and prevaricate. ‘We can’t afford it,’ is the oft-repeated refrain, even though the percentage of public debt to GDP was as high as 135% in the 1930s and 250% in 1945, and we managed to turn both of those debt millstones around. Today it’s around 95%. Incidentally, in 2024, the British public spent double on holidays what the government spent on defence and roughly the same as the defence budget on new cars.

Interestingly, the country in Europe with the highest expenditure on defence - Poland - has one of the continent’s fastest-growing economies, while Germany is now massively investing in defence and fully intending to kill two birds with one stone: to protect itself and boost the economy. The German government is currently spending around €100 billion annually, while between 2023 and 2025 it issued €188.4 billion on no less than 255 major defence procurement projects. And this is a crucial point: significant extra defence spending doesn’t need to spell economic disaster. There are means of borrowing the money at very low interest and paying back long term. I suspect few in Britain would object if there was every chance the borrowing would be paid back. For debt to be cleared, there needs to be economic growth, after all. So, let’s create growth by dramatically increasing rearmament. It really isn’t rocket science.

And there is the means to fund a significant boost to defence spending. There is, for example, the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) being worked up at the moment by creative Brits and championed by none other than NATO’s hero of the hour, Mark Carney, the Prime Minister of Canada. It provides super cheap loans for member states, super cheap loans to industry or innovator priorities operating within those members states, and also guarantees to member state commercial banks, investors and funds to incentivise the release of a stack of private investment into the DSR space at a scale not seen since WW2. Money borrowed under such terms can be used to give the economy a huge kick-start, provide growth and at the same time, make us safer. What’s not to like? It’s the Keynesian model and has a huge amount in its favour. But it requires action NOW.

Frustratingly, this is decisive action that is not emanating from the British government. In the movie, Jerry Maguire, Tom Cruise tells the sports star he represents, ‘Help me to help you.’ I want to scream this line to the Prime Minister and his cabinet. Act with purpose, vision and clarity. The DSRB was conceived here in Britain and there was a golden opportunity to host the bank with all the associated prestige and capital growth a global institution such as this would inevitably bring. Tragically, it is not to be, however. Unbelievably, some key officials in the Treasury were against it, largely because it wasn’t their idea, and what has followed has been a faceless strategy of empty chairing negotiations by UK officials to delay its development in favour of their own Multinational Defence Mechanism – an enterprise that is neither as ambitious or has had the take-up from fellow allied nations that has been enjoyed by the DSRB.

So, it seems the bank will not be based in the City of London, but in Luxembourg and Toronto. Seriously. Sir Keir Starmer, John Healey and even Rachel Reeves, it seems, are in favour of signing up to the DSRB. If so, they would be sitting alongside some 40 other NATO and global nations that are already in the process of doing so, while at least eight founding member states are currently crafting the first such banking charter that allows for serious deterrence funding. Yet despite continual championing by several Labour MPs and the House of Commons Defence Committee, they cannot get through to enough of those crucial civil servants at the Treasury to make it happen. A whopping parliamentary majority is not enough. It’s enough to make one weep. How could we be so short-sighted?

But this is why pressure needs to come from elsewhere. If the PM is impotent to act, then it must be left to others to wake up the nation from this sleepwalking. And there are faint signs of hope. The proportion of those who believe defence spending should be increased is now 44% up from 30% a couple of years ago. This rising figure is something those of influence should be working with now and urgently so. There is not a moment to lose. We should not be leaving it to the ‘formers’ but galvanising those with genuine influence to help change public opinion, just as a handful of writers and other public figures did in the 1930s.

This wonderful, beautiful, varied country, with its astonishing landscape and coastline, it’s rich culture and history, its incredible talent, and wealth of immensely creative people is so worth protecting. We have the skills, ability and wherewithal to make ourselves watertight safe, to thrive and blossom once more. Complacency - that terrible word - short-termism and an abject lack of resolve are threatening to undermine us. It’s time for us to wake up and move once more to the sunlit uplands.

Come on, people.

We can do it. But we need to act NOW.

Subscribe

author: James Holland

title: It's a Duty to Know Our History
html:
‘My expeirence in two world wars, the aftermaths and the endeavours to make a lasting peace makes me marvel at the regularity with which errors are repeated,’ noted Bernard Baruch, the eminent American financier and statesman. ‘One of the errors that most frequently recurs is failure to study and understand the records of the past.’ Baruch was Chairman of the War Industries Board in the First World War, predicted the Wall Street Crash of October 1929, and was a close adviser to President Roosevelt throughout the Second World War especially with the rapid increase of armaments production. He was also the US representative on the UN Atomic Energy Commission and a titanic figure in both Washington and Wall Street. In other words, he was a man worth listening to. It goes without saying that he was bang on the money with this line above.

There are those who claim that history is irrelevant, that now is now and the past was then, a different time entirely. The novelist L.P. Hartley famously began his iconic novel, The Go-Between, with the line, ‘The past is a foreign country. They do things differently there.’ Hartley was right to a point; the world moves and evolves constantly and yet the present is always shaped by what has come before. A brief study of the ruptures currently affecting us in the democratic west, for example, shows us that all have their roots in the past. The antagonism and mistrust of the Iranians towards America goes back to US involvement in the overthrow of Prime Minister Mohammed Mosaddegh over his attempts to nationalise the British-controlled oil industry in the country. It was compounded by American interference in the 1970s and US hostility to the Ayatollah’s revolution in 1979 and of US support for Iraq in the subsequent Iran-Iraq War.

Subscribe

History also helps us understand the tragedy of Gaza, the calamity of the War in Ukraine, of why the American military has since 1949 dominated NATO. What comes before, no matter how foreign it may seem to us today, leaves indelible footprints that shape the present and the future. History also tells us that in democracies, economic turmoil directly leads to political turmoil, and that the instability caused by the double whammy of economic and political crisis leads us closer to war. In 1919, there was the economic catastrophe of the First World War followed by the Spanish ’flu pandemic. A decade later, came the Wall Street Crash and the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of May 1930; the turmoil of the crash was made considerably worse by the start of a global trade war. This led directly to the collapse of the national banks in Vienna and Berlin and in turn to Germans rejecting the established order of the Weimar Republic and embracing Hitler and the Nazis. Democracy was abandoned and six years later, Germany and Europe was at war.

American Presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S. Truman understood that economic prosperity and international collaboration protect and nurture democracy. Out of the ruins of global war they were able to establish these foundations, which we in the democratic west have enjoyed since 1945. Those principles are now once again under threat: the economic costs of war in Iraq and Afghanistan, the 2008 crash, the global pandemic, and more recently American tariff wars - once again - as well as actual conflict, have destabilised democratic economies and severely challenged the political and global order. In other words, the lessons of the 1920s and thirties, learned the hard way in the west, appear to have been forgotten. While there is cheering in much of the west at the ousting of the autocratic Victor Orban in Hungary, the wrecking ball of the second Trump administration - a man with no regard whatsoever for the lessons of the past - continues to fracture western stability in a very alarming way.

I’ve recently been listening to the superb series on London’s Golden Age on The Rest is History podcast. My big brother, Tom, is one of the hosts and he and I were chatting about Samuel Johnson and James Boswell, the heroes of the series, and I mentioned to him how incredibly contemporary both men seemed. Tom disagreed; he felt they were products of an age which was now alien to us today. He’s right that the world was a different place then but was humankind? Both Johnson and Boswell, because of the hundreds of thousands of words Boswell, especially, wrote about his own life and that of his great friend, left a record of two men who shared all the characteristics we still feel to this day: passion, love, irritation, pain, frustration, happiness, ecstasy, temptation, anger, hate and kindness and compassion. These human emotions are also very much the background to the plays of Shakespeare, for example, or the novels of Dickens. Their universality ensures they remain relevant and are still enjoyed to this day. The world their characters inhabit may be different but in the case of Shakespeare, especially, the storylines are sufficiently familiar enough to be given regular renditions out of period and transported to the modern day.

When I began writing about the Second World War some twenty-five years ago there were still plenty of veterans to whom I could meet and talk. That is no longer really the case. My old friend and former Mosquito bomber pilot, Colin Bell, is still astonishingly cogent at 105, but uniquely so. More recently, I’ve been turning to diaries, letters and journals instead and what eye-openers they have proved. A detailed diary or set of letters was, in many ways, treated as a cathartic confessional and I can promise you the characters of the writers leap off every page. Their 21 year-old or 32 year-old selves become vividly real. They’re fully-fleshed, entirely recognisable people, with the same likes, dislikes, worries, fears, concerns, irritations, sense of humours and anxieties as we who live in the world today. They just happened to be living through the Second World War. Some have terrific senses of humour; others are pedantic fuss-pots; others spend most of the time feeling wretchedly terrified; while for others, the excitement and cameraderie outweigh the fear and anxiety. There is stoicism, despair, wit, resignation, hope, regret, and the entire rainbow of human emotions. Reading their words, men and women who long ago died become fully alive once more. It’s fabulously interesting.

If you accept, as I believe, that times change but we humans don’t very much, then the analogue study of history becomes even more important. Yet few, if any nations, make the study of history compulsory throughout the years of standard schooling. In the UK system, history is studied in ink spots - the Russian revolution, a bit on the emancipation of women, civil rights in America, the rise of the Nazis and something on an aspect of the Cold War, for example. How this all fits together is rarely emphasised, while the learning itself is based around hitting key points, fence posts and learning by rote. In other words, it’s often a bit uninspiring. Of the 5.1 million students taking GCSEs here in the UK each year, only 300,000 choose to take history, or around 6%. It’s not a lot.

Fortunately, history is one school subject that people often return to later in life, but really it should almost be a public duty to learn about the past. History doesn’t repeat itself - it can’t possibly because that was then and this is now and the world is constantly changing and evolving - but patterns of human behaviour most definitely do. The lessons are all there, whether it be the perils of financial crashes, or entering a war too dependent on air power, or viewing conflict through the prism of what a war leader wants it to be rather than what it actually is. Or how an autocratic regime following democracy will always make those who voted in the dictator poorer, both financially and in terms of personal freedoms.

And nor should the study of the past be a chore. We’re naturally drawn to human drama and history is full of it: a real soap-opera of tragedy, trauma, and the highs and the lows of human endeavour, of amazing, wondrous achievements and individual fortitude and bravery as well as human frailties, weaknesses and evil malevolence. It’s exciting, inspiring - and offers warnings for today and the future.

Every year during the June midsummer in a beautiful corner of Hardy’s Wessex there is the Chalke History Festival. I mention it because I’ve been involved with it from its outset. This year will be its fifteenth iteration and an extraordinary gathering it is too: an eccentric mix of talks, discussions, living history, performance, music, theatre, workshops and, of course, food, drink, stalls, and all you’d expect from a summer festival in the heart of the English countryside. An amazingly eclectic group of speakers and contributors take part in a line-up that is unique to Chalke and includes people from around the world. It’s a fabulous event, and not-for-profit: it was founded as a cause for good and aims to encourage more people to be inspired by the incredible stories of the past. It is an event that attempts to champion the urgent need for a better understanding of what has gone before. We mean for Chalke to inspire, enlighten and inform. We want people to live, see, breathe and smell history.

The festival is, of course, a pinprick, but in these tumultuous times an understanding of what came before has rarely been more relevant. The freedoms we in the west enjoy - freedom of speech, religion, of personal choice - were hard-won and should never be taken for granted, yet complacency and short-sightedness are threatening to undermine the liberty we cherish. Our long history is the greatest story of all and I would urge everyone to learn more about it. The lessons for both today and tomorrow, despite the ever-changing world in which we live, are all to be found in the tales of what has come before. History is there to help.
