title: The Tragic Tale of a Cricketing Genius
html:
I was in Sydney last week watching the final test match in the latest Ashes series between England and Australia.  As an Englishman, travelling halfway round the world to witness this, the result was disappointing but I’d long ago got over the terrible, shoulder-sagging disappointment of the losses at Perth - truly gut-wrenching - then Brisbane, which felt rather inevitable.  By the time the third test at Adelaide was over, familiar resignation had set in and I’d adjusted my expectations accordingly. Melbourne brought the first England victory in Australia since 2011, so I reckon I have been a lot more fortunate than the tens of thousands who have flooded here since that glorious tour and witnessed nothing but defeat.  By the time I arrived in Sydney, I was pretty sanguine: just happy to be witnessing all five days of a test match at this truly historic ground. Yes, there are new stands these days and the old grassy hill has gone, but the century-old pavilion and Ladies’ Stand are still here, look pretty as a picture, and offer just the right elegant nod to tradition and counterweight to progression.

And, to be honest, it was a thrill to watch Joe Root’s 41st test hundred, one had to admire Travis Head’s ton and also doff a cap to another great of the modern game, Steve Smith, with all his quirks and eccentricities.  After a bit of rain on day one, the sun beat down, the skies were brilliantly blue, the outfield looked effortlessly immaculate and the lighter green roofs of the old pavilion and Ladies’ Stand charmed gently from their corner of the ground from start to finish.  There was also the Barmy Army, those most doughty of travelling sports fans, who massively trumped the Aussie spectators in terms of consistency of noise, variety of repetitive chants and who never once gave up their sense of fun and enjoyment. It was a victory of sorts, and one I was happy to enjoy.

But without doubt, the greatest thrill of being here in Sydney was to witness Jacob Bethell’s first test hundred - a truly magic moment for any young batsman, but especially so here, in the cauldron of the SCG, a place that has floored many lesser mortals. It was a big hundred too, 152 gorgeous runs, that marked what must surely be the start of a glittering international career. The greatest batsmen have an aesthetic grace to their craft: they can hit a ball in a way lesser mortals simply cannot emulate. Commentators and former professionals have all been purring about Bethell’s innings and although I’m only a rank amateur, watching him it was obvious to see why.

Much has been made of the belligerency of England’s test match batting in recent years, but Bethell’s knock was all about balletic grace, timing and, frankly, a joyous kind of timelessness. He constructed his innings with painstaking patience but also sound judgement and with careful caresses that seemed to effortlessly send the ball hurtling to the boundary. Bethell is an old-school batsmen in modern form. No wonder the purists have been so lavish in their praise.

Which has set my mind wandering to another young prodigy who briefly lit up the world’s cricketing stage, but nearly a hundred years before the coming of Bethell. Sport constantly evolves just as the world evolves, but there are constants. Bethell’s innings was a reminder of that. Timing - the precise moment to lay bat on ball - concentration, the ability to absorb pressure, technique - the transfer of the body from one position to another without losing balance - and the stillness of the head over the ball: these are the skills understood by the cricketers of a hundred years ago just as they are today. Bats and protective equipment might have changed, formats might have evolved, but the the basics of batting - hitting a leather ball hurtling towards you and scoring runs without losing your wicket - remain exactly the same.

And it was these same skills that had many talking about Archie Jackson with the same gasps of delight that have been bestowed on Jacob Bethell this past few days. Like Bethell, he was charming, modest, fresh-faced and good-looking and batted with a rare elegance and grace. The tragedy for Archie Jackson, however, was that he never had the chance to fulfill that obvious talent and skill into a long and celebrated career.

Sadly, there was no high-definition television in Archie Jackson’s day, nor spider cam, nor even an iPhone with which to record iconic moments from high up in a stand. What does remain, however, is a sequence of seven photographs of Jackson batting in December 1929.  I'm a little bit obsessed with these images, although in many ways, they conform to type.  They're grainy, they're monochrome, and it's impossible to see the batsman's face. There's no high-resolution here, no tattoos leaking from under the shirt, or sun block, nor chin of four-day stubble. In all other respects, however, those shots look modern. They ooze style, grace, and silky-sweet timing. There's an orthodox cut, the follow-through firm but controlled in an unexaggerated way; there's a late-cut, and then a lovely back-foot drive, the batsman rocking back with perfect balance. Then come the off-drives: three of them, one with the batsman reaching, slapping a wide one through cover; another, with front-leg bent far forward, the arms suggesting this ball has been despatched just in front of cover point; while the third is an absolute thumper, a half-volley - or perhaps a good-length ball struck imperiously on the up - which you know, just looking at it, was the almost perfect cover drive. You can almost see it bumping over the boundary rope, and cracking into the picket fence beyond.

There is one other, and perhaps the most outrageous shot of all, more a home run hit by a baseball slugger; Jackson is leaning back, his arms and bat swung through and over his left shoulder.  It looks as though this extraordinary shot has sent the ball disappearing into the stands somewhere between long-on and midwicket; certainly, he did hit one six in the innings. It's the kind of shot we see time and again in Twenty 20 or in the one-day game. It is the shot of a batsman full of physical vigour, athleticism and brimming with confidence. A man totally in command of his game.

And in all these pictures, one thing is startlingly clear: in every shot, his head position is perfect. Still, balanced, over the ball. This is a batsman I would have travelled miles to watch, a batsman so exciting you just know he was turning batting into an art-form.  It's so obvious, so abundantly clear, in a way that photographs from 1929 are never normally able to demonstrate. There is poetry in this set of seven pictures and the body movement so beautifully posed that despite the graininess, and despite being taken more than eighty-five years ago, there is a palpable sense of excitement. You can feel that Sydney heat, smell the grass and dust and sweat and whitewash on the batsman's pads. They are among my most favourite cricket photos ever taken, of Archie Jackson, a young Australian only recently turned twenty years old.

That hot day, he scored 182, in an innings that included 27 fours and that one six. So completely in command of his game was he, it was thought by some watching him that he had played with a freedom bordering on indifference. Jackson was already being hailed as a batting genius, and a man with an impossibly bright future. An Australian legend in the making. Few of the five thousand watching that day would have had much reason to doubt that sunny prediction.

Strictly speaking, Archie Jackson was not Australian at all, but Scottish, born at 1, in Glasgow. He was the youngest of three children with two older sisters - a much-beloved baby brother. When Archie was nearly four years old, however, his father, Sandy, decided the family should emigrate and pursue a better life in the still-new country of opportunity: Australia.  Sandy set sail first, and over a year later, having found work and a house for them all, he wrote and called for his family. They left Glasgow and finally reached Sydney on 1 August, 1913.

The family house was in Ferdinand Street in the Sydney suburb of Balmain. It was a simple, Victorian terraced house with a tin roof and iron balcony. Another sister followed and the Jackson family soon settled into life in their adopted country; Sandy was doing well, working at the Cockatoo Dockyard, the children were healthy and happy and the move appeared to have been a good one. Archie's childhood was contented and largely carefree: he was greatly adored by his parents and sisters, there was enough to eat, he made good friends at school, and he was proving to be a talented sportsman, especially at cricket, encouraged by his kindly and easy-going father. Sandy even made a cricket bat for his son, complete with a cane handle.

Archie and his friend Bill Hunt lived for cricket and at lunch-time when matches were being played, would bunk off school and head to the Sydney Cricket Ground, using their threepence lunch money for their tickets. In the evenings they would play cricket at Birchgove Park, just a hundred yards from the Jackson house, and home of Balmain District Cricket Club.

By the time Archie was twelve, he and his friends were playing cricket whenever they could. Evenings were spent at Birchgrove Park, playing their own games with their own rules. Archie always proved incredibly difficult to get out, so they agreed that he should retire at a hundred. His response was to fly to ninety then stonewall. By now, he was already playing junior state cricket and soccer and had been started to play cricket for Balmain's lower grade teams. At twelve, he made four centuries for his junior school; two season later, he made a further three for Rozelle School, while at Balmain CC, the elders noticed people were being drawn away from watching the first team to see this young boy with the effortless footwork and all the shots stack up the runs for the lower grades.

At sixteen, Jackson became the youngest-ever debutant in first-grade cricket. Nor did he disappoint, despite playing against former Australian bowlers such as Jack Gregory, finishing the season with an average of 30.75. His cricket prowess continued to blossom, even though he was still a slight young man who looked even younger than his years.   The next season he scored his first first-grade century, and the season after that, 1926-27, when still only seventeen, he began in outrageous form: 111 in only two hours, then 143 and followed with another hundred, 158 against Mosman. The next moment he was playing for his state, New South Wales, and scored 86 in his first match, the innings ending only when he was run out. His first first-class century was not long in coming: one hundred exactly against Queensland, his century coming with an effortless off-drive and a skip down to the far end, his home crowd cheering raucously as this extraordinary talent and effortless caresser of a cricket ball crossed this latest mountain in his embryonic career.

This first first-class season was a golden summer. The sun shone, the runs flowed, and everyone in New South Wales, it seemed, and especially those in Balmain, had fallen a little in love with this young boy with the dreamy blue eyes, gentle face and balletic talent for batting. He finished with an average of 50 for New South Wales and scored more runs in the Sydney grade aggregates than any other, including five centuries and a further knock four short of a fifth.

His ability to score runs with apparent ease and at a rate bettered by few of his contemporaries showed no sign of abating the following season either, as Archie turned eighteen. Such was his talent and such were the flow of scores, he was picked for the Australian side to tour New Zealand. There were no test matches - New Zealand was yet to be granted that status - but he was now playing alongside his heroes; it was an Australian side that included Bill Ponsford and Bill Woodfull, Charlie Grimmett and Bert Oldfield - regulars of the test team. If Archie had been daunted by this he did not show it.  The runs continued to flow from his bat, including yet another century.

But what of the man he had become? He was undeniably handsome: lean-faced, pale blue eyes and with a gentle disposition. With his Scottish parents, he spoke with a British, rather than an Australian accent. Surrounded by adults since his mid-teens, he was also mature beyond his years, and thoughtful and bright; he loved to read and his letters were always articulate and carefully written. There were aspirations to write and perhaps one day become a cricketing journalist once his playing days were over.   

The Jackson family were close but despite the easy-going nature of his parents, they had brought Archie up to be respectful, polite and above all, modest. In Balmain, he was a hero, known to most, and feted accordingly, something he accepted with bashful gratitude. One of his greatest mentors was Alan Kippax, the Australian batsman and captain of New South Wales, who had singled out Archie from an early age. When Archie had been forced to leave school at fourteen and do his bit to help the family finances, Kippax had found him a job in his sports shop.

Kippax had also introduced Archie to A.B. R. Roche, a grazier from upstate New South Wales who opened the young prodigy's eyes to a world of literature, art and the theatre; for all his love of the game, Archie understood there was more to life than just cricket.  By the age of eighteen, Archie was a well-rounded and charming young man.

He was athletic, too, and in the field had gained a reputation as a fine slip catcher and lithe out-fielder with a whippy, lightning-fast throwing arm. Despite this, throughout his younger years, he had been plagued with ill-health. He had missed games during his final season at junior school and then again during the 1926-1927 season. And he always batted with his shirts rolled up just one turn, directly above the wrists, due to a psoriasis of the skin that troubled him not on his face but on his arms and back. He made sure he always showered privately at the end of a game so that none of his team-mates ever discovered the affliction.

Nonetheless, he was fit and well as he began the 1928-29 season - one in which the England MCC side were once again touring. Many of the cricket correspondents were clamouring for Archie to be called up for his first official test, but he failed in the test trial at the start of the season and despite scoring for New South Wales had to wait for the fourth test match at Adelaide to finally get his chance. He was still only just nineteen.

This was a fine England side, boasting players like Wally Hammond, Douglas Jardine, Maurice Tate and Harold Larwood, the ferocious Nottinghamshire paceman. Also still playing, despite being well into his forties, was the legendary Jack Hobbs. They were also a side that was thrashing an Australian team in transition; by the third test down, the English had won all three and regained the Ashes. With two to play, there was, however, still plenty of Australian pride to play for.

The Adelaide test began on Thursday, 1 February, 1929 with blue skies overhead and a scorching sun. England batted first and scored 334, with Hammond hitting 119 not out, so that it was not until mid-afternoon on the Saturday that Archie strode out to open for Australia alongside Bill Woodfull, a crowd of some 50,000 packed into the ground to watch the boy wonder. Within a matter of a few overs, however, Australia were in crisis at three down for just nineteen runs. Archie had watched all three wickets, including that of his friend and mentor, Alan Kippax, who was yorked for a duck.

Whatever nerves Archie must have been feeling on this momentous occasion, he never showed them, driving Maurice Tate with apparent ease and fending off the pace of Larwood without the slightest sign of concern. There was a brief scare when Tate appealed for a leg before, but he survived and continued to drive through the cover and whip through leg.  Soon, he was joined by Jack Ryder, the Australian captain, who repeatedly told him to 'Stick to it, son,' between overs. Another creamy four through the covers brought up Archie's fifty, and by the end of a sweltering day, he was still there, with Australia now 131-3 and still more than two hundred runs behind.

The following day, another scorcher, he continued where he had left off. Flicking disdainfully through leg, silkily driving through the covers and cutting past point. Ryder was out early, and another young star, Don Bradman, joined him at the crease. By lunch, Archie was on 97, having reached the nineties with a delicate late-cut. A chance to cool down and freshen up and then he was out in the middle again, to face Larwood. Standing in his crease, Archie waited as the paceman reached the end of his long run, turned and began bounding towards him. A whirl of the arm and the dark red ball was hurtling towards him, just outside off stump. Archie's head moved in line, his front foot went forward, and through came the bat and arms, all in perfect balance.  Bat on leather, and the ball was streaking past cover point towards the boundary fence in front of the Members' Stand. He had reached his century and in doing so had become the youngest test centurion - he was still on nineteen and he, remains, to this day, the youngest player ever to score a test century on debut for Australia. While Archie smiled coyly, the packed crowd erupted. Hats were thrown into the air as the spectators got to their feet and cheered and applauded.

Any timidity Archie had shown earlier that day now vanished.  In what seemed like no time at all, he had reached 150 - with a classic leg-cut for three - and was only finally out, leg before, on 164. Like Bethell’s a Sydney, it had been a stunning innings, but one that had helped lift Australia's score past England's. It was not, however, enough, for the home still managed to lose the test by twelve runs, with Archie scoring only 36 in his second innings.  Honour was, however, salvaged in the final test at Melbourne, as the home side finally won and with Archie scoring 30 and 46.

The accolades followed: the palm for the best innings of the series, a set of cut glass from the South Australia Cricket Association, and a public meeting in Balmain Town Hall where he was honoured by the mayor and told he was a credit to his country.  He was famous now, not just locally, but nationally.  Bradman was a hugely exciting prospect, but it was Jackson who was the boy wonder: an outrageous talent and one of the most naturally gifted and beautiful batsmen Australia had ever produced.

With no Australian test matches during their winter, the next opportunity Archie Jackson had to shine was in the test trial of December 1929. His stunning 182 ensured that he was an automatic choice for the 1930 tour to England. After a long and leisurely sea voyage via Tasmania and then Naples in Italy, the Australians reached Dover in early May and soon began the first of some thirty-one first-class fixtures. Archie would score over a thousand runs during the English summer but throughout those long months he was ailing, chronically ill for much of the time. There were coughs and flu-like bouts, which sapped his strength and, on occasion, left him bedridden. Unsurprisingly, it affected his form. There were starts, but in the matches leading up to the first test, he had not done enough, and while there were flashes of genius, the spark and effortless ease with which he had dominated bowlers had gone.  Archie’s batting had become laboured. 

Picked for the third test, he score just one, while Bradman amassed 334. He was dropped for the fourth, then scored a century against Somerset at Taunton, and picked for the fifth, at the Oval, in August. Bradman scored a double-hundred this time, and Archie seventy-three in 311 balls. For a batsman known for his free-scoring nature, this was a markedly slower innings. It was also one in which he had been repeatedly roughed up by Larwood, taking a number of body blows. And by now, the cough that he had been unable to shift had become more pronounced, more audible.

Back in Australia, his health showed no sign of improving, and although he brushed it off and tried to carry on playing with the same intensity as ever, his stamina was sapped. The West Indies toured that Australian summer but after runs in the first test, he had been forced to leave the field through illness on the third day of the Brisbane test, but managed to recover in time for the fourth. A week later, he was once again too ill to play, this time for New South Wales against the tourists. Neither he nor anyone else knew it at the time, but the prodigy, still only twenty-one, had just played his final ever game of first-class cricket.

Nonetheless, for Archie, life had taken something of a turn for the better by the spring of 1931. He was feeling a little better and had fallen in love with a ballet dancer, Phyllis Thomas, from Brisbane. He also felt sufficiently fit to join Alan Kippax’s New South Wales tour of North Queensland and appeared to have returned to his best, scoring six centuries on the trip including a 158 in which he hit the last fifty in ten minutes of furious strokeplay and a fifty not out struck in just eight minutes.  Few had ever seen batting like it. Yet, despite being so far north, the tour had been interrupted by frequent bouts of rain. It had done his health no good at all.

Even so, he was part of the New South Wales team that travelled north to Brisbane for the first match of the new season the following September – even though he was only just recovering from a bout of ‘flu. Among those who had come to watch was Archie’s girlfriend, Phyl, who was alarmed to notice that Archie had not taken to the field with the other New South Wales players. Wondering where he was, she saw Alan Fairfax, one of the NSW players, approach. Archie, it seemed, had coughed up blood, collapsed and been rushed to hospital.

It was now clear that he was suffering from full-blown tuberculosis. A stint in a sanatorium in the Blue Mountains was his immediate sentence after his release from hospital. Bored and frustrated, he frequently absconded, turning up at home or at friends’ houses unannounced. Nor was there much sign of long-term improvement; the 1931-32 season was lost to him. So too was that of 1932-33. There were glimpses – small signs of brief recovery, but then came an all-too inevitable relapse. Early in February 1933, having moved to Brisbane for both the warmer air and to be with Phyl, he felt sufficiently improved to play a game of cricket, but had suffered another collapse and had been rushed to Ingarfield Private Hospital. The prognosis now took a dramatic turn for the worse: the TB was rampant in both lungs and he was sinking fast. Phyl and Archie had become engaged: tragic, ill-feted lovers who were destined never to share a life together, for despite her bedside vigil, it was clear that Archie was slipping away. Telegrams were sent to his parents to come quickly. His childhood friend and fellow New South Wales and Australia cricketer, Bill Hunt, also flew up to see him, sitting by his bed and reading him the cricket reports. ‘I want to get back, Bill,’ Archie rasped.

He never would, however.  On 15 February, Archie fell into a deep sleep. Just a quarter of an hour after midnight the following morning, his short life was over.  He was just twenty-three.

His body was brought back to Sydney by train and when the coffin arrived at the Central Railway Station, the Australian XI were there to form a guard of honour. The casket was then taken to his parents’ home and from there began a four-mile funeral procession to the Field of Mars cemetery. ‘The funeral passed through densely packed streets,’ reported the Sydney Morning Herald. ‘As it went by Gladesville Park, a number of young lads were playing Jackson’s favourite game. As soon as the cortege was sighted, played ceased, and was not resumed for a time.’

The pallbearers were all drawn from the Australian team, Bradman, Woodfull, and Ponsford among them.  The nation, and the entire cricketing world, seemed utterly stunned, almost disbelieving in their grief. It seemed so impossible that such a talent, such a graceful, elegant, and beautiful young batsman had been lost to the world. ‘It was hard to believe,’ wrote Harold Larwood, who was in Australia playing the Bodyline series at the time. ‘We knew that our loss was Australia’s too.  Privileged were those who had known him.’

All too briefly, Archie Jackson had lit up the cricketing world. Kind, generous, and self-effacing in character, he had even sent Larwood a telegram of congratulations on his Ashes bowling feats just days before he died. On the pitch, his batting was something close to artistry, and it is one of the game’s enduring tragedies that the cricketing world was denied more. Looking at the photographs of those seven shots played during his remarkable 182, it is impossible, even all these years later, not to feel a pang of wistfulness.

With the Sydney test over, I took the chance to head across the harbour from Bangalore to Balmain on one of the amazingly efficient ferries that criss-cross Sydney Harour. Balmain used to be a distinctly working class area back in the day, habituated by men like Archie Jackson’s father, who worked at the various wharfs and docks that marked this small peninsula of Sydney.  Now, though, it has become considerably gentrified - a place of leafy terraced streets, detached houses and lazy coffee shops. The sea is never far away. As I walked down Ferdinand Street barely a soul ventured nor a calm rumbled by. All was quiet calm.  Number 14, where Archie and his family lived, is still there: a narrow terraced two-storey house with a small balcony on the first floor. There’s no blue plaque, no marking or indication that a great cricketer once lived there.

The street drops gently down a hill towards the sea but before the water is what is now called Birchgrove Oval, the same cricket ground where Jackson played as a boy and as a teenage prodigy. I’ve seen old photos of this ground and to be honest, it’s barely changed and remains a beautiful, charming place to play this most wonderful of sports. It was not hard to picture Archie and his friends playing here in what was another constant of the game: youngsters who have become bewitched by cricket will always find places to obsessively obsessively.

I was glad to have seen it, and happy to have been able to picture Archie there, his shirtsleeves rolled up just the once. Ever since I learned of this habit of his, it’s one I’ve adopted myself whenever I play; my own personal nod to this tragic hero of the game. Cricket - and sport - is always punctuated by moments of  brilliance and triumph as well as failure, by chance and opportunities taken but also missed. It was a treat to watch Jacob Bethell announce himself here in Sydney and I’ll now be following his career with even greater interest. But it’s also been good to pause and consider another young extraordinary talent, to search out some of his old haunts and to ponder what might have been had Archie Jackson been living today.

title: GOOD NEIGHBOR
html:
It was a cold, windy, grey day in Washington DC on 4th March 1933, the day Franklin D. Roosevelt was sworn in as President of the United States.  Wearing a morning suit and top hat, Roosevelt was escorted gingerly the rostrum, at the east front of the Capitol, by his son, James.  Having been struck down by polio over ten years earlier, Roosevelt had been paralysed from the waist down and could only walk with the greatest of difficulties and by strapping metal callipers to his legs.  Although it was a fifty yard walk, however, he had been determined to make it and not begin his presidency from a wheelchair. And make it he did, albeit a little stiffly.

Having completed his solemn oath he then turned to the crowd of more than 150,000 facing the Capitol and tens of millions more listening on the radio, and began his inaugural address.  The United States had been reeling since the dark days of October 1929; until then, while the rest of modern world struggled to overcome the ravages - both economic and physical - of the  Great War of 1914-18, America had become rich.  The 1920s had been a time of astonishing growth, with the advent of the mass-market automobile and plentiful American oil.  Towns had grown and spread, so too had roads as America boomed.  There was plenty of work, lots of money to be made, and with it came credit - too much credit.  Banks lacking legislation were lending more than was in their vaults and so, when the bubble burst with the Wall Street Crash in October 1929, the collapse was both considerable and protracted.

The United States had wanted to turn inwards, and pursue a more isolationist strategy but it was the richest nation in the world.  The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of May 1930 was designed to protect the US market but had catastrophic consequences around the world: a global trade war was no way to get any nation out of the economic mire of the Great Depression, least of all the United States itself.

As he stood addressing the nation, Roosevelt was very aware that a dramatic change of tack was needed if America was to re-emerge as the economic powerhouse it was destined to become once more.  It was time, he told the American people, to speak the truth, both frankly and boldly.  Their great nation would revive and prosper.  ‘So, first of all,’ he said in his patrician, East Coast, tones, ‘let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.’ As he went on to point out, plenty remained on their doorstep and the perils they faced now were not as terrifying as those of their forebears.  What was needed was a sense of national effort and plenty of action right away.  People needed to get back to work; new laws needed to be put in place to ensure no crash such as the one they had experienced could ever happen again, and he intended to get going right away.

There was, however, another, critical, pledge he made. ‘In the field of world policy,’ he added, ‘I would dedicate this Nation to the policy of the good neighbor – the neighbor who resolutely respects himself and, because he does so, respects the rights of others – the neighbor who respects his obligations and respects the sanctity of his agreements in and with a world of neighbors.’

This was a firm signal not only of Roosevelt’s future path with regard to foreign policy but also his own world view.  To his core, FDR was an internationalist, despite having won the election on an isolationist ticket.  And while a new President brought renewed hope, his inauguration came at a time of further collapse. There was two thirds less money in America than there had been before the Crash, more banks were collapsing and a fresh panic convulsed the country in February 1933.  Most expected Roosevelt to do a worse job than his predecessor, Herbert Hoover, the majority of Americans looked to him and his new presidency with little confidence.

Yet, Roosevelt’s first Hundred Days brought first, a sense of real hope, then renewed trust in their executive leader, and with it, a rise in confidence.  Roosevelt believed himself to be a man of vision and destiny – just as in Germany the new Chancellor, Adolf Hitler, also believed himself to be.  The great difference, however, was that Roosevelt had a profound desire to help steer America towards a better future, one that he felt certain he could achieve.  And he wasted absolutely no time.  In five days, a banking bill was ready and rushed through in just eight hours of debate.  Eight days into his presidency, he broadcast his first Fireside Chat on the radio.  Radios were still something comparatively new, but FDR became a master of this new form of media.  He had a calming, soothing voice, and now spoke to the nation like a family friend, using terms and analogies so that everyone could clearly understand what he was saying.  First up, he announced the Federal Banks would be reopening the following day and that thanks to his Emergency Banking Act, cash held there would be safe.  The day after, deposits exceeded withdrawals, stock prices rose by 15% and $1 billion returned to the vaults over the ensuing weeks. It was the start of what became the New Deal.

While Roosevelt was overturning prohibition and the Smoot-Hawley tariff act and also introducing a raft of new public works initiatives and social services for the first time, he also never lost sight of the pledge he’d made during his first inaugural address to forge a Good Neighbor Policy towards the rest of the Americas and especially Latin America.

The United States’ relations with Latin America had been bullying, overbearing, and, frankly, imperialist in outlook. The Monroe Doctrine, articulated by President James Monroe back in 1823, claimed that the Americas were for Americans only and that the United States would no longer tolerate European influence and interference.  In reality, however, it meant the US dominating its neighbours with growing aggression and condescension. Latin Americans were widely perceived to be racially inferior, handicapped by a succession of authoritarian, corrupt and backward leaders, and with a climate not conducive to progress. From the late 1890s under President McKinley, through the presidency of Teddy Roosevelt to even the progressive Woodrow Wilson, US policy had been to regularly intervene.  McKinley’s war with Spain in 1898 saw American troops invade Cuba as well as take the Philippines in South-East Asia.  Theodore Roosevelt then introduced the so-called ‘Roosevelt Corollary’, announcing that the United States could intervene in the affairs of Latin American countries if they thought such intervention was needed.  In reality, this was a licence to flex military muscles if the US felt its debts were not being paid swiftly or if American business interests were being threatened, or access to resources impeded.

And the United States repeatedly did apply the Corollary.  Wilson sent troops into Mexico in 1914, to Haiti the following year, the Dominican Republic in 1916, to Cuba in 1917 and repeatedly again in Mexico.  The later World War II general, George S. Patton, for example, led the first ever US motorised operation during the Pancho Villa Expedition into Mexico in 1916.  For much of Wilson’s administration, American troops also occupied Nicaragua, having installed a president of their choice who would continue to sign treaties favourable to the United States.  Americans convinced themselves they were brining modernity, prosperity and civilization to these backward folks, but they were kidding no-one.

Nor was it just military intervention but also financial ‘dollar diplomacy.’ Senate hearings that began in 1933 to investigate the lending practices of New York’s financiers during the 1920s revealed shocking levels of greed and corruption associated with Wall Street loans to South America.

FDR was now determined to pursue an entirely different and far more progressive and enlightened path.  At the Montevideo Convention in December 1933, Cordell Hull, Roosevelt’s Secretary of State, backed a declaration that, ‘No state has the right to intervene in the internal or external affairs of another.’ That same month, FDR also backed up the declaration.  ‘The definite policy of the United States from now on,’ he announced, ‘is one opposed to armed intervention.’ In quick order, US Marines were withdrawn from Haiti, and the Platt Amendment overturned an aggressive intervention treaty with Cuba originally signed in 1903.  At an inter-America conference in Buenos Aires in December 1936, FDR effectively made his debut on the international stage, and used his speech to promote democracy and higher living standards throughout Latin America. ‘Men and women,’ he said, ‘blessed with political freedom, willing to work and able to find work, rich enough to maintain their families and to educate their children, contented with their lot in life and on terms of friendship with their neighbors will defend themselves to the utmost but will never consent to take up arms for a war of conquest.’ This was Roosevelt’s vision for a better world in a nutshell. Democracy would help to improved living standards, which would lead to greater political stability and, in turn, peace.  A peaceful, stable Latin America would be easier to trade with than one in turmoil.  This in turn would benefit the United States, both in terms of exports and imports.

Two issues were now coalescing in FDR’s mind: that the rise of authoritarianism posed a threat not just in Europe but also the free world, and that an advanced form of progressive democracy, championed by the United States, could and should be promulgated globally. A progressive democracy that eschewed imperialist ambitions, that rejected oppression.  A form of democracy that offered greater economic as well as political equality.  Greater prosperity would lead to greater political stability.  Greater political stability would help the agents of peace.  They were all connected.  These were themes he had also raised six months earlier, in Philadelphia, on his nomination for a second term. ‘I cannot, with candor, tell you that all is well with the world,’ he told hist audience. ‘Clouds of suspicion, tides of ill-will and intolerance gather darkly in many places.  In our own land we enjoy indeed a fullness of life greater than that of most nations.  But the rush of modern civilization itself has raised for us new difficulties, new problems which must be solved if we are to preserve to the United States the political and economic freedom for which Washington and Jefferson planned and fought.’  He called upon his fellows to follow a higher moral purpose, in which every man had equality of rights but also of the market place. ‘Here in America,’ he told his audience, ‘we are waging a great and successful war. It is not alone a war against want and destitution and economic demoralization. It is more than that; it is a war for the survival of democracy. We are fighting to save a great and precious form of government for ourselves and for the world.’

A touch of political melodrama, perhaps, but he was quite right.  Dark forces were massing, and the world would need a man of vision like Roosevelt. By the time he was sworn in a second time, having carried all but two states, another major war was once again looming.
excerpt: When the USA Had a More Benign Approach to Its Neighbours
author: James Holland

title: THE COLOSSEUM OF CRICKET
html:
I’m sitting high in that vast concrete temple to sport, the Melbourne Cricket Ground. Above, the sky is cloudlessly azure blue after a cloudy and chilly first couple of days here in town. Below, is the immaculate chequered green bowl of the cricket ground itself, the dun strip at its heart and around which are dotted the white-dressed players. Cricket has been played here since 1853; the first test match between England and Australia back in 1877. It’s obviously changed a fair bit since then, not least in the immense scale of the stands. Yesterday, on the first day of the 4th test match in this current series of the oldest rivalry in sport, there was a record attendance: over 93,000. Blimey!

And what a day it was. I’m currently reading Ian Leslie’s fabulous book about the Beatles, or rather, about the songwriting duo of Paul McCartney and John Lennon, John & Paul: A Love Story in Songs. These two clearly were both geniuses, two of England’s most talented-ever sons and exports. The same cannot be said for the current England cricket team, although Joe Root has unquestionably been touched with greatness and Harry Brook has a touch of cricketing genius about him. Brooky’s a bit like Lennon-McCartney in 1964: already brilliant and different but not yet fully matured. Here’s hoping.

Subscribe

Leslie’s book takes different Lennon-McCartney songs and dissects them, placing them in their wider context, explaining their complexities both brilliantly and with literary panache. And utterly absorbing his treatment is too. I’ve got to A Day in the Life and I Am A Walrus, both surreal, wistful, and in turns joyful and tragic. These songs were heavily influenced by the amount of drugs both John and Paul were using at the time, John especially. Watching yesterday’s play it was as though test cricket was also on its very own acid trip: lots that was familiar but definitely not test cricket as we know it. Twenty wickets in a day; England’s shortest test match innings since 1904. Back then, pitches really were rough, but not these days, not even with 2mm more grass left on the track than normal. We were sitting right at the very top of this enormous collosseum, up there with the gods, and right behind the bowler’s arm in the Shane Warne Stand. The ball clearly moved about a bit but not that much. Try playing at Chalke Valley CC in the first weekend of May! The ball wobbles all over the place! So, goodness knows what got into these elite cricketers on this Boxing Day here at the MCG.

The play was frenetic, mad, and so was the crowd. Outside the ground there are statues of former Australian sporting heroes, and not least Bill Ponsford and Sir Donald Bradman, men who graced the game either side of the Second World War. A different age, of course. Back then, the aspirations for masculinity were effortless charm, suave urbanity and an ability to dance well. Now, that aspiration is to drink vast amounts of beer, grow amply around the girth and - at the MCG at any rate - eat tepid fried food with your hands out of disposable cardboard. Stained, after-eaten cartons and plastic cups are dropped under the consumer’s seat. It’s revolting, really, but now totally normal behaviour.

Back in Ponsford and Bradman’s day, players would swap flannels at the end of the day’s play for a sharp suit and recomb their hair. Spectators, too, would be wearing suits, ties and sports jackets and the ladies elegant frocks. Progress has been made since; we’re no longer so buttoned up. Back then, 99% of spectators would be Australian; in today’s modern world, with the ease of air travel, I reckoned at least 20% were England supporters who had travelled halfway round the world to watch this brand of amphetamine test match cricket. England and Australia were easy to distinguish: one tribe mostly wearing yellow, the other tribe white and shades of blue. The taunts were tribal and I’d say, on balance, that the England supporters out-sang the Aussies. Well, ‘singing’ is probably over-stating it, but a victory, I suppose, of sorts.

In other regards, the cricket-loving male here at the MCG was much of a muchness and a sign of how much sartorial standard’s have slipped since Bradman’s day. Some wore amusing Hawaiian shirts, usually mocking the opposition. Most wore sporting tops of some kind. Shorts - not flannels! - are now de rigeur, along with the paunch, facial hair of some kind, and tattoos. In our modernity, we’ve regressed. Earrings, nose studs, hoops, bracelets, neck chains, all adorn the modern sport-loving fan in a way that would have been unthinkable eighty years ago. If blokes turned up wearing woad body paint, no-one would bat an eye.

In a further homage to carboard and instant food, KFC are handing out fried chicken buckets everywhere you turn. These are not full of finger lickin’ fried chicken, however. They’re empty, and predominantly green in colour and have an image of the Ashes urn on them as well as the acronyms ‘KFC’ and ‘FLG.’ What’s the purpose of these? To put on your head, of course! Why? Why would anyone want to put a cardboard KFC bucket on their head, even one with a faint nod to cricket? It’s a mystery but countless among the 93,000-plus were doing so.

In fact, the only person I saw yesterday looking as urbane as the cricketer of yesteryear was Stuart Broad, former England cricketing hero and now cricketing broadcaster. He was down at the boundary’s edge issuing words of wisdom for Channel 9 before the start of play. Broad has the kind of suavity and charm of which David Niven would have been proud and looked refreshingly urbane. ‘He’s very good looking,’ said my daughter, who bizarrely doesn’t seem attracted by balding but otherwise hairy, ink-festooned and overweight blokes drinking beer, whether whiter versions from Blighty or home-grown here in Autralia. What is she like?

The cricket continued at its breathless pace. Josh Tongue, also looking as though he was from an earlier age and about to break into a rendition of YMCA, helped skittle out Australia for next to nothing. He’s superb - oozing joie de vivre and excitement to be playing in this monstrous stadium - and hope was desperately forcing its way through the deep, inner bastions of pessimism that told me that if Australia had been all out of 152, then England would probably ensure they scored even fewer. I so wanted to England to be just one or two wickets down by the close of play. Do that and they would then be comfortably placed to win this fourth test match. I didn’t want the England team to be weak men. I wanted them to recognise the advantage they held over the old-enemy and ruthlessly take advantage.

Of course, it wasn’t to be. Harry Brook played with that touch of genius he has, ambling about and smacking 90 mph deliveries nonchalantly for six as though he were playing a village beer match; but it didn’t last. Once he was out, the rest quickly followed. England all out for 110.

The crushing sense of disppointment sat on my shoulders like a dead weight. Why should I care? Why should anyone? It’s not a war. No-one’s dying. It’s just sport. It does matter, though, for reasons that are hard to articulate, and here I am, back at the MCG, on Day 2, with Australia already looking like they’re in the ascendency, but my tendrils of hope still trying to work their way to the surface…

title: Don Blakeslee - Legendary WW2 Fighter Pilot
html:
One of my great heroes is the fighter pilot, Don Blakeslee, a man who flew more combat missions and fought the Luftwaffe longer than any other American bar none. He chalked up well over 1,000 combat hours - forty-five solid days’ worth - and flew the best part of 500 missions; most pilots were sent home after completing around 200. He flew with the Canadians in the RAF and then with the Eagle Squadrons, then became Exeuctive Officer - second-in-command - of the newly created 4th Fighter Group in England in the autumn of 1942 and then its CO, leading them during Big Week, on D-Day and commanding the longest-range fighter mission of the war, to Russia, in June, before finally being grounded - very much against his wishes - in September 1944. One of the 4th Fighter Group’s ground crew looked at the Mustangs lined up one grey and misty morning and commented, ‘I guess Colonel Don must have been born under one of those planes.’ He outflew everyone and took the notion of ‘leading from the front’ to new levels. By the time he was done he was still only twenty-seven but had become one of the greatest fighter combat leaders of both the RAF and USAAF. He was, quite simply, a force of nature: charismatic, clever, outspoken, profane, aggressive but also self-effacing and the ultimate team player. Ferociously good looking with dark hair and piercing blue eyes, Blakeslee was a man who imposed his spirit and personal magnetism on all those who came into contact with him. He was, quite simply, an inspiration.

Like a lot of those who volunteered to fly at the start of the war, Blakeslee had fallen for flying as a boy in Ohio when he’d been taken to see the Cleveland Air Races. Seduced by the glamour, excitement and thrill of this still new form of travel, he and a friend worked at the Diamond Alkali Company in Fairport Harbor and saved up until they could afford a Piper J-3 Cub. Not long after, however, his friend pranged it and although was able to walk away, the Cub was a wreck. Broke and with no further prospects of flying, Blakeslee then joined the Royal Canadian Air Force in Ontario in August 1940, promising his mother he would only ever take on a role as an instructor. It had meant resigning his commission in the US Army Reserve but with America not yet in the war, Blakeslee was impatient not just to get flying again but also to get into the action. He had never had any intention of honouring the promise he had made to his mother.

Subscribe

Gaining his coveted wings in March 1941, he had then been shipped over to Britain to complete his operational training unit on Spitfires and then to join 401 Canadian Squadron at Biggin Hill, south of London. Over the course of the next year, Blakeslee flew 200 hours, mostly fighter sweeps over France. The pickings were comparatively slim and he only shot down a couple of enemy aircraft in that time but by the beginning of July 1942 he was tour expired and told he was to be taken off frontline flying to finally become an instructor instead. By this time, there were three ‘Eagle’ Squadrons - American fighter squadrons within the RAF. Blakeslee had always rather looked down his nose at them. ‘They were punks,’ he said, and preferred sticking with the polyglot unit of Canadians, Brits and others. However, the United States was now in the war and the Eighth Air Force was being created and would be based in England. It was agreed that the Eagle Squadrons would be transferred lock-stock and barrel to the USAAF to become part of VIII Fighter Command. Blakeslee was told that if he joined 133 Squadron he could continue flying. Punks they may have been in Blakeslee’s eyes but it was better to be with punks and still fly combat missions than to languish in the backwaters as an instructor.

Blakeslee duly joined 133 Squadron as a flight commander in the second week of July 1942. Everyone knew the switch to the USAAF was about to happen but they were still part of the RAF when disaster struck on 26 September that same year. Escorting some B-17 bombers to Morlaix in Brittany in France, they ran into heavy cloud but also a 100 mph tail wind, which caused them to fly far further than planned and beyond the range of their fuel tanks. Only one of twelve managed to make it back, and he crash-landed. The other eleven were all lost - four killed, six taken prisoner and one escaping on the run. Although there were double that number of pilots in the squadron, it felt as if the guts had been ripped out of it as result of the losses and made worse because the CO, Red McColpin had transferred to the United States Army Air Force that very same day. A number of new pilots turned up the following day, but the beating heart of the squadron had gone. In truth, the squadron had always been something of an outlier, for while 71 and 121 had been formed first the previous summer, and were based together at Debden, south of Cambridge, 133 Squadron was the last to be created and were based at a satellite airfield at Great Sampford. A few Nissen huts and a large grass field was all 133 Squadron’s base had to offer. Somehow, the squadron had to be picked up, given a shake, and rapidly find its sense of esprit de corps. The man given the responsibility for achieving this was Don Blakeslee, who had not been on the flying slate that fateful day.

His approach, on his first evening in charge, was to forego any speeches but instead stand on the bar in the Mess and announce that the drinks were on him. ‘He was a great believer in the RAF tradition of hard drinking and high living,’ noted Jim Goodson, who joined 133 Squadron at that time and who became a mainstay of the 4th Fighter Group too, ‘and never permitting either of them to interfere with constant readiness to fly, and fly well, at any time.’ At well after one in the morning, by which time the pilots were mostly semi-conscious, Blakeslee announced they all needed to be ready to fly at 6am.

It was usual for fighter planes to take off in pairs or, at a push, in fours, but that next morning Blakeslee ordered them to take off together – all sixteen of them – in formation. After the spontaneous gasp of horror, Blakeslee yelled at them to move and they all headed out to their waiting Spitfires. And somehow, they all managed to do exactly as he’d demanded. ‘Tighten up!’ yelled Blakesleee. ‘Let’s show these bastards!’

The bastards in question were the other Eagle Squadrons at nearby Debden, and sure enough, before most of the 133 Squadron pilots had had a chance to think too much about what was happening, the squadron was flying in perfect formation at five hundred feet. And right over Debden. By the time they landed back down again, everyone was talking excitedly with a palpable sense breathless pride. ‘That evening,’ added Goodson, ‘Blakeslee wasn’t the only 133 pilot with the belligerent swagger.’

Soon after, the Eagle Squadrons were transferred into the US Eighth Air Force, and with new squadron numbers too: 133 Squadron became 336 Squadron in the newly formed 4th Fighter Group, and the old RAF rondels were scrubbed out and repainted with US Army Air Force stars. Blakeslee had been happy to keep his Spitfires and was none too amused when, the following April, he was told they would be re-equipping with Thunderbolts. On 15 April, 1943, Blakeslee was leading the squadron on a ramrod over Belgium when they spotted a couple of FW 190s. These German pilots dived out of the way and the the squadron followed from a height of around 20,000 feet. By the time Blakeslee pulled out and blew one of the Focke-Wulfs to pieces, he was at just 500 feet and almost flying into Ostend. It was, however, the first recorded victory ever in a P-47 and it was entirely appropriate that this victory had been achieved by a Fourth Fighter Group pilot and by Blakeslee in particular. Back at base, Goodson, who before the mission had tried to persuade Blakeslee of its virtues, said to him, ‘I told you the Jug could out-dive them!’

‘Well, it damn well ought to be able to dive,’ Blakeslee replied, ‘it sure as hell can’t climb.’

Not long after, Blakeslee was made Excutive Officer of the entire Fighter Group, although only on the condition he could keep flying – and that meant combat flying. ‘We love fighting,’ he once said. ‘Fighting is a grand sport.’ He continued to love drinking too. When the mess secretary complained the pilots were smashing too many glasses, Blakeslee replied, ‘Good show. Shows their spirit.’

Although Blakeslee’s own personal score was gradually mounting, he never painted swastikas on his fighter plane like most others, and never gave his personal mount a name or any kind of decorations: just ‘WD C’ on the fuselage. Unlike many pilots, he was not superstitious either. ‘That’s kid stuff,’ he said. Nor did he get much better at shooting. ‘Hell, I can’t hit the side of a barn,’ he told a reporter. ‘There’s no sport in it for a guy who can shoot straight. The sport comes when somebody like me has to pull up behind ’em and start shooting to find out where the bullets are going.’ In a dogfight, he was everywhere – twisting, climbing, rolling and bellowing and blinding. Blakeslee swore like a trooper. But first with 336 Squadron and then with the 4th Fighter Group, he was venerated as a fighting air leader par excellence – so much so that by the fall of 1943, his fame had spread throughout the Eighth. One time, he came back with no less than 71 bullet holes in his plane.

In many ways, Blakelsee was the embodiment of the spirit of the Fourth, possessed with an obsessive love of flying combined with a stubborn single-mindedness and an unshakeable thirst for adventure. He was once asked whether he ever felt like quittting. ‘The first time Isaw a plane falling in flames, I was hard hit,’ he replied. ‘It was a good friend of mine. What am I doing here? I asked myself. That’s the first and last time that’s happened to me. You miss a man when he goes, but it doesn’t affect you in the same way.’

As a combat leader in the air, he was without match. In a melee, he would be everywhere, blaspheming, bellowing, warning and always able to maintain a very clear understanding of what was going on and where the rest of his pilots were. Once, over Berlin, he was given command of all the fighter planes accompanying the bombers, which amounted to 800 aircraft. He was also peerless in terms of his energy and inexhaustible zest, which he managed to maintain despite often spending late nights in the mess; Blakeslee adhered to old RAF tradition of fighting hard, playing hard and enjoying a drink. Combat flying was incredibly draining, both physically and mentally, but not for Blakeslee. ‘You don’t think about pilot fatigue,’ he said, ‘as long as you’ve still got your enthusiasm.’ Somehow, this never seemed to dim with Blakeslee.

In December 1943, the newly arrived 354th Fighter Group were the first to be given the new Merlin-powered P-51 Mustangs and Blakeslee was sent over to Boxted to give these new boys a lesson in fighter tactics. Blakesleee loved what he saw of the Mustang and immediately it was the plane for him - a thoroughbred like the Spitfire but powerful like the Thunderbolt. The Mustang was everything he wanted from a fighter plane: sleek, highly manoeuvrable, extremely fast and long-range. As soon as he took command of the 4th Fighter Group, Blakeslee began furiously lobbying General Bill Kepner, the commander of VIII Fighter Command to allow the 4th Fighter Group to be the first to convert to P-51s. Kepner was dubiou, however, because his fighters had never been busier and he didn’t want to lose one of his most highly prized fighter groups to retraining. Blakeslee’s response was typical. ‘How much time can you give us to switch, sir?’ No more than 24 hours was Kepner’s reply. ‘General,’ Blakeslee told him, ‘give me the Mustangs and I give you my word. I’ll have them in combat in 24 hours. I promise!’ Of course, the entire group was ready in that time. It was entirely unprecedented but Blakeslee repaid the faith Kepner had placed in him and his men.

There were fundamentals to fighter tactics: use height, the sun, speed and manoeuvrability to your advantage. Never fly straight and level for more than a second or two in the combat zone. Keep watching all the time. Flying needed to be instinctive and based on muscle memory, so the brain could concentrate entirely on shooting the enemy and saving your own skin. ‘Goody,’ Blakeslee once said to James Goodson, one of his squadron commanders, ‘why do they talk so much about strategy and tactics? Hell, what you do depends on what’s happening at that moment. What good’s a strategy when you’ve got three 109s on your ass?’ Blakeslee put fighter strategy down to seven words: “Find the enemy and shoot him down.” Blakeslee was fortunate in that the moment he took command of the 4th Fighter Group in January 1944, the Mighty Eighth had a new commander in General Jimmy Doolittle, a man who believed every bit as much as Blakeslee that aggression was vital for his fighters and that they should be given every latitude to operate to the best advantages of the machine. That meant abandoning any earlier notions of close escorting bombers and instead determinedly pursuing the enemy fighters as hard as possible: in the air, on the ground, any way they could. Doolittle and Kepner had the wit to allow their group and squadron leaders the freedom to use their initiative and skills as they saw fit. It was a form of air combat mission command, to use a more modern military term: give the commanders the objective but allow them to achieve any way they thought fit. It allowed Blakeslee, for one, to flourish, and with it, the 4th Fighter Group.

On 21 June, 1944, the Eighth Air Force needed its fighters to escort bombers on a new concept: Operation FRANTIC, a long-range shuttle mission. three-leg shuttle: first to Poltava in Russia, then to Italy, and then back to England again. It was a 1,600 mile epic just to Poltava and needless to say, command of this long-range mission was given to Don Blakeslee. The plan was for the bombers to hammer a synthetic fuel plant at Ruhland in eastern Germany, refuel and rearm in the Soviet Union, then fly south to Italy, join forces with the Fifteenth Air Force there, then bomb Budapest, and then back to England. Armed with sixteen different maps, Blakeslee got them to Russia and then on to Lucera in Italy. Over Budapest they ran into one of the greatest Luftwaffe fighter groups, JG52, which included the top three fighters aces of all time. For once, the Mustangs were outnumbered but Blakeslee still added to his score. In what was arguably one of the greatest dogfights of the war, the 4th Fighter Group more than held their own. What’s more, he got almost all of them back home again. How successful the shuttle raids of Operation FRANTIC were has been debated but they proved that no part of the air over the Third Reich was safe from Allied planes.

Blakeslee was the last of the original combat leaders of the Eagle Squadrons to be flying when he was finally grounded in September 1944. Many of his old fellows were now dead, or POWs or had long since been rotated back to the States. By the time he was done, the 4th Fighter Group had already nearly shot down a thousand confirmed enemy aircraft and had passed that score by the war’s end. They were a maverick unit led by a brilliant, inspirational and maverick commander, who had forged this famous unit in his own spirit. That in turned had been forged during the days of the Eagle Squadrons and the experience of fighting with the RAF and which was carried over and developed in the celebrated 4th Fighter Group. It was fitting, too, that they ended up flying the P-51, a fighter commissioned by the British and which, once married with the genius American-designed airframe with the brilliant British-designed Rolls-Royce Merlin, created arguably the most decisive aircraft of the entire war.

He chalked up well over 1,000 combat hours - forty-five solid days’ worth - and flew the best part of 500 missions; most pilots were sent home after completing around 200. He flew with the Canadians in the RAF and then with the Eagle Squadrons, then became Exeuctive Officer - second-in-command - of the newly created 4th Fighter Group in
