title: US Tariffs & the Road to World War II
html:
The United States had spent the 1920s getting drunk on illegal hooch but also on money.  That all came to end, however, on 29 October, 1929.  By the time the Wall Street stock exchange closed at 3pm pm on Black Tuesday, 810 billion dollars had been wiped from the US market, which was twice the amount of currency in circulation in America at the time.  It was an economic catastrophe of unprecedented proportions with some of the biggest companies in the country collapsing.  A generation lost their savings; people who had been millionaires the week before found themselves without a dime.  There was the faintest of recoveries but then the slide continued, down and down.  The shares of US Steel, one of the single largest companies in the country, went from $262 a share before the Crash to just $22 by 1932.  Over 100,000 businesses were made bankrupt, banks across the country collapsed and unemployment rose from 1.6 million people  before the disaster to 14 million by 1933 – which equated to 25% of the working population.

The days of credit were over with all confidence in the security of stocks and shares shattered.  Because so much of the wealth that had been generated was effectively debt, there was no longer enough cash in circulation.  Wages couldn’t be paid, bills couldn’t be paid, loans couldn’t be honoured.  Building projects were halted, consumers stopped spending, and the heady years of boom and excess came to a halt as sudden as if they had crashed into a wall of concrete.

President Herbert Hoover desperately tried stop the rot, urging business leaders not to lower wages or halt orders and trying to give the economy the confidence shot it so desperately needed. Briefly, in early 1930, after the Federal Reserve cut interest rates, and Congress agreed a bail-out of $100 million, the market rallied.  Then came an act of astonishing short-sightedness.  Two Congressmen, Senator Reed Smoot and Representative Willis C. Hawley, had proposed, back in May 1929, yet another tariff act on industrial and agricultural goods to specifically help American farmers; this had been in response to an election pledge Hoover had made while running for President the previous year.  It was well intentioned and meant to safeguard jobs within the US, but it should have been halted in its tracks the moment the Crash brought economic disaster.  It was not, however.  The House had earlier passed the act, but the Senate continued to debate it until March 1930 and rather than swill it down the sink with the dishwater, the Smoot-Hawley Tariff narrowly passed by 44 votes to 42.  Protectionism, however, was not going to work.

In shocked horror over a thousand economists signed a petition imploring Hoover to veto this craven piece of legislation.  Yet, although Hoover was personally against the tariff, he was bludgeoned and coerced by a combination of cabinet members, Republicans and businessmen and so felt compelled to sign it into law.  The consequences were just as the thousand-plus economists had warned.  Confidence in the President’s ability to weather the crisis plummeted making him a lame-duck and worse, showing to the rest of the world that the world’s richest nation could not provide the vision, rationality and clear-thinking so desperately needed in this calamitous moment in history.

Already, the economic depression had spread around the globe, and just as the United States had rejected the League of Nations in 1919, so it once again rejected the chance to work together with other international partners. It was all very well looking inward, but America was an international player whether it wanted to be or not and already the richest country in the world.  Working with, not against, other nations at this moment of world crisis was what was urgently needed, especially since it had been prompted by their own reckless irresponsibility in the first place. The Wall Street Crash, like previous such calamities, had been entirely avoidable. Hiking up tariffs even further was what the world did not need.  In France, for example, US tariffs imposed on its Great War ally rose on average to a cripplingly high 38%.  Predictably, other countries and trading partners responded in kind, raising their own tariffs in response.  Any chance of stimulating the US economy by foreign demand had been dealt a hammer blow.  All around the world, commodity prices continued to tumble.

The consequences were incredibly dangerous not just for global prosperity but also for security.  Economic collapse prompted political collapse not just in Germany but in many other countries besides.  In Brazil and Argentina, confidence in democracy was wrecked and authoritarian autocrats seized power.  In Europe, the crisis peaked in 1931 when Austria’s Creditanstalt Bank in Vienna collapsed followed by the Darmstädter und Nationalbank in Germany.  One bank after another began selling sterling in a vain attempt to increase their gold reserves.  This led to a run on the pound; Britain tried to maintain the exchange rate but between mid-July and September suffered cash withdrawals of more than £200 million. With the Bank of England’s gold reserves now running perilously low, the government decided, once again, to abandon the gold standard, as it had during the last war.  In truth, Britain was in a better position than most, partly because sterling still remained such a dominant currency despite this tumble, but also because it had the resources of the empire and extra-imperial assets as well as the mutual support of the Dominions. Even so, sterling lost a quarter of its value in 1931.  Having become rich thanks to its enduring support of free trade, Britain also now imposed a general tariff of 10% in March 1932, followed swiftly by a protectionist deal with its Dominions.

This was the harsh reality of tariffs in an expanding and progressive world: they escalated rapidly and worked only to reduce the flow of capital and elasticity of economies.  The Great Depression in Europe continued into the following year, 1932.  France initially rowed the storm a little better.  This was largely because the franc was already undervalued before the worst struck the rest of Europe, and because it already had protectionist measures in place for its farmers and food production. Yet France could not avoid the slide either.  The tariffs ensured its export market shrunk dramatically; even in 1936, exports were half what they had been in 1929, while production only returned to the levels of the late twenties by 1939.  One by one, a succession of French coalition governments fell; in all, there were no less than thirteen and eighteen prime ministers between 1930 and 1939. Political instability, social unrest, the long shadow of the Great War, tariffs imposed by the US and others and a refusal to further devalue the franc, all combined to ensure France had become and remained an uncompetitive market.  France’s economic doldrums continued.

Gross domestic product – the total value of goods and services produced by a country’s population – was and remains an indicator of a nation’s economic strength.  Throughout Europe, GDP tumbled.  Between 1929 and 1935, it fell by around 5% in Britain; in that resurrected state, Poland, the drop was a staggering 25%.  France’s GDP fell by around 15% but the decline continued longer.

In Austria and Germany, however, the effects of the turmoil was far more calamitous.  In Germany production had halved by 1932 with unemployment rocketing.  Morre than a third of the population was without a job - some 8 million.  ‘The whole nation is enveloped in distress,’ one German observer noted. ‘Official interference is of no avail; the people live in a veritable hell of meanness, oppression and disease.’ The picture was much the same for that other defeated nation, Austria.  Unemployment was rampant.  In one village south of Vienna, three-quarters of the population became unemployed after a textile factory was forced to close.  ‘He has no hope left and just lives from one day to the next without knowing why,’ noted a report on one young unemployed man who had a wife and two children. ‘The will to resist is lost.’

 

For the most part, those countries with long-established democracies managed to maintain the status quo but the converse was also the case.  Democracy had already effectively collapsed in Poland, while in Japan, which had seen a dramatic rise in terms of industrialization and urbanization, the crisis now prompted a lurch to ultra-nationalistic autocracy and militarism.  Unable to trade successfully with the United States and now finding itself critically under-resourced, Imperial Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931 in what marked the beginning of the country’s quest to gain raw materials through conquest rather than through trade negotiations.

Meanwhile, in America, the situation worsened, and President Hoover, at heart a humane and decent man, was not the man to lead the nation from the mire. His vain attempts to instil hope when all around was despair, and his signing of the disastrous Smoot-Hawley Tariff, showed him to be a man both ill-equipped for the gargantuan challenge he faced and hopelessly out of touch.  Ideologically, Hoover was wedded in the long tradition of American individualism; after all, it was what had led him from a rural upbringing in Iowa, to become a mining millionaire and then to win the presidency.  Quite profoundly he believed it was not the task of the state to be responsible for ensuring the citizens of the United States were given jobs, food and shelter.  To do so would be to go against the tradition of graft and enterprise and entrepreneurialism that had made America great.

Such ideals now made him impotent and increasingly a figure of mockery.  Tent cities and shanty towns sprung up and were ironically known as ‘Hoovervilles.’ The economist, John Maynard Keynes, for one, was urging governments to spend more and run a deficit in order to bolster the economy and boost growth and jobs, but Hoover preferred to keep a balanced budget and so brought in the Revenue Act in 1932, which raised taxes across the board and brought a highest tax rate of 63% of net income on the very people most likely to kick-start the economy.  Needless to say, his austerity measures didn’t work.

And the situation was made worse by a natural disaster that was also a direct result of the time of plenty a few years earlier.  A particularly brutal drought began in 1930 that affected the prairies and Great Plains of the mid-west; the better weather of the twenties had led to over-farming – it had been the time of plenty after all – and the over-farming had led to a lack of pasture and an excess of exposed soil.  One of the meteorological consequences of the drought was a series of brutal dust storms, which stripped topsoil through the central farming heart of the United States and dumped this precious life blood as far afield as Chicago and Washington DC.  In so doing, vast areas were ruined, the essential nutrients to growth carried away on the wind. The drought continued through the 1930s, wrecking farmland, ushering in profound rural poverty and creating what became known as the Dust Bowl across the Great Plains.

Nowhere, though, were the consequences of the Depression greater than in Germany. Defeat, and the abdication of the Kaiser and the overthrow of the Imperial government in the November revolution of 1918, led directly to the establishment of the Weimar Republic, Germany’s first experiment with democracy.  And, perhaps against the odds, Weimar had begun to thrive during the ‘Goldene Zwanziger’ – the second half of the golden twenties. Germany even joined the League of Nations, settled festering border disputes with the Locarno Treaties, and introduced a series of social reforms, including education for all children, improved health insurance, an eight-hour working day and the abolition of any kind of press censorship.  Even paid maternity leave and a national unemployment scheme were introduced in 1927, while more than two million new homes were constructed between 1924 and 1931.  Germany was one of the most progressive nations in the world, from which blossomed an astonishing cultural renaissance too.  This was the age of the Bauhaus movement, of cabaret and jazz bars, of street theatre; Berlin became a hub for intellectuals, writers and artists.

None the less, support for liberal democracy, especially from the military and political elites, had always been somewhat superficial.  Once America’s loans dried up and the Depression spread globally, the fragility of Germany’s democracy began to be exposed.  The bedrock of democracy is transactional: it depends on the contract between the people and the politicians that the latter will deliver economic stability and the chance for long-term progress.  Economic stability gives people a pioneering sense of hope.

For ordinary Germans, the Depression suggested that existing democratic parties were no longer delivering thier side of the bargain, and so they began to turn to the extremes of the right and left. In March 1930, the five-party coalition collapsed, and the President, the former field marshal, Paul von Hindenburg, used emergency powers to bring in economist Heinrich Brüning as an independent and unelected Chancellor.  Brüning was another favouring austerity over government spending and found his emergency reforms twice rejected by the Reichstag, the German parliament.  His response was to then dissolve the Reichstag, which prompted another election.  That September, 1930, the Nazis increased their vote to 18.3% and the Communists became Germany’s second largest party.  They were only kept out of power by another and equally fragile five-party coalition.  Brüning now pushed through his series of debilitating austerity measures which undid many of the progressive welfare reforms of a few years earlier, and which only increased popular antagonism and despair.  He then made it clear to the Americans that Germany could no longer pay reparations.  Against the wishes of the French, President Hoover agreed a one-year pause, which was then extended.  It meant that reparations were now effectively over.

Yet while that was a win for Brüning, there was no lessening of the austerity measures, and the political and economic turmoil continued. The Young Plan of 1929 to reduce reparations and extend the period of repayment had not allowed the Reichsmark to be devalued but the government now introduced internal devaluation by forcing the economy to reduce prices by 20%.  Mounting contempt and mistrust of democracy followed as the impoverished and brow-beaten masses reached breaking point. Maynard Keynes had predicted this scenario in his Economic Consequences written back in 1919. ‘Physical efficiency and resistance to disease slowly diminish, but life still proceeds somehow,’ he wrote, ‘until the limit of human endurance is reached at last and counsels of despair and madness stir the sufferers from the lethargy which precedes the crisis.’ The ordinary man, seemingly forgotten, ignored and much reduced, began to channel that frustration and anger.  Support grew, not for the traditional ruling elites, but for new, more extreme political parties: the German Communists and Hitler’s Nazis. Recognising he had lost the support not only of the country, but also of von Hindenburg, Brüning resigned at the end of May 1932.  Appalled by the dramatic rise of Communism in Germany, the old Prussian field marshal now tried to steer Germany back to the right with a succession of hand-picked and right-wing Chancellors he appointed himself.

A political vacuum was emerging as five successive and short-lived governments failed to stop the unrest.  This explosive crisis was now ruthlessly exploited by brilliant propaganda and the rhetoric of a man who had learned how to encapsulate the anger, frustrations and fears of a swathe of disaffected Germans.  Adolf Hitler spoke to them with passion and rage, but also hope, his hands clenched and grabbing the air, his pale eyes glowering.  Each speech – and Hitler was the first person to use air transport to criss-cross the country at breakneck speed – spoke of the betrayals and the stab in the back, but also offered an extraordinary vision of a far, far brighter future.  For those who believed him, who found answers in his ideology, he was mesmeric – and, crucially, unlike anything they had seen or heard before.

And so it came to pass. From being at best a fringe political figure just a few years earlier to at worst a joke, Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 after a democratic election had taken place the previous November.  What followed was the comparatively swift dismantling of democracy. By July 1933, following the passing of the Enabling Act, all legislative powers were passed to the cabinet and, as a consequence, directly to Hitler.  He wasted no time in banning all political parties other than the Nazis.  The Reichstag – the German parliament – was then dissolved and a snap election called.  Inevitably, because no other parties were allowed, the Nazis then won 100% of the seats.

The Nazis came into being because of the First World War, but they rose to power as a result of the global economic crisis offset by the Wall Street Crash of 1929 and by the instigation  of a global tariff war initiated by the United States.  The consequneces of the Depression in Germany was a reminder of just how fragile democracy could be in a time of economic turmoil.  From seemingly nowhere, Hitler and his acolytes had snatched complete power and immediately threatened the world order.

title: THE LAST GREAT HERO
html:
A short while ago, I was talking to a fellow historian, Luke Turner, about notions of manhood and how much they’ve changed since the Second World War. He pointed out that today, it’s about looking ripped, showing off on social media, covering oneself in tattoos that will look dreadful when they’re old, drinking huge amounts of beer and playing sport. Back in the war, however, charm, urbanity and being a marvellous dancer were character traits far more highly valued. The ideal man was effortless good at everything, courteous at every turn, and, most importantly of all, modest. Showing off – shooting a line – was deeply frowned upon.

Subscribe

On the weekly World War II podcast I co-host with Al Murray, We Have Ways of Making You Talk, we are currently running a series on the best Second World War generals to have commanded in the western theatre. We’ve produced a long list, which Al and I have been going through, and are then putting these lists to the vote. Of course, all the big names are there: Montgomery, Patton, Eisenhower, and Rommel, but there’s one who particularly stands out for me. I first came across him as a boy when I read an article about the Battle of Alamein in a magazine – long since disappeared – called Look and Learn. There was a picture of General Sir Harold Alexander, as he then was, and in my boyish naiviety I decided he looked like a nice man: pale, blue eyes, and laughter lines extending from each side. For some reason that picture, and his name, lodged in my mind.

Over the years, I’ve studied his career in very great detail. I am, in fact, commissioned to write his authorised biography, although for various reasons that hasn’t quite happened yet. This has, though, given me the chance to look at many of his private papers, much of which are still held by his family, and all of which have confirmed my first impression as a boy. Alexander was a wonderful man. He was also the living example of what constituted the ideal hero of eighty years ago: effortlessly brilliant at everything, charming, handsome, urbane, and surely the most modest of all senior commanders to have emerged from the war.

When Field Marshal the Earl Alexander died on Monday, 16th June 1969, so passed one of the last great British heroes. He had been the most experienced battlefield commander of any side during the Second World War, having commanded in combat at every rank of command from subaltern to field marshal. He had fought along the Western Front, commanded German troops in the Baltic in 1919, and had carried out colonial policing duties in the Middle East, India and the North-West Frontier. At the beginning of the Second World War he had been the last officer to leave Dunkirk, had brought the British and India army back from Burma into India, commanded British forces in the Middle East and North Africa, and had been the British and American commander-in-chief when 250,000 Axis troops had been captured with the German and Italian surrender at Tunis in May 1943. He was c-in-c in Sicily, and throughout the Italian campaign. It was in Italy that the first German unconditional surrender was signed in May 1945. Post war, he served in Churchill’s second government and as Governor-General of Canada, where he granted thousands of displaced European Jews the chance to create new lives.

And then he retired, living out his final years simply. A highly talented artist, he painted and travelled, embarked on building projects and spent time with his family. He rarely looked back. Despite a life that stretched from the reign of Queen Victoria to Elizabeth II, and despite a career that had taken to the far corners of the globe, that had seen him face death innumerable times, Alex was always a man who looked forward, who embraced the ever changing world.

No-one who met Alex – as he was always known - ever had cause to doubt his integrity; moreover, there were few people more prone to self-deprecation and less likely to blow their own trumpet. Such unassuming modesty had been drummed into him as a child, a childhood in which he had been brought up to respect notions of honour, duty and impeccable manners in all things and at all times.

Born the third son of the Earl of Caledon, Alex’s background was distinctly aristocratic. His childhood was spent shooting, fishing and painting on the large Caledon estate in County Tyrone in Northern Ireland. At fifteen he was sent to Harrow, where he excelled at sports. In his final year, he played in Fowler’s Match at Lord’s, the most famous Eton-Harrow cricket match ever to have been played. From there, he went straight to Sandhurst, passing out in July 1911, aged nineteen. As a fiercely proud Ulsterman, he was determined to join the Irish Guards. The ‘Micks’ were a young regiment, created by Queen Victoria in only 1900; nearly all its number were Irish. ‘They were my bosom friends,’ he later said. ‘In the Micks there is a great feeling of matiness between officers and men. The Irish love their leaders, as I had found as a boy, and they have natural good manners.’ He was yet to excel as a soldier, but was certainly developing into a handsome, highly athletic young man, and the perfect gentleman. Between duties, he found plenty of time to go to dances and the theatre, to hunt, shoot, box and play polo, as well as cricket and golf. He even went motor racing at Brooklands, and in Easter 1914, entered - and won without breaking sweat - Ireland’s most famous sprint, the Irish Mile.

The four long years of the First World War developed him as a soldier. He quite openly enjoyed it, despite – or rather, because of – spending almost the entire war with fighting troops. At the First Battle of Ypres in November 1914, he was seriously wounded in the thigh and hand and invalided home. He recovered well and, determined to get back to the front as soon as possible, walked sixty-four miles in one day to prove to a cautious doctor that he was fit enough. Sure enough, by February 1915 he was back and later that summer led his company at the Battle of Loos. His reputation was growing rapidly, notably for his exceptional personal courage, but also for his extraordinary imperturbability and the gift of quick decision. Always leading from the front and with no regard to his own personal safety, he soon had the complete devotion and respect of all those who served under him.

He was wounded twice more, survived the Somme, Cambrai, and Passchendaele, and in 1917, aged just twenty-five, became acting Lieutenant-Colonel commanding the 2nd Battalion. By the armistice, he had earned a DSO and bar, an MC, the French Legion of Honour, and had been mentioned in despatches five times. Nor did his combat record stop with the end of war. In 1919, he was sent to command the Baltic Landwehr, part of the Latvian Army, in the war against North Russia. Since most of the men under his command were of German origin, he was unique amongst British commanders of the Second World War in having commanded German troops in battle. Staff college and staff appointments were followed by stints of further action along the North-West Frontier, where his superior at the time, Brigadier Claude Auchinleck, took note of his cool efficiency and began a lasting friendship.

By the outbreak of war in 1939, this gilded officer was one of the army’s youngest Major-Generals and commanding 1stDivision. He went with them to France, and after the British retreat in May 1940, was left behind to supervise the final withdrawal of British troops, only leaving on June 3, the last day of the British evacuation, and only after travelling the length of the beaches in a launch and with a megaphone calling out to any men still stranded. It made him literally the last man out.

Remaining in England for the next two years of war, Alex realised that the vast majority of infantry troops under his command were simply not ready for battle. He subsequently began to develop Battle Schools in which men were taught simple forms of battle drill to which they would react automatically in times of stress – simple orders such as, ‘Down, crawl, observe, fire.’ He also recognised that some kind of battle inoculation was needed before submitting green troops to the terrors of German dive-bombing, shelling and machine-gunning. This could only be done with live ammunition. Thirdly, he realised that it was essential that all troops were battle fit. However obvious this may seem now, the Battle School system was considered quite innovative at the time and became the basis of future infantry training.

It was particularly during his time commanding Southern Command that Alex came to Churchill’s notice. The Prime Minister was certainly influenced by Alex’s aristocratic background, but also by his calm control and a military record that was second-to-none. Even in Burma, yet another retreat from defeat, Alex had impressed with his unflappability and ability to make the best of a bad situation.

And he looked the part, too. Modest though he was, Alex had a streak of the dandy about him; he always dressed immaculately. On leave during the First World War, he spotted a Russian officer wearing a high-peaked cap, with its visor dropping over his eyes. Alex liked the design so much he went straight to his hatter in St James and had him make an exact copy. It was a style he kept throughout his career simply because it had style.

There was also plenty of charm. He never swore: describing something as ‘tiresome’ was the closest he got to cursing, and only once was he ever seen to lose his temper, and that was when some of his men refused to give two dying Germans a drink of water during the Battle of Passchendaele. He drank but was never drunk; he would sketch and paint whenever he had the chance; spoke a number of languages including German, French, Italian and Russian. In 1935, he was appointed to command the Nowshera Brigade on the Northwest Frontier. It was unusual for a Guardsman to be given a command in the Indian Army and to begin with he appeared to conform to type in the eyes of the old India hands, disappearing every afternoon for what they assumed was a siesta. At the Brigade Sports Day a couple of months later, however, he stood up and addressed the entire brigade in fluent Urdu.

He also had a very sound sense of judgement, and perhaps even more importantly, understood the men under his command. He understood how much men could endure and what could be expected of them. He understood that armies need confidence and experience in combat, and that the approach to battle – the preparation and the closing-down of potential stumbling blocks – was the key to victory. This held him in good stead as Eighth Army began to claw their way back across North Africa in the summer and autumn of 1942. Although Alamein is seen as Montgomery’s victory, it was Alex who, on arriving in Egypt in August 1942 announced there would be ‘no more retreats.’ It was also Alex who steered Monty away from his first plan for the second part of the Alamein battle and on to what proved a highly successful course. Alex was Monty’s boss and he deserves every bit as much credit for that crucial turning point in British fortunes. Meanwhile, a joint Anglo-American force had landed in North-West Africa, but by early 1943, had become bogged down, with the Americans suffering their first battlefield defeat. Alex was brought in as army group commander and in ten days had reversed the defeat. Eight weeks later came the triumphant final victory in North Africa. He had shown a rare ability to handle coalition forces, a skill he continued to demonstrate as he led Allied forces first to victory in Sicily and then into southern Italy.

In Italy, he became great friends with Harold Macmillan, who would later become Prime Minister. Macmillan would often accompany him on tours of the front. One time, at the end of January 1944, they called on the American General Geoffrey Keyes and French commander, General Alphonse Juin and climbed a hill from which they could see the battle playing out in the valley beyond. Macmillan was fascinated to observe Alex’s technique of suggestion rather than directly ordering. ‘These are put forward with modesty and simplicity,’ he noted. ‘But they are always so clear and lucid that they carry conviction. It is a most interesting and extremely effective method.’ He was also conscious that away from the front, Alex would always talk of other things as much as possible – politics, ancient art, Roman antiquities, country life. ‘He hates war,’ Macmillan had added in his diary.

The battles of Cassino and the landings at Anzio are often seen as low points in the Allied war with Germany, yet the shortage of troops, equipment and above all, shipping, combined with atrocious weather were factors that were out of Alex’s control. What is undeniable is that on June 5th 1944, when Rome finally fell, the month-long campaign had been the Allies’ biggest battle to date and had wrought a devastating defeat on the German forces in Italy. Alex’s strategy for the rest of the campaign in Italy was one that was subsequently hampered by the precedence given to D-Day and the campaign in North-west Europe. However, during his time as army group commander then Supreme Allied Commander, Alex managed to not only win a complete victory in Italy but at the same time averted civil war in Greece. In Italy, he commanded twenty-three different nationalities, and not one of his subordinate commanders ever had a bad word to say against him. The Americans, in particular, were frequently at loggerheads with their British coalition partners, but not one US commander had anything other than praise for Alex. Indeed, Eisenhower wanted Alex, not Montgomery, to lead Allied ground forces on D-Day.

He also had a terrific sense of humour. Throughout the war, he wrote regularly to his young children back home in England. These letters survive and are full of cartoons and illustrations. ‘It’s about time we have another baby, as you are all growing up,’ he wrote in a letter at the end of February 1944. ‘Ask Mummy what she can do about it, but tell her not to do anything until I get back.’

Bragging was anathema to him and he deplored any kind of publicity about himself, preferring to deflect any praise onto others. It is one of the main reasons that this remarkable man has been, to a large extent, forgotten. In his time, however, he was one of the greatest generals of his age – if not the greatest in the Western theatre. He made his mistakes, but his achievements were immense. For these, but also for his modesty, self-deprecation, his profound sense of honour and duty, and for the incredibly impressive standards he set himself he deserves to viewed as one of the great British heroes, along with Drake, Marlborough, Nelson, and Scott. Really, there has been no-one like him since. He is someone I still look up to and admire like no other. To me, Alex remains a hero – a truly great hero.

title: The Power of Friendship
html:
In this week of the eightieth anniversary of the end of the Second World War , I’ve been thinking much about that time and the absolute awfulness of the war against Imperial Japan. I have, of course, been contemplating the seismic decision to drop the atomic bombs and the terrible fate of those living in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. I’ve also been thinking afresh about the fighting that took place over those long years – from remote Pacific islands to the jungles and plains of Burma and north-east India. And I’ve also been thinking of the truly horrific ordeal of those unfortunate enough to have been taken prisoner. Richard Flanagan’s The Narrow Road to the Deep North is the most stunning novel I’ve read in the past decade or so and focuses in a large part on the experiences of those forced to construct the Thai-Burma railway as POW slave workers of the Japanese. It’s fiction, but watching the dramatization now being screened has made me pause for thought too; it’s a reminder of how brutal life – and death – could be and once again I’ve been feeling grateful not to have been a young man in that era.

But my thoughts have also gone back to a more uplifting story and one told to me by a former prisoner of the Japanese who was born and bred in my home town of Salisbury, in Wiltshire, and who was still living there in his late eighties when I got to know him. And he taught me something: that no matter how grim or brutal the Second World War might have been, most combatants were able to draw a few positives from the experience. Chief amongst these was the sense of camaraderie that developed amongst men thrown together entirely because of the war. When young men were living, sleeping, eating, and fighting for their survival together the intense bonds of friendship that developed were often all that kept them going.

Subscribe

Very many terrible things could befall a young serviceman in the Second World War, but for sustained misery and pain, becoming a Japanese prisoner of war must count as a particularly unfortunate fate. Most faced brutal treatment by their guards, extremely harsh conditions, as well as starvation and disease. Death rates of Allied prisoners in German POW camps were around four percent; in Japanese camps, this figure was between twenty and thirty-seven percent – at best a one in five chance of survival. A good friend could make the ordeal easier, however; good friends could offer one another solace, humanity, and physical and mental support during the darkest of moments. Sometimes, a pal could make all the difference between living and dying. And this was most certainly the case for John Leaver.

John had been into a working class family, the second of three sons. At fourteen he’d left school and begun work in an outfitters’ shop. He was still there when his call-up papers arrived in May 1941. Two brothers were already in the army, but John was told he would be joining the RAF. After initial training – square-bashing and route marches in Weston-super-Mare – John was sent to St Athens in Wales and was due to be sent on an armourer’s course when, in September 1941, he suddenly received orders to report to Liverpool Docks. He, along with a number of other RAF ground crew, were to be shipped overseas.

As instructed, John reached the quayside and reported to a hut alongside the docks. The only other person there was another man of similar age, who immediately came over, shook John’s hand, and introduced himself as Fred Walsh. They got talking and immediately recognising a kindred spirit in one other, stuck together until they boarded their ship the following day. In fact, they remained pretty inseparable throughout a very long three-and-a-half month journey.

They had been told they were to become the ground crew for 84 Squadron, but catching up with the squadron proved to be something of a wild goose-chase that took them round the Cape to Durban – where Fred introduced John to his rich uncle - then on to Bombay, back through Iraq, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt and eventually, at long last to the Far East, by which time, John and Fred had become extremely good friends.

Fred was from Guernsey in the Channel Islands, the son of a policeman. He’d left the island before the Germans occupied it in June 1940, and although not much older than John, was already married with a young son. The voyage was a very new experience for them both, for although Fred had been to sea when crossing the Channel between Guernsey and the south coast of England, neither had ever really spent much time away from home and neither had ever left the United Kingdom before. Nor did they have any idea how long they might be away or when they might next see their families. The knowledge that there was a good friend to share this adventure across oceans and continents made the separation from home much easier.

They never did catch up with the rest of the squadron, however. By mid-February 1942, they were steaming towards Singapore, when news arrived that the British there had surrendered to the Japanese. Their ship was promptly diverted to Sumatra instead, in the Dutch East Indies. ‘We couldn’t believe Singapore had fallen,’ John told me. ‘We had enough manpower there. If they’d just stood firm…It still irks me, because I think they should have fought on, I really do.’

John and Fred arrived in the Far East amidst the panic and mayhem of the biggest military defeat in British history. On Sumatra, the squadron’s ground crew were split up. Half were told they would be sent to Rangoon in Burma, the other half were to stay on Sumatra. John and Fred were amongst those told to stay, although four days later they were on the move again. Against the advice of the ship’s captain, who suggested they sail straight on to Australia, the RAF officer in charge decided they should do as they’d been ordered, and fight on in the best way they could. That meant landing at Morak in Java and helping the Dutch pilots at Bandoeng airfield, who were still desperately holding out against the Japanese onslaught. Once again, the squadron was divided: some of the men were ordered to man the guns around the airfield, while the rest worked on the surviving planes. But yet again, John and Fred stayed together, singled out to help keep the aircraft flying.

Theirs was now a lost cause, however. John remembers that one day they were attacked by no less than seventy-two Japanese bombers. ‘Lucky for us, they all attacked the far side of the aerodrome from where we were,’ he said, ‘but you could see hundreds and hundreds of bombs coming out of these planes, then the most terrific explosions and the ground shuddering. The aerodrome was flattened – the hangars were down, the planes there were on fire and there were bits of bodies all over the place.’ They held out for a few more days, cannibalising the wrecked aircraft to keep the remaining two planes airborne, until on March 8, several British army lorries reached the airfield. “Don’t you know there’s bus-loads of Japs coming?” the soldiers yelled at them. On the back of the trucks were several Bofors anti-aircraft guns, but instead of training them onto the advancing Japanese, the soldiers were heading for the port. ‘They baulked,’ said John, ‘and that really sticks in my throat. They were being bloody yellow.’ With nothing left to fight with, the ground crew grabbed whatever kit they could and clambered aboard the lorries. ‘I suppose the idea was to try and get a ship to Australia,’ said John. But there was no ship to take them, and they were left with no option but to wait for the Japanese to arrive and then surrender. Both John and Fred could scarcely believe what was happening. ‘I felt bloody sick about it,’ admitted John. Their active contribution to the war effort had lasted less than three weeks.

After they had surrendered, they were ordered back to Bandoeng airfield to fill in the bomb craters. When they got there, they saw that those men from the squadron that had been ordered to man the guns had been killed. ‘They were all dead,’ recalled John. ‘Every one bayoneted.’ But despite such scenes, John told me he had little idea then of how they would be treated as prisoners of war. ‘Actually, to begin with, they weren’t too bad,’ he said of the guards, although conditions were far from comfortable. He, Fred and the remainder of the squadron’s ground crew were initially put into a holding compound on Java; then in August, they were moved to another POW camp at Batavia, where around two thousand Allied servicemen were interned. Fred had kept an occasional diary ever since leaving England, and incredibly he managed to keep it going throughout their incarceration, writing with whatever he could find on scraps of paper. ‘Food scarce,’ he noted on their arrival at Batavia on August 17, 1942. ‘Bad sanitation and cramped billets…Rumours that we will not be here long.’

The rumours were correct. Towards the end of October 1942 they were herded onto a ship and taken to Singapore. Once there, they were disembarked, hosed down, then ordered to board another ship, an old, rusting hulk called the Dai Nichi Maru. It was a freighter, built on the Clyde in Scotland at the end of the previous century and not designed to take passengers at all. The Japanese, however, were planning to carry more than a thousand prisoners and slightly more Japanese troops on board. Keeping close to one another, John and Fred climbed the gangplank up onto the deck then followed the line of prisoners slowly scaling down a vertical iron ladder into one of four holds on the ship. John and Fred were two of nearly three hundred men crammed into their hold, and it quickly became very apparent that the Japanese viewed the prisoners as nothing more than cargo, no different from the damp bed of bauxite ore that lay at the bottom of the hold and onto which the bewildered men now stood and squatted.

Conditions had become progressively worse the longer they had been in captivity, but the Dai Nichi Maru was truly appalling, a degrading, dehumanising, claustrophobic hulk. There were only a few toilets and these were wooden structures built on to the outside of the boat. In order to use them, a prisoner would have to climb up the iron ladder onto the deck, then clamber over the side to the latrine. The holds were also dark and dank, with tarpaulins covering over most of the open roof. Food was given twice a day in large tubs lowered from the deck and was usually a thin, watery gruel or red fish. The men ate it with whatever they could – an old mess tin or enamel mug, for example. There was no way of cleaning them afterwards. The water ration was also severely restricted and the water of bad quality. ‘We got two cups of water a day,’ said John. ‘One in the morning and one in the afternoon and that was it. Your mouth was parched up dry – it was horrendous.’ As for the fish – well, he cannot even look at a fish bone now. ‘It’s daft, but I still hate red fish,’ he told me. ‘To me they’re vile.’ To make matters worse, most men, like John and Fred, were still dressed in KD – khaki drill, the RAF’s twill cotton tropical kit – with no spare clothes. Facing a journey of unknown length and to an unknown destination, in winter, and in a ship that was so inadequate it would disintegrate the moment it was hit by a torpedo, John and Fred could do little but pray their ordeal would soon be over.

The Dai Nichi Maru was one of the notorious ‘hell ships’ that transported Allied prisoners from the Philippines, Dutch East Indies and Singapore to camps elsewhere in the Japanese Empire. Apart from the infamous Burma-Thailand railway, these ships were the greatest cause of death amongst Allied POWs. Japanese reports suggest that more than 10,000 of the 50,000 prisoners transported in this way died en route.

John vividly remembered the voyage as one of barely comprehendible horror. Many prisoners had boarded in a weakened physical condition, but soon disease became rife, with dysentery crippling many just a few days into the voyage. The stench – of faeces, sweat, oil and fish – was appalling. ‘By God, it was terrible,’ he said. ‘You’ve got those with dysentery, being sick all the time, and plenty that were dying. And the moaning – that’s all you could hear.’ Later, Fred noted in his diary, ‘More and more chaps were fainting daily. I shall never forget it. There were no medical supplies on board. Chaps were lying sick and dying all around.’

The first man to die in their hold was an army captain. They couldn’t leave him there and so they tied a rope around him and two men clambered up the vertical ladder and hauled up the body. One of the officers then said a few prayers and they tipped his body over the side ‘I still get bloody bad dreams about that,’ admitted John. ‘Towards the end there were three or four deaths every day, regular as clockwork. Sometimes even five or six.’ Some prisoners, John reckoned, simply gave up the will to live. ‘You saw their spirit drain away.’

After calling into port at Formosa (now Taiwan) they continued northwards and ran into storms, which brought more misery. Huddling together to keep warm as the ship rolled, the condition of many of the prisoners dramatically worsened. The food – both the quantity and quality – deteriorated further, as did the water available. Although few men had the stomach to eat anything, they were slowly but surely dying of starvation and thirst, as well as dysentery.

They finally docked at Moji in Japan on November 24, nearly a month after setting out from Singapore. John was in better condition than most, but Fred had started to get ill; a few more days aboard and the death toll would have been far greater. ‘We were lucky,’ said John. ‘Because Fred and I were put in the same hold, we were able to keep each other going.’

At Moji, a hundred names were called out, and once again, good fortune ensured that both John and Fred were among those listed to be taken to a small, new, POW camp on the tiny island of Mukaishima, some thirty miles east of Hiroshima. The Japanese had built the camp there for two reasons: first, it was almost impossible to escape, and second, the prisoners provided a very useful labour force for the Hitachi Shipyard on the island.

Not that they were in the best physical shape after their ordeal on the Dai Nichi Maru. Fred was taken to hospital with serious stomach problems, but most of the seriously ill were, as he noted in his diary, ‘too far gone.’ Within a few days of their arrival at the end of November, the first man had died. John helped the medical orderly measure up the dead man. Soon after, the Japanese produced a rough coffin. ‘We had to carry him out of the camp and up a track,’ said John, ‘then dig a hole and fill it with wood. Then we put the dead lad on top and set fire to it.’ Further deaths swiftly followed. By the end of the year, twelve men had died; by the end of March 1943, that figure had risen to twenty-one.

Life on the island was monotonous in the extreme. The camp itself was small, a compound of about 75 feet wide by 150 feet long, enclosed by an eight foot high wooden fence. The prisoners lived in long huts, made of rough wood, unpainted inside and out and without any form of heating. The men slept on a raised wooden deck; the latrines were outside: a wooden box with six holes covering a concrete pit that had to be emptied every week. The urinal was tacked onto the end of the living block and separated from only by a partition wall, and particularly unpleasant for the prisoners sleeping at that end.

Every day, they got up at around 6am, then were marched the two miles down to the port. The working day began at seven. They were allowed a ten-minute break in the morning and half an hour for lunch, or ‘tiffin’ as it was known, and another ten-minute break in the afternoon. They finished work at 4.30pm and then were marched back to the camp. Every four weeks, they were given a day off. Fred worked in the welding shop all day long, but John was part of a six-man gang who pushed carts of supplies from the ships around the island. ‘There was one guiding the front,’ he said, ‘two each side on the ropes and two at the back pushing.’ As slave labour went, it wasn’t too bad. ‘At least we were on the move all the time,’ he said, although the work was exhausting. ‘In the summer we were black as the ace of spades,’ said John. ‘We’d sweat like hell and we were absolutely knackered all the time. Your legs would go. There’d be blokes screaming at night their legs hurt so bad.’

As John is the first to admit, their camp was not as brutal as some. ‘Ours was a doddle compared to what some had to contend with,’ he pointed out, but even so, theirs was still a very tough, uncomfortable, existence. The summers were hot, but the winters were cold; they only had one set of clothes, which were filthy and worn. The island was fairly bare: grassy with sandy soil, and with few trees. During the monsoon they got absolutely soaked with little opportunity to get their clothes dry, whilst in the summer there was almost no shade at all.

Nor were they ever given enough food. Meals consisted of a tiny bowl of rice each first thing in the morning and some watery soup, the same again at lunch and on their return to the camp in the evening. ‘Sometimes they put these tiny minnows – dried fish – in as well,’ said John. On a good day they’d eat maybe as much as 700 grams of food, but it could easily be as little 350 grams. It simply did not provide enough energy for the kind of hard physical work they were doing. John told me they spent much of their time dreaming and obsessing about food. ‘You would be lying on your bunk at night and you’d say, “I could really do with a nice plate of beef,” and someone else would say, “I could murder a treacle pudding,” then others would shout, “Shut up!”’ Every day on his march down to the port, he would pass a small factory. He had no idea what was made there, but the smell tantalisingly reminded him of his mother’s treacle pudding. ‘Every day I had to smell that,’ he says. Only once the war was over did he discovered they had made mustard pickle there.

Any opportunity to supplement their meagre rations was readily taken. One Saturday in winter, they were marching past a field of frozen swedes. There was a guard with them who was kinder than most and he told them to hide behind a wall where no-one could see them, then passed them some swedes. ‘We struggled to break the bloody things,’ said John. ‘We smashed them against the wall and trod on them and eventually got some bits, and we sat there chewing them.’ Two hours later, however, they all suffered terrible stomach aches.

On another occasion, John was helping take cart loads of wooden faggots to the kitchens at the dockyard. ‘We got there just after a mealtime,’ said John, ‘and this Jap was scraping the crust of rice off the edge of his wok, and he gave it to us.’ They all ate a small bit, then carefully hid the rest in their clothes and took it back to the camp. Once there, John told Fred about his extra rations and together they went to the latrines to eat it. ‘We took it in turns to eat it while the other kept watch,’ said John. ‘Can you imagine? It was horrible in there – it really stank. The things you did for a tiny bit of food.’

The second time he was given some rice scraps, he was caught, however. By this time, John had been in the camp long enough to know what to expect. Sure enough, he was taken out and beaten with a pick-axe handle. ‘It was like being hit with a baseball bat,’ says John. They hit him on his body and across the back of his head, which knocked him out. ‘When I came to,’ he told me, ‘I was in a wheelbarrow being pushed back to our barrack block.’ Punishments were frequent and often for the slightest misdemeanour, and although prisoners were not beheaded or used as bayonet practice as in other camps, their guards could be still act with ruthless cruelty. ‘A favourite punishment was to put people in a box,’ said John. This would be just a few feet square and the prisoner would have to sit crouched up. ‘The agony would start after half an hour,’ he said, ‘but you could be in there for days.’ On November 9, 1944, Fred noted, two prisoners were put in boxes for ten whole days for breaking into stores near their billets. Another punishment was to make prisoners kneel on strips of bamboo, with further strips placed on the back of their legs with the weight of the body resting on them. ‘There was no way you could relieve the pain,’ explained John, then added, ‘God, they were sods for what they did.’

And whilst some of the guards were all right, others were most definitely not. Towards the end of 1943, one of John’s friends, John Yateman, became ill. One day, John was talking to him in their barrack block when one of the guards came up to them and told Yateman that he’d heard the doctor talking about him. “You’re going to die very soon,” the guard said with relish. “They can do nothing for you.” ‘Yeatman was a big lad,’ said John, ‘about six foot four, but when he heard this he just cried and cried. He was a hell of a nice kid, and he didn’t want to die. I was so angry I could have grabbed that guard’s rifle and stuck his bayonet into him right there. The bastard.’ Sure enough, Yeatman did die - of tuberculosis - on 7 January, 1944. ‘I’ll never forget it,’ John remembered, ‘seeing him crying his heart out.’

Occasionally, Red Cross parcels would reach them, which would be shared out. Typically, these included clothing and tins of meat, cigarettes and chocolate, but it was not until April 1944, a year and a half after they first arrived on Mukaishima, that the first letters from home reached the prisoners. The sense of isolation and of being out of touch with all that was familiar could easily sap morale, but as John pointed out, the ongoing friendship between he and Fred helped sustain them. Then in the summer of 1944, Fred became ill again. He’d never properly sorted out his chronic stomach problems that had begun during the voyage on the Dai Nichi Maru. Incredibly, he’d been taken to hospital early in 1943 but the operation had not been a success. In August 1944, he left the island for another operation, and to John’s great relief, not only did he return soon after, but his treatment appeared to have been a success.

Although more than a hundred American prisoners joined them in September that year, the British prisoners knew that by then the tide of the war had turned. One of the prisoners could read Japanese and he used to read out bits of Japanese newspapers to the others. ‘We heard about D-Day and so on,’ said John, ‘and about the Americans retaking the Mariana Islands. After that we started to see the Superfortresses flying over.’ He remembered one time when he was down at the dockyards and suddenly a huge din of aero engines could be heard. ‘We looked up and saw 80-100 aircraft coming over. It gave us the most incredible lift.’

But the closer they got to the end of the war, the worse their condition became. By the autumn of 1944, both John and Fred weighed well under nine stone, and rations were getting worse. Red Cross parcels gained ever-greater importance. The prisoners were almost delirious with excitement when 200 parcels reached the island – almost one each! - but having unloaded them and carried them up to the camp, the camp commander told them they could only have a small portion of them every two months. The rest were locked up.

The twenty-third prisoner out of the original one hundred died in February 1945. Mukaishima may have been less severe than other camps, but nearly a quarter of them had died. The victim had contracted pneumonia, as had several others. Most had suffered chest infections and other ailments during what had been a particularly cold winter. But somehow the surviving prisoners had kept going, bolstered by the knowledge that the Allies were slowly but surely winning the war. On May 9, just a day after VE Day, word reached them that the war against Germany was over.

Meanwhile, they were seeing more and more American aircraft flying over. Moreover, there was increasingly less work to do at the dockyards and, John noticed, nearly all the Japanese workers on the island had gone – presumably called up as replacements for the Imperial Army. ‘It suddenly went very quiet,’ said John.‘There was hardly any work being done and then one day one of the guards said, “Yesterday one bomb, 120,000 killed.” He looked like he could kill us there and then because we were happy. So we shut up quick.’

In fact, after the first atomic bomb, the whole island, prisoners included, were told to stand by to evacuate. The order to leave never came, but some of the Japanese guards told the prisoners they would kill them all. ‘We were scared,’ admitted John. ‘We really thought they might.’ Nor was John in good physical shape. His weight had dropped further and he was suffering the vitamin deficiency disease, beriberi fever. For ten days they waited with mounting apprehension. Then at one o’clock on 17 August, 1945, the camp commander told them the war was over. A minute later, the British officer in charge led the prisoners in a rendition of ‘God Save the King.’ ‘I have never heard it sang so well before as it was today,’ noted Fred in his diary. ‘A wonderful feeling… so came the day we had been waiting for for three and a half years.’

There was a short while to wait until the Americans came to liberate them, but on September 12, they left the island for good and were taken to Yokohama Harbour. From there, they boarded an American aircraft carrier that took them to Sydney. ‘There were thousands on that ship,’ recalled John, ‘but even then Fred and I were called out and put on the same deck and mess table together. It was incredible but that’s how it was throughout the whole war.’ When they reached Sydney there was no ship to take them back to England, so the Red Cross billeted the former prisoners with Australian families while they waited for their passage home. Once again, John and Fred remained together. ‘They were the nicest people,’ said John of the family that took them in. ‘And to be honest, staying with them was just what we needed to get back to normal. They took us out – to the opera, to the races. Looked after us like we were their own family.’

After a month of recuperation, they boarded a ship together bound for Southampton. The two of them had been together almost every day from the moment they left Liverpool in September 1941, to the moment they arrived home in January 1946. ‘Fred was a hell of a nice man,’ says John. ‘The best friend in the world. In all that time we never once had a cross word. Not once.’

With the war over, however, they finally went their separate ways. Reunited with his wife and son, Fred initially returned to Guernsey. But his father had died and Fred found it hard to settle down. He had been very taken with Australia, however. Furthermore, the family he and John had stayed with in Sydney had told them that if they ever wanted to move to Australia, they would guarantee them both a job and a place to live. ‘They were as good as their word,’ said John, ‘and they sorted Fred out, and he stayed there for good.’

The world is a much smaller place now, but in the decades following the end of the war, it was no easy matter keeping in touch with a friend on the other side of the world. And anyway, John had his own life to sort out. His return was marred by the news that both of his brothers had been killed in France shortly after D-Day.‘That knocked the stuffing out of me,’ he admitted – for a year and a half, he’d had no idea they had been killed. Unsurprisingly, their loss also left his parents heartbroken. John remembered coming home one night and seeing his mother crying at the kitchen table. ‘She could barely hold a cup of tea,’ he says. ‘I talked to my father about it and he said, “She’s like this most days.”’

John, on the other hand, initially adjusted well. Soon after the war, he met and married his wife, Jean, and together they had four ‘super kids.’ He had a good job and was content, living in Salisbury with his parents nearby. But then one day, some years later, he suffered a sudden and catastrophic breakdown. The combination of his wartime experiences and the loss of his brothers had finally got the better of him. He was in hospital for months. ‘I’d never talked about the war, and nor had anyone asked me about it,’ he told me. ‘I later discovered that people had been told not to talk to former POWs about what they’d been through. I’d always wondered why they hadn’t.’ Gradually, however, he began to improve, although for years after he was taking Librium, ‘like they were Smarties,’ a drug he fears may have done him more harm than good. ‘It affected my memory,’ he admitted. ‘There’s quite a lot I can’t remember from when the kids were younger.’

He was fortunate to have a very close and supportive family, however, and made a full recovery, but as the years passed by he often wondered what had become of his old pal who had helped him through the long years of war. He regularly made enquiries but it took a number of years before he finally tracked Fred down via their respective Rotary Clubs. That was in 1982; they had not heard from each other for thirty-seven years. With the friendship now rekindled, a few years later, in 1989, Fred made a trip over to England and the two were reunited. Fred spent a month in England, ‘and we got on as well as we’d ever done,’ said John.

But by then Fred’s health was in decline; he had recently had yet another stomach operation. ‘You see, the war affected my nerves,’ said John, ‘but it affected Fred too – with his ulcers and ongoing stomach problems.’ Fred’s visit to England was the last time the two saw each other. In 1998, John received a call from Australia to say that his friend had lost his battle with cancer and had passed away. ‘I’ve never cried in my whole life,’ John told me and his eyes were moistening again ‘Not when I heard my brothers had died nor when my mother and father passed away. But when I heard that Fred had gone, I sobbed my heart out.’

During Fred’s last visit they spent a lot of time reminiscing and talking about the war years. They recognised that they had been lucky to have survived, but they were both in agreement as to why. ‘Fred said to me, “Without you, I don’t think I would have lived,”’ remembered John, ‘and I know that but for Fred, I’d wouldn’t have made it either.’

The power of friendship in a time of war…

title: Where Are You, JFK?
html:
A great friend of mine recently told me he has a framed print of President John F. Kennedy’s inauguration speech, delivered in Washington DC on 21 January 1961. It was, he told me, an extraordinary speech. ‘It has an incredible line,’ my friend pointed out, then quoted: “And so, my fellow Americans: ask not what your country can do for you – ask what you can do for your country.” Needless to say, I followed this conversation by looking it up and reading it through several times. And my friend Peter was quite right. It is an impressive speech, even more so when put alongside the most recent presidential inaugural address - and when read today, in our dramatically different and rapidly changing world.

Back in January 1960, the Second World War was not yet fifteen years done, but already America had emerged as the leading superpower in the world, more prosperous, more modern, more aspirational than any. The emerging world was split into two powerhouses: the western world of progressive, liberal democracy, and an alternative world of communism that was really autocracy, and in which individual freedoms were suppressed and the populations oppressed by state control. I joined this former, western world, just over nine years later in 1970; it’s the world I was brought up in and to which I remain avowedly attached, as do the vast majority of people in the Western world today.

Kennedy was making his speech at a time when daggers were drawn, except that instead of a duel of knives, the weapons were nuclear bombs. Tension between East and West was ratcheting up and during his brief presidency, the world arguably came as close as it was ever going to get to an all-out nuclear war during the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962. Thankfully, the crisis passed, but in January 1961, Kennedy’s speech not only presented a very clear Christian-based and western world-view but also a striking mixture of hope and fear. It was also a speech to the people about the people; there is just one paragraph in which he uses the first person, for example. “In the long history of the world,” he said, “only a few generations have been granted the role of defending freedom in its hour of maximum danger. I do not shirk from this responsibility – I welcome it. I do not believe that any of us would exchange places with any other people or any other generation. The energy, the faith, the devotion which we bring to this endeavour will light our country and all those who serve it – and the glow of that fire can truly light the world.” His vision is of a collective effort – one that will lead to a better world.

What he was also outlining was a global mission for the United States: one in which Americans prospered at home but also lit the way beyond America’s shores. His grand aim was to alleviate poverty, bring peace and co-operation. “Together,” he added, “let us explore the stars, conquer the deserts, eradicate disease, tap the ocean depths and encourage the arts and commerce.” The United States, he pledged, would have the strongest military in the world, “For only when our arms are sufficient beyond doubt can we be certain beyond doubt that they will never be employed.”

The new president warned that his vision would not be done in the lifetime of his administration, nor perhaps, even in his lifetime; in this he was, of course, proved horribly correct: just under three years later he was assassinated in Dallas. Nor did the history of the world pan out as he hoped. Following his death came the catastrophe of the Vietnam War, Watergate, the Iran-Contra Affair, yes, the collapse of the Soviet Union but only a fleeting embrace of democracy in Russia, civil war in the Balkans, famine in Africa, genocide in Rwanda, global terrorism directed on the US and the West, more catastrophic wars, global warming, another financial crash, civil war in Syria, the rise of populism in the West, the global pandemic, the West’s ignominious and terrible retreat from Afghanistan, war in Ukraine, turmoil in the Middle East, not to mention famine, illness, and further civil war aroud the globe, not least amongst many of the United States’ neighbours. This was not the vision JFK was painting.

So, here we are now, the world in a state of flux, uncertainty abounding and the threat of further economic crises, political and social unrest in the West, and even an increased prospect of war. It’s all a bit depressing, to say the very least.

And yet, we in the UK and Western Europe – not to mention the United States – are richer than ever. There have been advances in technology and medical care that have prolonged our lives and made them easier too. We travel more, go out more, enjoy more holidays than any previous generation. We have more information at our fingertips than any of our forebears. Our lives are given considerably more luxury and entertainment than any other previous generation: the access to music, to film and TV, to sport, to vehicles and household appliance that make our lives better.

I wonder, though, whether we’ve all become a little spoiled here in the West, and with it complacent. John F. Kennedy, when he made that speech, was addressing a voting population that had all lived through and experienced World War II. “The graves of young Americans who answered the call to service,” said Kennedy, “surround the globe.” He was quite right about that; from the waters of the far Pacific to the mountains of Italy and hedgerows and towns of Northwest Europe to the ice of the Arctic Circle and deserts of North Africa, American servicemen had died in that most terrible of world conflicts. Kennedy himself had served – and heroically too – in the US Navy in the Pacific. Even those who had not seen action had lived through and experienced the hardships and privations that came with the war, and, of course, the losses and grief. Too many sons, lovers, husbands, and fathers had been lost.

In the case of the USA, the war had, though, led to greater employment and growing prosperity as the nation emerged from the Great Depression through the production of arms and armaments. The B-29 Superfortress project, for example, brought jobs and growth to parts of the country that were in dire need of investment and urgent ‘levelling up’; Wichita in Kansas, for example, at the edge of what had been the Dust Bowl, became an industrial centre almost overnight.

Yet as servicemen and -women returned home after the war’s end, there was a growing sense that a wonderful opportunity had arisen to fulfil the promise of the American dream – a responsibility, or even a debt that was owed, to those who had sacrificed the most. A social contract: not to squander the peace but rather, to make first the USA, and then the world, a better, more prosperous place. It was also a Western world based on Christian values: to be neighbourly, to protect the poor, to show charity, but also one that valued the family and hard work.

This is not to suggest that everyone felt the same way or that every citizen in the United States was a paragon. Far from it, but there was a wide sense of hope, societal responsibility and optimism. This was present in Britain too, despite six long years of war and economic calamity. Those returning to Britain after the war demanded a better, fairer country and the new Labour government pledged to comply. Cheaper housing, a welfare state and a National Health Service were part of this new landscape. This latter project was designed to help keep British people healthy – to offer better medical care so that people could continue working and lead full lives. When Prime Minister Harold Macmillan – himself a veteran of the First World War and key political figure in the Second – announced that Britain had never had it so good, he was saying nothing less than the truth. But with these post-war changes came the understanding that Christian values, working hard, thrift and responsibility to both community and nation, went hand-in-glove.

Even so, the USA was no Utopia and Britain most certainly not. My memories of growing up the seventies and eighties are of bland food, soulless cafes, Formica, and misogyny; but they are also of more cohesive communities and very little sense of entitlement; expectations were comparatively low and there was an innate understanding that one took out what one put in. And hovering in the background was The War. If I spread too much butter on my toast, my mother admonished me with the line, ‘In the war that would have lasted a week!’ or some such. School was known as ‘Colditz’ after the infamous German prison camp. All the middle-aged people and above spoke of it: this collective experience all had lived through. And no matter how much Britain’s fortunes might have faded since then, I knew, even as a comparatively small child, that the country was now an infinitely better place. That can only have rubbed off from the adults around me.

There is nothing to be gained from being nostalgic, but reading JFK’s speech today has made me pause for thought. It’s certainly inspirational, and it’s certainly got vision, two factors sorely lacking in Western politics today. It makes me wistful – that the generation who fought through the war and who sacrificed so much are slipping away and with them the sense of a higher purpose. Eighty years on, we seem to be as fascinated by the war as we ever were but it’s still a comparatively small number of people who share that fascination. ‘The War’ is certainly no longer part of the vernacular. That’s a good thing in many ways, but not if it stops us from valuing the peace that was so hard won, because that would mean we’re taking the prosperous and peaceful world we live in for granted.

And that is most definitely not a good thing. It also feels like the sense of a social contract has gone. A friend of mine was a midwife in Lambeth and told me that no matter how poor some of the homes she visited were they all had widescreen TVs, computer games but, crucially, no table. People demand ever cheaper food but that has also come to mean more convenient food too – food that can be eaten instantly, on the go. Eating from paper and packaging has come at the cost of conversation. Multiculturalism also appears to be teetering; the UK has always been a nation of immigrants – and the same is true for the US – but it worked because those coming to Britain to make new lives were expected to absorb British customs and values as well as continue those from where they came.

When the British Prime Minister tried to slash a bloated welfare system in the United Kingdom he presented it as a means of cutting costs. Yet clearly the welfare system is being abused. Had he suggested he was cutting back on those cheating the system, he might have got a little further. How a policy is presented really counts; words matter, as JFK’s speech showed, as Roosevelt understood. And as did Churchill, for that matter. We’re emotional beings and respond when our hearts are lifted, our emotions raised. The Prime Minister does not seem to understand this, and so, the nonsense of vast amounts of money being spent on too many who neither need nor deserve tax payers’ help continues. According to the Department of Work & Pensions, an incredible 9.9 million people of working age claimed some form of benefits in 2024 out of a total of just over 34 million. That’s almost a third. That’s preposterous. Yet, collectively, as a nation, we buy more new cars than ever, travel further, and have more disposable income than the generations who came before us. A Gen Z twenty-something might bemoan the cost of housing but they still have their smart phones and all that comes with those. Live sport has never been more expensive and yet more people attend such live events than ever before.

Kennedy was speaking in 1961, sixty-four years ago, but it’s hard not to feel the excitement his speech must have evoked at the time. The sense of hope, of optimism, that together, incredible things could be achieved. Like Franklin D. Roosevelt before him, Kennedy was a superb communicator. His charisma was obvious and his vision presented with clarity. Charm, warmth, and clarity of vision – these were and remain three essential values for an effective leader. ‘

“Better the occasional faults of a Government that lives in a spirit of charity than the constant omission of a Government frozen in the ice of its own indifference,” Roosevelt declared back in 1936.

And there is much in what JFK pledged in 1961 that still strikes a chord today. His determination to fight the common enemies of man: tyranny, poverty, disease and war. The notion that together we are stronger. That strong defence leads not to war but is the bulwark against future conflict. And, of course, not what the country can do for the individual, but what the individual can do for the country. He followed that line by asking his ‘fellow citizens of the world’ a question too: “Ask not what America will do for you, but what together we can do for the freedom of man.”

It's heady stuff, but isn’t that what we need? Here in the UK, we must shake ourselves out of the ice of our own indifference. The complacency and the sense of entitlement need casting off. The excessive litigation and threat of litigation, and the nimbyism that stifles progress, need to be kicked into the long grass. We need to return to the post-war belief in public service and in collective responsibility – a change of tack that has been very successfully introduced in Sweden, incidentally. We need unity – of purpose and of an understanding of the threats that now overshadow us. Much of what we appear to consider important right now – or what seems to provoke barely contained outrage when challenged – will seem like very small beer indeed should we find ourselves under sustained terrorist attack or worse, at war with Russia.

It is not good enough to simply say, ‘We can’t afford it.’ We can. There are solutions for everything in a rich, technologically advanced nation like the UK and our fellow democratic nations in the West. We need to embrace the excitement of possibility, of self-belief, of optimism. If ever Britain – and the West – needed political leaders to inspire and offer a credible and exciting vision for the future, it’s now. Where are you, JFK?
