title: Honouring Brave Men
html:
It was early last June, a few days before the 80th anniversary of D-Day, that I found myself climbing up a winding hill overlooking the southern side of the River Noireau in Normandy.  The road was lined by lush fields and then we reached the treeline as the road continued up through a steep escarpment.  Emerging a short while later onto a high plateau of rolling pasture, we came upon a Calvary at a junction with a track, set a little way back from the road, Christ’s figure upon the cross looking pained and forlorn as well he might be.

           

We drove on a little way towards the quiet village of Berjou and were approaching the village when we paused and got out to see a strange anomaly in the hedgeline to our left.  I’d first seen this a month earlier, and on that visit it had been startling to see: a clear rectangle, perhaps twelve yards wide and three deep around which the hedge deviated from its parallel course to the road.  It was no less startling this second time, and we were still looking at it when a wartime jeep rolled up and stopped.  At the wheel was Louis Bon and his father, who together run a small but wonderful museum at the far side of the village, honouring the battle that was fought here back in August 1944.

           

‘This is where the tank stood,’ Louis told us. ‘It was shunted off the road and rolled over.’  The turret of the Sherman had been blown off, he told us, so it was only the hull that had stood there – and it had remained there for years.  The hedge had simply grown around it.  Louis had found a cap badge of the Sherwood Rangers Yeomanry on the ground there.  Clearly, it had been on the beret of the one of the men killed that day; as the tank had been rolled upside down the metal had fallen out.  That cap badge had survived, but the wool of the beret and the man wearing it had been incinerated.  ‘But,’ Louis added, ‘Galvin’s tank was hit a bit further back.’

 

About twenty yards further back.  I paused and wondered.  What had hit it?  An anti-tank round? A panzerfaust? And from what direction?  What was certain was that Lieutenant Frank Galvin’s crew had emerged from the wood escarpment, rumbled on down the road to the village and then been hit.  They’d not fired a shot at this point and so the Sherman had been full of ammunition and still plenty of fuel.  A high-velocity charge ripping through the outer still would have sent globs of white-hot metal bursting around the inside of the turret, any one of which could have hit the shells lining the inside, which in turn would have triggered a profound internal explosion.  The turret burst off like a champagne cork and the five men inside were incinerated.  The only comfort is that they almost certainly would have known nothing about it.  Tank warfare was – and is – absolutely brutal in its violence.

           

I was digesting this when Louis, rummaging around the hedge, produced a hunk of rusted steel. This was from Galvin’s tank, blasted there eighty years earlier. I followed and soon found plenty of other debris; it was just there, in amongst the grass and hedge, a relic of that moment of destruction. I felt a lump in my throat and wandered on down the road, feeling an urge to be alone for a few moments.  A month earlier, when I’d last been there, one of my companions, a wine merchant called ‘Tuggy’ Meyer, suggested building a memorial at this site. Now, being there a second time and with a mangled shell casing in my hand, I knew Tuggy had been right. These men needed their own memorial. They deserved not to be forgotten…

 

Wednesday, 16 August, 1944, was a dark day for C Squadron of the Sherwood Rangers. The Normandy campaign was nearly over but although the Allies were smashing the German armies, the fighting remained savage.  The objective for the Sherwood Rangers that morning was to reach Point 337, a low hill on the high ground above the escarpment, and the village of Berjou.  Armour – tanks – always operated alongside the infantry, and for the day’s assault they were attached to the Duke of Cornwall’s Light Infantry, part of the 43rd ‘Wessex’ Division.  The Sherwood Rangers had fought alongside the Wessex men plenty of times since D-Day but not the DCLI before.  This was to be a new partnership.

 

Trouble had been brewing before that day, however. A couple of weeks earlier, the army commander, General Dempsey, had fired a corps and divisional commander for being too slow. This had swiftly filtered down the chain so that all senior commanders in Second Army were feeling the pressure.  Major-General Ivo Thomas, the 43rd Division commander, was an especially humourless and tough task master.  Stanley Christopherson, commander of the Sherwood Rangers, disliked him intensely and called him ‘Von Thoma’ after the German Afrika Korps commander captured at Alamein. Others referred to him simply as ‘Butcher.’  At any rate, the day before, Thomas had sacked one of his brigade commanders, Brigadier Nomran Leslie, also for being slow. Christopherson, for one, had been outraged. It meant, though, they were all under the spotlight more than usual. Orders for the Sherwood Rangers were to get to Point 370 as quickly as possible, but after successfully crossing the river, the DCLI soon became bogged down with fighting German outposts down along the river rather than climbing up to the ridge as ordered. C Squadron of the Sherwood Rangers, leading that morning, now found themselves in an invidious situation: pause and work alongside the DCLI or do as ordered and climb the hill? When challenged by a DCLI captain, Lieutenant Stan Perry, in the lead tank, radioed back for clarification. Get the ridge was the order. 

           

So, that settled it, but it meant they were now advancing up a winding road with no infantry support. Tanks provided the fire-power but infantry offered vital eyes and ears. It was hard, even with a tank commander’s head and shoulders out of the turret, to see or hear hidden enemy troops.

 

They were winding their way up, along the high-hedged road, when Perry heard a loud bang and suddenly the radio aerial slithered like a whip over the turret and disappeared, hit by a panzerfaust round; it could have been so easily very much worse, but while their own intercom still worked, Perry now had no radio contact with either the rest of the troop or anyone else in the squadron or regiment – a significant problem since he was leading and because tanks were more effective when working together.  On balance, though, he thought he should continue on his way but lay off the track in case of mines. This meant working his way into the fields and through the trees, but he reckoned it would be safer; he just hoped the lads behind would follow even though they could no longer hear him.

 

Visibility in this close country was still difficult. Small arms were chattering and mortars falling and exploding as the infantry further down the slopes tried to push up onto the ridge. Perry scanned carefully for panzerfausts but didn’t spot the second warhead fired directly at them, but there was another loud crash and the lap-gunner cursed that his trousers had been burned. It seemed a panzerfaust had been fired and punched a glob of steel through the front glacis and straight between the legs of Perry’s co-driver. It was something of a miracle that apart from his singed trousers, no-one was hurt. 

 

Finally emerging through the wood at the top of the ridge, Perry saw a junction up ahead and aware these were good places for hidden anti-tank guns, moved off the road again and into field, rejoining the road near a roadside calvary shrine.  His gunner, a devout Catholic, asked if he could get out an offer a prayer.  ‘I drew the line at him dismounting,’ said Perry, ‘but I did stop to let him say a prayer.’

They rumbled on a short distance, but he couldn’t see the other two tanks in his troop, which meant his tank was the only one up on the ridge, and already attracting a barrage of mortars and small arms. Bullets and shrapnel clattered against the hull.  ‘It was getting pretty hairy,’ admitted Perry, who decided it would be prudent to half close the twin lids on his turret. As he put out his arm to pull back one of the covers, he felt a stab of pain and thought he’d been stung by a bee or wasp.  But his arm flopped down his side and then he saw he’d been shot – a sniper bullet had hit him in the arm but had been stopped by the bone.  It hurt a bit but wasn't bleeding too badly and Perry had enough of his wits about him still to order the line of poplar trees up ahead to be sprayed by their machine-guns and blasted with HE. ‘And the first one we did,’ said Perry, ‘a figure dropped out of it, and I think that was the sniper who got me.’

 

Despite his wound – and very nearly being drilled in the head – he ordered his tank to press on. This was incredibly perilous: for all their fire-power and steel plating, tanks were very vulnerable when isolated. Nor did Perry have any idea where the tanks following him were and without his radio could do nothing to call them up. His arm hurt all right, but he reckoned it was going to hurt whether he was there on the ridge or back at the RAP.  His operator made a splint for him and forward they went towards Berjou. 

 

The enemy, men from the 3. Fallschirmjäger – Parachute – Division, were demonstrating just how effective they could be with a handful of machine-guns, mortars and panzerfausts in this countryside of woods, dense hedges and lines of trees.  Perry’s tank had not progressed much further when they were hit by a third panzefaust warhead, this time in the track drive sprocket on the driver’s side.  This meant they could now only drive on one track, damage that would have been enough for most crews to bale out.  ‘But I had a very good driver,’ said Perry, ‘and by inching forward then braking a bit, and then inching forward a bit more, he could drag the dead track and still move a bit.’ A little while after, the wireless operator managed to rig up a secondary aerial and although they still couldn’t make contact with the other two tanks in his troop, Perry was able to speak to Jack Holman – who told them to try and get back to the river.

           

Tank warfare could be confusing at the very best of times but for Perry, cut adrift from both the rest of his troop and the squadron, it was particularly alarming. He was wounded, so too was his tank, and travelling on one track the couple of miles back to the river was a torturous prospect. ‘We went back cross-country again,’ he said. ‘I was supposed to take the road but I was always a bit wary of roads.’

 

Third in line in C Squadron was Lieutenant Stuart Hills’s troop; his tank had been the seventh to ford the Noireau.  The plan had been for Stan Perry’s troop to get up onto the ridge then turn left into a field that marked the highest point round about, and which overlooked Berjou a half-mile further on. Lieutenant Galvin, who had briefly commanded Hills’s tank at Hottot, led the next troop and was due to push on towards Berjou from the left.  Hills’ troop were then to drive on straight down the road and into the village. For Hills and those crossing the Noireau further behind Perry’s troop, the start had not been half as bad as they’d feared. Leading 4 Troop, Hills had had no trouble at all as they’d climbed the road and gone through the wood; clearly, the enemy had been pushed back up onto the high ground beyond.

           

But up on the ridge it was all going horribly wrong. Unbeknown to Perry, his troop sergeant had already been knocked out on the way up to the ridge, which had held up those following.  Corporal Arthur Brooks had been a little way behind and eventually emerged onto the high ground, although by that time Perry’s tank had turned back into the woods. By now, however, Brooks was on his own up there and over the net was frantically asking for urgent support. It was late morning; actions like this always sucked up time. Brooks didn’t know what had happened to Perry but knew his troop commander’s radio was down and that he’d almost certainly been hit. Clearly, Brooks needed reinforcing and quickly, so it was agreed that Lieutenant Galvin would push forward with his troop and turn left onto a rise in the ground overlooking Berjou. Then Hills would follow with his troop and push on through to the village. 

 

Hills waited in the wood for news that Galvin and his troop were safely onto the high ground but time ticked by and no word came. They tried to raise him on the net but got no response. Brooks was still frantically asking for urgent help. Inwardly cursing Galvin, Hills decided to press on. He wondered where on earth they were – and cursed the lack of infantry too. Brooks reported that he had a handful with him but nothing more. Over the radio it was clear that Jack Holman, still back down near the river, was having a difficult time trying to get the infantry to play ball; they were still clearing the woods and the slopes where the tanks were not able to venture. It was frustrating. Once again, going into action with an unfamiliar infantry battalion had led to poor co-operation. 

           

As Hills rumbled forward and emerged from the woods, it was clear the plan was falling apart badly. There was still no word from Galvin. Now, as Hills’ troops pushed out into the open farmland, mortars and small-arms crashed around them. Turning left, the three tanks climbed up towards the high ground where Brooks was valiantly trying to hold on. Hills tried to keep his head down as much as possible and told his crew to keep swivelling their periscopes watching out for panzerfausts, but within moments a fizz of a sniper’s bullet whipped past his head, just inches away. 

Mortars continued to rain down and shells too, seemingly from a wood on the far side of the village. Brooks had wounded men from Perry’s second tank on board, and so having safely joined him, ordered him to move back towards the wood and radioed for the Essex Yeomanry to shell the likely enemy gunners. Meanwhile, they opened fire on a thick copse just a hundred yards or so ahead of them. With shells crashing around them, mortars bursting and clattering against the the hulls, and smoke drifting over the battlefield, all they could do was fire HE and spray the trees and hedgerows with their Brownings and hope for the best. 

 

‘The next five minutes,’ noted Arthur Reddish, the co-driver in Hills’s crew, ‘were horrendous.’ First came word of Frank Galvin.  It seemed he had not turned up onto the hill but instead had pushed on towards Berjou and been hit – by what was not clear, but his tank had been brewed up and the entire crew killed in the inferno. Moments after this news had reached them, Corporal Brook’s tank was hit as he returned towards the woods, the blast blowing him clear of the turret.  Seeing this, Sergeant Guy Sanders, who had rescued Lieutenant Campbell’s burning tank just two weeks earlier, jumped down to help Brooks. It was an act of immense bravery but as he did so a renewed flurry of mortars crashed down and both Sanders and Brooks were cut down and killed. Around the same time, Sergeant Sleep, Galvin’s third tank, was drilled in the head by a sniper’s bullet. 

 

Hills sat in his commander’s seat while this carnage unfolded, aware that he was every bit as vulnerable. ‘I had no idea what lay in front or what might happen,’ he wrote. ‘The fatal shot might come from anywhere and I was constantly expecting it.’ Infantry were now catching up and three tanks together made a difference; what’s more, the remaining troops began to arrive and shells from the Essex Yeomanry began to crackle through the air; the wood beyond disappeared amidst of swathe of explosions, dust and smoke. If there were enemy tanks, none were seen; the greatest danger in this countryside and from these German rear-guards was from the ambush; that moment, had now passed. 

           

With the arrival of infantry and artillery support and increased numbers of tanks, Hill 337 was overrun later that afternoon and the village liberated early the following morning, 17 August. Another battle was over, albeit a comparatively small engagement in the big scheme of things. But a dead man was a dead man, whether in a big battle or small.  A life snuffed out, cut short. And eight men in C Squadron were now dead and seven wounded.  Six of those casualties were tank commanders, four of which had been killed, including one of the squadron’s legends, Sergeant Guy Sanders, MM. 

           

Sanders, Brooks and Sleep were recovered by the Sherwood Rangers’ indefatigable padre, Leslie Skinner, on the 17th, and he buried them and carefully marked their graves, just as he had every man in the regiment who’d been killed. Galvin’s tank was still burning, however. It would a few days before it had cooled enough for him to gather the carbonized remains. ‘Complete brew,’ Skinner noted in his pocket casualty book. ‘Bodies unidentifiable – all ash/bones (5 pelvic bones).’

 

All eight Sherwood Rangers now lie in a large Commonwealth War Graves Cemetery to the south-east of Caen. Galvin and his crew are buried together because their remains were indistinguishable. The idea of a memorial to these eight, here at Berjou, really started to take root, however. I had written a book about the Sherwood Rangers and remain very attached to those ordinary but extraordinary men, who endured so much and yet battled their way so incredibly courageously across north-west Europe. But I was also haunted by the eight men who had been killed that day near Berjou.

 

Guy Sanders, for example, was loved, respected and revered. He’d won a Military Medal – the equivalent of a Military Cross for those not officers – at Alamein and only a fortnight before Berjou had performed another breath-taking act of heroism. At the hamlet of La Bigne, their column had been toe-to-bumper climbing up a road through the village. A leading tank had been hit, was on fire, and began rolling backwards. Seeing this would crash into the vehicles behind, Sanders leapt ont the stricken tank, leant into the driver’s compartment and steered the burning beast clear. That action had saved countless lives. Now, trying save yet another man, he’d paid the ultimate prices.  He won a posthumous bar to his MM for this.

 

And then there was Frank Galvin and his crew. There’s some very vivid footage taken by an  Army Film Unit of Galvin and his crew taken near Hottot on around 9 July. They’re readying their tank – the gunner cleans his barrel, the driver nimbly clambers into the driver’s hatch, and Galvin adjusts the headset as he sits in the turret. They all look young, but Galvin wears a slightly anxious expression. No-one within the Sherwood Rangers fraternity could tell me much about him or his crew, but a couple of weeks after my visit to Berjou I was at the Chalke History Festival when I was approached by a man who told me he was called Rupert Brown and that his wife was Frank Galvin’s widow’s niece. I was dumbfounded and delighted in equal measure. Rupert subsequently sent me copies of letters between Galvin and his wife, and photos too. His wife even had the last letter Galvin’s wife had sent him, posted on 15 August, which had been returned to her unopened.  It remains unopened to this day.

This serendipitous meeting with Rupert made me more determined to ensure there was a lasting memorial to these brave, tragic men.  A great friend, Stuart Bertie, a brilliant architect, conceived a stunning design: sheets of steel, to reflect the nature of the tanks they served with, but with the silhouettes of the eight men stamped out and also their names, dates, the regimental crest.  After all, this is about them: young men, not inanimate Sherman tanks. It’s fabulous: striking, profoundly moving, and, I hope, will ensure these men are not forgotten. That they’re still in people’s thoughts even after all these years. I, for one, am truly grateful for the sacrifice they made. 

So now the money has to be raised. It’ll cost around £14,000 all told, so myself, David Christopherson – Stanley’s son and a great friend – historian Saul David, ex-Guardsman Rob Gallimore, my oldest friend Giles Bourne, and our brilliant architect, Stuart Bertie, will be walking from the landing sites on Gold Beach where the Sherwood Rangers came ashore on D-Day and following their route all the way via Bayeux, Tilly-sur-Suelles, Caumont and Ondefontaine and Proust to the River Noireau and the climb to Berjou. Hopefully this 70-mile walk, following in the footsteps of those those band of brothers will ensure this fitting memorial will soon be fixed where those eight men lost their lives back on 16 August 1944.

 

Please do help if you can: https://gofund.me/fbf7cee0

Trooper William John Brownlee, aged 24

Trooper Douglas Dixon, aged 23

Lieutenant James Francis Galvin, aged 24

Sergeant Guy Sanders, aged 35

Sergeant William Arthur Ernest Sleep, aged 32

Trooper Robert Wright, aged 28

Lance-Corporal J. Young, aged 21

title: The Real Lessons of WWII 80 Years On
html:
I had a busy week both taking part in the commemorations for the 80th anniversary of VE Day and talking about the end of the Second World War. There was a new book out, Victory 45, and I was also involved with some of the BBC’s coverage, both on TV and radio. The week saw me travelling from my home in Wiltshire to London to Salford and back again. In between, there was a visit to No. 10 to interview the Prime Minister and I also met a number of public figures, most of whom had been alive to remember VE Day when it actually happened. It’s always an honour and privilege to be part of the BBC’s programming of such events and no matter one’s views on our national broadcaster they do always cover these occasions exceptionally well. And to be part of the commentary team under Paddy O’Connell for the VE Day procession last Monday, 5th May, was pretty special. He’s a master at this: thoughtful, pithy, and with just the right hint of levity when required. Live TV is exciting to be a part of and especially at poignant and moving occasions such as those of last week’s commemorations.

My mind has been full of thoughts, some contradictory, as I ponder those few days. One of the questions I was repeatedly asked was, ‘Why is this 80th anniversary so important?’ I always got the impression the answer the questioners were looking for was something to do with the twilight of the wartime generation. As Paddy commented about veteran Alan Kennett, who formally gave permission for the procession to begin last Monday, ‘He was one of many millions, but is now one in a million.’ That was beautifully put but while it’s certainly sad that those who fought in the war are now slipping out of living memory, I think the anniversary is more important as a reminder as to what can happen if war is allowed to escalate. The origins of this most cataclysmic conflict the world has ever known are not complicated: rising living standards as well as urban populations and a growth in modern technology meeting sudden and dramatic economic crisis, followed by immense political upheaval. History tells us that economic crisis invariably leads to political earthquakes and that when that happens, war is much more likely to follow. Countries tend not to go to war when they’re prosperous and politically stable.

Subscribe

So, my answer was: it’s important because tens of millions were killed as a result of the war, tens of millions more were displaced, borders redrawn, there were untold levels of destruction, misery, mayhem and cruelty, the global order was totally rewired, and we’re still feeling the consequences to this day. The Second World War should forever be a warning of what can happen in our fragile world. That’s why this eighty-year anniversary is important. The war and its consequences should act as a constant reminder of what can go catastrophically wrong.

And yet, here in the UK - and no doubt elsewhere - a survey by LBC Radio showed that 4 in 10 Brits have no idea what VE Day was about, a figure that rises to two-thirds of 18-24 year-olds. I also went on LBC to talk about this. To be honest, I’m never that bothered by polls that show how little younger generations know about history, and I don’t really share the outrage of the Daily Mail and others. When I was a teenager and a young adult I knew nothing about the war, except as a reference point: school had been Colditz, Germany was jokingly referred to as ‘enemy territory’ amongst my friends, and there were war movies to watch on damp winter afternoons on the telly. But I had no idea about the course of the war at all and had never paid it much interest, despite studying history at A-level and at university.

I think my first spark of interest was in 1995 when I and friends attended the 50th anniversary commemorations in London. My Damascene conversion came only when I was twenty-nine; I was playing cricket and a Spitfire flew over. That it was this iconic aircraft had to be pointed out to me by the umpire, but that was it. I’ve been obsessed by those six long years ever since.

I think my late start is far from unusual. Few people take up physics or chemistry in their late twenties but lots who abandoned history at school suddenly become interested a bit later in life. That’s because young folk mostly have very narrow world views: their friends, home, sport, romance, partying and so on. Who cares about the boring old past? Who cares about politics, for that matter? But as life progresses and one’s horizons broaden, understanding how one fits into the great pattern of life becomes more interesting, more relevant, and has more direct bearing on one’s own life. History can provide many of the answers.

On the other hand, as a nation, our horizons, still, broadly seem to be that of the teenager: insular, domestic, and relating to what is immediately in front of us, rather than the bigger threats to our day-to-day lives that are bubbling away further beyond our borders: global warming, shifting world economics and politics, emboldened enemies.

Our defences, however - and those of Western Europe - have become horribly depleted. We’re short of manpower, short of weapons, short of equipment. I know a number of young men who have applied to join the Army and RAF and not been able to find a place despite being university graduates and, as far as I can tell, bright, fit and competent. What??? How can this be? Aren’t we understrength? All are people who would have waltzed in a decade ago. That, I suppose, is what comes of outsourcing recruitment to a private company. One aspiring female officer - supremely fit, clever, keen, and a Cambridge history graduate - was told she’d not made the cut because her mother had had cancer. No wonder numbers in the Army, already low, are lower still than they should be.

After the morning procession last Monday, my podcasting co-host, great friend and now co-author, Al Murray, and I went to No. 10 Downing Street to interview the Prime Minister for our We Have Ways of Making You Talk podcast. It’s a WWII-themed show, rather than one about contemporary politics but we were there to talk to the PM about VE Day and what it meant to him. Our producers had warned me not to be a Rottweiler and to ask fairly anodyne questions. We agreed we’d kick off with, ‘Prime Minister, you’ve been in post for ten months now and understand the pressure of the job, but what do you think it must have been like to be a wartime prime minister?’ Sir Keir admitted it would have been immense although had witnessed President Zelenskyy at first hand and saw the pressures he was under. He then rather unexpectedly launched into his defence manifesto. He pointed out that the first duty of the PM is to defend the country and its people. Yes, absolutely, I thought. I’ve pointed this out to whoever will listen umpteen times in the past. We need to work together with our European neighbours, he added. Again, yes, we absolutely do. Sir Keir also said that while there’s a tendency to move as fast as the slowest in the train, there is now an urgent need to move a lot faster. Time is of the essence. Small and medium size businesses as well as larger industrial concerns have a part to play. All of this was music to my ears.

The USA made itself rich on the back of becoming the Arsenal of Democracy, I pointed out. Couldn’t we in the UK make arms and boost economic growth? Yes, he said, the two went hand-in-hand. And what about mobilizing the people? I mentioned that in the autumn of 1938, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain did not go to war in large part because 92% of this democratic population did not want to. How could we mobilize Britain now, I wondered? Sir Keir replied that he thought people were coming round to the idea and that the need for increased defence spending was more widely understood.

I’m not so sure, and I reckon this is the biggest challenge facing not only the UK but also France, Germany and other Western European countries: how to galvanize their populations and get them to support far, far greater defence spending and mobilization. The priority for most people is what is closest to home: health, cost of living, cost of housing, crime. Statistics from August 2024 showed there were 24 million people in the UK claiming some form of benefits. Of these, 13 million were retired and receiving state pensions, but 9.9 million were of working age. Additionally, 3.9 million people received some form of health-related benefit in 2023-24. That’s nearly 10 million people out of a total population of 68.3 million on welfare. It’s a lot, and a huge chunk of the government budget that cannot be spent on defence, or a host of other urgent requirements for that matter.

There are other solutions, as I’ve outlined in previous columns on Substack: a new European defence bank, for example, which raises capital on government bonds - so, effectively long-term, low-interest loans - but which don’t need to appear on annual government balance sheets. Yet, it seems to me that much of what is needed in the UK, whether urgent defence requirements, cleaning rivers, rebuilding our network of roads, youth schemes and how to find a labour force to replace the vast number of migrant workers coming into the UK, are all vying for a dwindling pool of government cash and rising national debt against what most people view as entirely different and more important concerns.

Something has to give. My impression of the Prime Minister was that he’s committed, sincere, and knows what he needs to do. Whether Starmer can convince the voting public, however, especially with Reform dangling impossible-to-achieve policies in front of the population, is another matter. The response to our interview on social media was fascinating. About 80% appeared to think it was interesting and a good thing to have done, but 20% or so accused us of becoming ‘woke’ and of betraying ourselves by talking with a ‘traitor.’ Most of this was little more than contradictory and non-sensical bile but it was amazing to discover a certain part of the population really believes that speaking to a prime minister, whatever his political affiliation, was some kind of betrayal. This is what our political leaders have to deal with: a barrage of conflicting but vehemently held views, while trying to steer a course that will enable the PM to fulfill his most important task: protecting us, the population of the UK, from outside threats.

As a historian, though, the patterns of history worry me, and the stark reality is this: that the USA is now demanding that NATO’s European members provide 70% of its numbers and 50% of its materiel supplies - ie, arms and weapons, whether it be missiles, drones, ammunition, tanks or jet aircraft. Oh, and by the way, should matters kick-off in the Indo-Pacific, that figure will rise to pretty much 100% in both.

Is Europe ready for this? At present, not in any way. And is the population of the UK, for one, prepared to play its part? No, not if it means cuts elsewhere, whether winter fuel allowance or welfare.

This is the price of the 80 years of peace, so hard fought for, at such gargantuan cost, eighty years ago. Peace is so standard, so expected and accepted, no-one in the UK can imagine existing in any other state. As a consequence, the threat is not taken seriously. We’ve become an inward-looking and complacent society, and one where the best part of 10 million take from the state rather than adding to the coffers. That’s nearly 15% of the total population and more than a quarter of working age adults in the UK. And while it is undeniably true there are far too many people living in poverty in the UK, the vast majority of this country have never had it so good. There are an average of 1.9 television sets per household, and some 34 million cars for a total population of 68 million of all ages. Sixty years ago, 33% of total household spending went on food, now it’s around 10%, but we still want it to be cheaper. Nearly £100 billion was spent on holidays last year and £54.2 billion on new cars – incidentally around the same figure as the UK defence budget.

No-one, though, wants to take a cut, or a step backwards. Not when life still seems much the same on a day-today basis, with the local pub still serving pints, a plethora of coffee shops in every town, McDonalds, cinemas, endless streaming services offering even more endless TV dramas, reality shows, sport in high definition, and social media offering an unstoppable array of cute dogs, beautiful people and everyday folk living the dream. Footage of the horrors in Ukraine or Gaza or elsewhere might galvanize some to drive a van of supplies to Lviv, but most put it to the back of their minds. After all, such scenes happen elsewhere, not here. And I entirely sympathize with this; I like my comfortable life too. It’s embarrassing to think how much I spend on having fun compared with my parents, for example.

There is a way round this dilemma, however, and that is to fund dramatic defence increases by a Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, or a European Defence Bank; they’re two concepts much the same. The UK is set to sign a defence deal with the EU, which is all to the good. Starmer appears to have an excellent relationship with his fellow political leaders in Europe.

But what is also needed is far greater dialogue on this. Workers still need to man the factories; an urgent sense of national purpose and pride – nationhood not nationalism - has to be forged. The very real threat we face, and the fragility of the peace we so enjoy, has to be underlined. And people should be told that only by dramatically rearming, by creating a strong conventional deterrent that does what it needs to do - deter our enemies - can our long-term peace be safeguarded and secured. It has never been easier to sell a message than today. ‘Repeat, repeat, repeat,’ was Josef Goebbel, the Nazi propaganda chief’s mantra. What he would have done for the 21st century’s information tools.

So, this is the lesson of the Second World War and what we need to focus on 80 years after it was all over: that it should never have happened in the first place, that the consequences of allowing our defences to become so depleted directly led to it starting in the first place, then evolving and sweeping across the planet like wildfire.

Because we must never, ever reach that state again.

title: VE Day 80 - We Must Learn the Lessons
html:
There had been a palpable sense for all the Allied troops advancing through Germany in the second half of April 1945 that it was surely now only a matter of time before the war was over.  No-one wanted to die but somehow especially not when peace was so obviously close at hand.  For the Sherwood Rangers Yeomanry and their accompanying infantry that meant advancing cautiously and shooting up and spraying with machine-gun anything that looked likely to pose a threat.

It hadn’t stopped the killing, however.  On 19 April, just south of Bremen, Lieutenant Denis Elmore and two of his crew, Troopers Charlie Harkness and Denis Miles, had been killed when their Sherman tank had been hit by an anti-tank round.  The three men in the turret had stood no chance as the tank had immediately burned fiercely, so that it was only three days later, on 22 April, that the indefatigable regimental padre, Major Leslie Skinner, had managed to recover the carbonised remains and then bury them.

That same day, having been in state of numb shock for a couple of days, Lieutenant Stuart Hills sat down to write to Elmore’s mother. Hills and Elmore had been the very best of friends for years; Hills’ parents had lived in Hong Kong and he’d been sent to boarding school at Tonbridge, where he’d met and immediately bonded with Elmore.  The two had even opened the batting together during a school cricket match at Lord’s, Hills had spent much of his holidays with Elmore’s family, and they’d both joined up and been posted to the Sherwood Rangers together, landing with the regiment on D-Day.

Until recently, Elmore had been the regiment’s intelligence officer and could easily have avoided further front-line action.  He had pleaded, though, to be given another chance to lead a troop before the fighting was over. It had cost him his life.  He’d been just twenty-one.  

‘I loved him better than anyone else in the world,’ Hills wrote to Elmore’s mother, his raw grief bursting off the page, ‘so I know just how you feel, and the bottom has been knocked out of my world.  His popularity in the regiment both with officers and the men was so great, that a sort of shadow seems to have beset us all – in spite of the fact that we have all become hardened to death.’  He told her that Denis had every quality that was best in a man.  He was so very sorry and sent his deepest sympathy. If there was anything at all he could do for her, he would. ‘The supreme sacrifice, as Denis and I always remarked to each other,’ he added, ‘was ‘the luck of the game’ and Denis made it very, very nobly; he will never be forgotten.’

How hard it was to bear, all these terrible losses.  The commander of the Sherwood Rangers, Lieutenant-Colonel Stanley Christopherson wrote to her too, as did Padre Skinner, and as did Myrtle Kellett, the widow of the former commanding officer, ‘Flash’ Kellett, just as they had every time a man had been killed.  They did the same for Troopers Miles and Harkness too, although it made a big difference when they knew the men personally, as Christopherson and Skinner had Elmore.  Christopherson acknowledged just how inseparable Denis had been with Hills and another officer, Dick Holman, and how hard his loss had hit them.  ‘But as I told them,’ he wrote to her, ‘Denis had so much good in him that such goodness simply can't just end – it must go on in some form.’

I’m writing this on 5 May 2025 and have been thinking much about the eightieth anniversary of the end of the Second World War.  The losses suffered - the tens of millions dead, the even more millions more displaced, the immense destruction, are barely comprehendable.  With the enemies of democracy growing bolder, this anniversary seems suddenly more relevant and poignant than others.  It should be a warning: this is what can happen if we don’t do all we can to prevent it.  ‘Success in war,’ as Matthew Syed wisely wrote a little while ago, ‘is not just about how much you have, but how much you are prepared to give up.’  War again in Western Europe still seems very distant to the vast majority, which is why we’re dragging our heels with rearmament. We don’t want to give up our affluent lifestyles.  In his groundbreaking book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, the great economist, Maynard Keynes, began by writing about the golden age before 1914, when Britain seemed prosperous and the modern world appeared to be uninterruptible.   A Londonder, he marvelled, could telephone friends, travel cheaply and easily, and could sample products from around the world. ‘But most important of all,’ he noted, ‘he regarded this state of affairs as normal, certain, and permanent, except in the direction of further improvement, and any deviation from its as aberrant, scandalous, and avoidable.’

Catastrophic war followed this moment of comfortable complacency as it did again a generation later, which was why Denis Elmore had his life cut short on an unremarkable street in a Bremen suburb that April day in 1945.  In 1914, Europe had largely been in that happy state of peace for ninety-nine years.  It’s now eighty since the Second World War yet it feels, suddenly, as though many of the old certainties are imperilled.  And as in 1914 and 1939, a future war for us in the west is entirely avoidable.  We should all be thinking this week about what the war caused, the misery, suffering, pain and carnage. And we should all strive harder to ensure nothing like this ever happens again.

I often think of the men of the Sherwood Rangers partly because they achieved so much in the war but also because they were such ordinary, everyday people, most of whom had never expected to go to off and fight; the majority would not have worn a uniform had it not been for the war.  Their diaries, letters and journals, especially, show what fundamentally humane, decent people they were.  Reading their words their characters and personalities are so identifiable.  They really were the very best of British: self-deprecating, with a love of the ridiculous, of pranks, of letting their hair down when allowed, taking war seriously but not life too much so.  At Christmas 1944 they saved up their sweet and chocolate rations to give them to the local Dutch children.  Two of the men dressed up as Father Christmas and an elf, and on a hastily fashioned sled, towed by a light Stuart tank, they drove through the town and handed out their gifts.  In February, near the German town of Cleve, Stanley Christopherson carely noted in his journal spotting his first snowdrop. And this despite the death, carnage, violence and destruction. How can one not admire these people?

The fighting continued during those last weeks.  Bremen fell and then the Sherwood Rangers pushed north-east into the heartland between Bremen and Hamburg. They suffered their last death on Wednesday, 2 May.  The area round about was low lying, and sodden, often boggy, peaty ground.  Roads had been blown and booby traps and mines laid.  Progress was slow as engineers tried to pick a way through or fill in and bridge craters.  Trooper Lawrence Carter was in A1 Echelon, but along with a military policeman was trying to direct traffic around a crater when they were both shot and killed by a sniper.  ‘Buried both by roadside,’ noted Padre Skinner.

The next day, the regiment crossed the Hame-Ooste Canal and took the pretty village of Karlshöfen without opposition.  It was a small farming community with a number of large brick eighteenth and nineteenth century houses and barns, as well as a church and war memorial to those from the village killed in the last war.  It was decided that its houses and plentiful barns and yards made it an ideal place to set up RHQ. 

The sun was shining that third day of May.  Summer was on its way.  The three large oak trees at the mouth of the farm’s entrance were just starting to come into leaf.  There was dust amidst the cobbled stones that led to the large old farmhouse Christopherson had chosen as his own billet.  Jeeps, Dingos and lorries were parked up in the yard as were Robin Hood, the CO’s tank, and Maid Marion and the other RHQ tanks.  The village had a touch of Englishness about it – an architectural style and leafy ambience reminiscent of Lincolnshire and parts of Norfolk – and blissfully intact.  Really, there was little sign of the war at all and nothing whatever to suggest the horrors of Sanbostel less than ten miles across the fields.

Brigadier Pryor-Palmer, the commander of 8th Armoured Brigade, to which the Sherwood Rangers were attached, called in for tea that afternoon to brief Stanley on the next operation, which was an assault on the coastal port of Bremerhaven.  Once again, the brigade was to be supporting the 43rd Wessex Division.  Once Pryor-Palmer had left the rest of the afternoon and evening was spent making plans.  It was around 8.30pm that night that Christopherson was summoned from the farmhouse to Robin Hood and where he was told an important message had arrived for him from Brigade.  Sergeant William Pick was waiting for him and handed over a scrap of paper torn from an exercise book.

‘This message has just come over the air from Brigade Headquarters,’ Pick told him.  He looked flushed and a little agitated. Christopherson’s first thought was one of slight irritation at the scrap of paper and badly hand-written scrawl.  Then he read the words that had been written down.  ‘No advance beyond present positions. Stop.  No further harassing fire. Stop.  No further tactical move unless ordered. Stop.  BBC News Flash confirmed. Stop. German Army on 21 Army Group front surrenders WEF 08.00 hrs 5 May 1945.  Stop.  Details as to procedure later. Stop.’

The war was over. 

‘My first reaction,’ he noted, ‘was a feeling of profound relief, followed by indescribable exhilaration, and finally a sorrowful longing for those special friends, no longer with us, with whom I wished to share this moment.’ It was, none the less, a moment for celebration.  A large stock of captured champagne had been given to them by the 51st Highland Division after crossing the Rhine and this was now brought up and many bottles opened – and drunk.

Stuart Hills had been out with his troop that afternoon and it was getting dark as he headed back to RHQ in his Dingo.  Suddenly, hundreds of brightly coloured Very lights were shooting up into the air like fireworks. ‘That’s either a signal for a night attack,’ he said to his driver, Bert Crowhurst, ‘or else peace has been declared.  Step on it and we’ll find out.’ At RHQ, it was mayhem, the party already in full swing.  Hills felt stunned with relief and overwhelming joy but then, after about half an hour or so, he missed Denis more than at any other moment and so he went to bed instead. 

Hills woke the next day in a bed with sheets and with the sun pouring through the windows and birdsong filling the air.  They had all been waiting so long for this morning.  ‘No more death, shooting or loud explosions,’ he noted.  ‘We could rise from our beds and go to breakfast without fear of being blown to bits.  Everything that for so long had held us down and ruled our lives had now been shattered in an instant and we were free – we were at peace.’

But at what a price.  In all, the Sherwood Rangers, who had gone to war in 1940 and who had fought through much of the North Africa campaign before north-west Europe, lost 148 men killed and 299 wounded just in the eleven months from D-Day to 5 May 1945.  That amounted to some 40% of the entire regiment and 150% of those actually serving in tanks at any one time.  It was a hideously large number.  Stanley Christopherson was one of only two officers who had set off for Palestine in January 1940 still serving with the regiment.  On one occasion during the war in north-west Europe, he’d been sheltering in a slit-trench trying to make himself as small as possible, and feeling wet, cold and frightened as shells rained down. ‘I made three resolutions,’ he wrote, ‘which I was determined to keep after the war - should I survive. First, never to be bored; second, never to be frightened again; and third, when slowly slumbering into a steaming hot bath, to say, “Thank God for this Hot Bath - Amen”.’

So, let’s hope this week of commemoration we use it not just to remember the immense sacrifice made for the eighty years of peace we have enjoyed, but also to realize and accept the fragility of that freedom.  Let’s not make the same mistake as that generation of the Golden Age before 1914 or those who acted too late to prevent war in 1939.  We must not sleepwalk through complacency but act now, with purpose, urgency and with the full recognition that  the freedoms we so cherish are worth making some sacrifices for now, so that we don’t have to pay an even greater one.
excerpt:
There had been a palpable sense for all the Allied troops advancing through Germany in the second half of April 1945 that it was surely now only a matter of time before the war was over.  No-one wanted to die but somehow especially not when peace was so obviously close at hand.  For the Sherwood Rangers Yeomanry and their accompanying infantry that meant advancing cautiously and shooting up and spraying with machine-gun anything that looked likely to pose a threat.

It hadn’t stopped the killing
author: James Holland

title: The Battle for Berlin 1945 - Part 2
html:
“We are in a vast cauldron,” noted the seventeen year-old boy soldier, Helmut Altner. “In front of us, around us and behind us, is an enveloping hell as the Russians drum on our trenches.  The explosions go on and on.  Our ears have long since been deafened.  Hardly anyone speaks.  Only when a fountain of dirt and steel erupts close by does an angry word escape that one can read from their lips.”

It was a little after 5am, and Marshal Georgy Zhukov’s barrage to open the Battle of Berlin was suddenly, earth-shatteringly, under way.  Altner had only been a soldier for a little over a fortnight but even the veterans had rarely, if ever, experienced such an intense rain of fire as this.  Altner was with fellow teenagers and fifty- and sixty-year-olds in the Grenadier Training and Replacement Battalion 309, hastily formed, even more hastily and cursorily trained, and then packed off to the Seelow Heights, forty-five miles east of Berlin and overlooking the River Oder and the massed armies of Zhokov’s 1st Belorussian Front.

From his trench in the reserve lines, Altner could see burning barns and villages standing out in the distance like torches in the night.  Refugees were flooding back, dragging their belongings in prams and handcarts, or on their backs.  Altner watched as a dazed woman stumbled past him wearing a dressing gown, her hair loose and wild, eyes wide and blank.  Her mouth was moving but made no sound.  Ammunition and supply carts surprised by the attack were also racing back along the road, the drivers wilding whipping their horses while shells screamed overhead.  Altner thought the refugees looked like creatures of the underworld – women, children and old men surprised in their sleep, some only half-dressed. In their faces he saw both despair deadly fear.

Then, after half an hour of this torrent of steel, the shelling abruptly stopped.  For a while, Altner could barely hear a thing, so deafened was he from the barrage.  Gradually, his battered ears adjusted and he became aware of heavy small arms fire.  Then shots were whipping by, a bursts of machine-gun fire was ringing out.  He and his new comrades were unsure what to do, because although they weren’t in the forward lines they had still to be issued any weapons…

From his command post on the Reitwien Spur, the end of the fish hook that swung east from the rest of the ridgeline of the Seelow Heights, Marshal Zhukov felt certain few German troops could have survived such an opening onslaught.  He was possibly right had they been where his artillery had been aiming, but General Heinrici, the German army group commander, had correctly predicted Zhukov’s opening move and had already pulled his men in the German Ninth Army back to the secondary lines.  As a result, casualties had been remarkably slight despite the shock and awe.

At 5.30am, with the guns suddenly and dramatically silent, a single searchlight had been directed vertically into the sky, the signal for the other 140 to shine theirs horizontally with the effect of a billion candlepower.  This cunning plan, was, however, a total debacle.  As anyone who has ever driven in fog will know, strong beams simply bounce back off smoke and mist and this was exactly what happened; the searchlights blinded only the attackers rather than the Germans.

General Chuikov’s 8th Guards Army stumbled forward over the flood plain, becoming increasingly bogged down in the mire, made rapidly worse by the weight of vehicles on such soft and boggy ground.  No-one could see anything much until daylight and then it was German observers who had the best view; they could look down on the massed Red Army forces. Chuikov’s men were bunched together and sitting ducks.  Rarely had the under-strength German artillery had such easy targets.  Carnage ensued.

Meanwhile, to the south, Marshal Konev’s 1st Ukrainian Front also attacked.  Zhukov’s rival in the race for Berlin had half the forces and was to the south-east of Berlin, and, on paper at any rate, had a tougher challenge.  The River Oder had weaved its way to the south-east, but a tributary, the River Neisse, wiggled roughly south-north and unlike on Zhukov’s front, Konev’s men had no bridgehead over the river at all.  On the far side was the flood plain, which was a few hundred metres deep in some places but several kilometres wide elsewhere, before rising to a lower ridge than that of the more pronounced Seelow Heights.  The Germans had prepared plenty of trenches here with machineguns and mortars with interlocking fields of fire as well as laying coils of wire and minefields.  The river was only around 20 yards wide, but still presented a sizeable obstacle to overcome.

Konev’s plan, however, was far better than that of Zhukov’s bull-in-a-china-shop approach.  Before the attack began, combat engineers were ready for mine-clearance and bridging at no less than 150 points.  Konev’s preliminary artillery barrage was also longer and fired deeper, allowing the infantry to wade over and move across in boats and start moving forward behind the rolling artillery fire.  By 9am on 16 April, Konev’s engineers had the first of the bigger bridges across, capable of taking a 30-ton load, while 60-ton bridges, able to hold the heaviest tanks, followed soon after.  It was a remarkable acheivement.

By the morning of 17 April, Konev’s front  was already halfway to Cottbus – they’d advanced some 6-7 miles and had crushed the German front lines.  At the same time, Zhukov’s forces were still struggling across the flood plain, continuing to get bogged down in the mud and drainage ditches and still being hammered to German artillery by being too bunched together.  Increasingly frustrated, Zhukov then threw his tank armies into the fray; as was the case with the Allies, most tank regiments were organized and designed for exploitation. Infantry and engineers - and some tanks - were to blast a hole in the line, then the armour would be thrown in to make the breakthrough.

When Stalin learned that Zhukov had committed his armour before the breakthrough had happened he was furious - and baited his senior battlefield commander that he might well give Berlin to Konev instead.  As Stalin was well aware this was precisely what Zhukov feared most.  Rather than pausing and reconsidering his battle plan, however, Zhukov merely threw yet more troops into the breech.  With the clock ticking inexorably, he knew the race was now even more firmly on that it had been at the outset.  He would bludgeon his way forward, battering a way through with the lives of his men.  Casualties were horrendous, but Zhukov could afford it.

To the south that day, 17 April, Konev’s forces managed to get over the River Spree as it ran south-east of Berlin.  Bridging equipment hadn’t caught up with his lead troops but they discovered a fordable stretch where the water was only one metre deep - a depth that T-34 tanks could easily wade through.  One tank brigade after another made it across against ever-crumbling opposition.   

While Zhukov remained in his clay bunker on the Reitwein Ridge watching his massed forces getting hammered by German guns, Konev was living it up in luxurious schloss near Cottbus.  Late on 17 April, Konev called Stalin and asked permission to turn his tank armies – the Third and Fourth Guards – towards Berlin via Zossen.  Stalin asked Konev whether he knew that Zossen was the Headquarters of the Oberkommando der Heeres, the German Army..  Konev replied that he did know this.  “Very well,” said Stalin. “I agree. Turn your tank armies on Berlin.”

There was now an argument for putting Zhukov’s 1st Belorussian Front onto the defensive, and holding the crumbling German Ninth Army where it was, while Konev snuck in behind and into the city.  It would certainly have saved a lot of Red Army lives. Zhukov, however, was never going to let this happen and with news reaching him of Konev’s advance, he ordered his armies to bludgeon their way forward even harder, no matter the cost.

On 18 April, the third day of the battle, Zhukov’s men finally fought their way over and off the Seelow Heights, Helmut Altner and the dazed and battered men - and teenagers - of the 9. Armee pulling back in understandable disarray, but in severe danger of being cut off and surrounded; after all, Konev’s 1st Ukrainian Front was now to the south and ahead of them to the west, while Zhukov’s armies were starting to sweep around to the north too.

Meanwhile, Konev’s troops were now speeding towards Zossen.  His men had a far greater distance to go than those of Zhukov, but had one massive advantage: running from Cottbus to Lubben to Berlin was one of Hitler’s first Autobahn’s built in 1930s.  This road is now the A15 and A13 – but in 1945, it was a big, wide, concrete roadway that allowed a massive flow of armour and vehicles, including 15,000 US trucks. It was no wonder Konev’s men were making such progress.

The Red Army casualties already lost - approaching half a million, dead, wounded and missing - almost defied belief yet there was still plenty of fighting to come, as I’ll be writing about in my next piece on the Battle for Berlin.

title: MAKE EUROPE STRONG AGAIN
html:
A couple of weeks ago I was at NATO Headquarters in Brussels for a workshop to discuss the future of the organization’s defence challenges. There were two dozen of us: former generals, intelligence operatives, politicians, diplomats, academics, defence analysts, tech bros and even senior scientists, and drawn from across NATO members. It’s fascinating - and troubling - that while everyone in that room was utterly convinced of the need for European NATO members to dramatically rearm, the wider public of most countries in the west are far less troubled. Rather, for most people, worries and anxieties are more local: the challenges of day-to-day life and what is immediately in front of them. The most recent Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN) in the UK, for example, listed the cost of living, the NHS, the economy, crime, housing, and climate change and the environment as the top five concerns, and in that order.

Much further down the list are worries about defence and whether Putin’s Russia - or any other of our enemies - poses an existential threat. Yet, the global order is shifting, our enemies are becoming emboldened and our stoutest and most important ally in Europe, the USA, is going through a seismic shift in outlook and approach. The ideals of Presidents Roosevelt and Truman, who profoundly believed in democracy, global prosperity, low tariffs and free trade and then of President Eisenhower, who chose to have the USA be the military dominant partner in NATO, have all been dramatically kicked into the long grass since 20 January this year.

Subscribe

NATO’s European members remain inextricably linked militarily to the United States through satellites, shared systems and, of course, intelligence. This cannot be unpicked, and nor should it be, but much has changed: Europe now needs to stand on its own two feet militarily. The US is expecting European members of NATO to provide 70% of the footfall and 50% of the materiel to defence on the continent going forward. It doesn’t matter what President Eisenhower wanted back in 1952; it’s now 2025 and the current President wants this to change. Yet right now, NATO’s European members are a long way from 70% footfall and 50% supply. What’s more, those figures being demanded by the US apply now or in the near future, could easily change again. If America gets drawn militarily further into the Indo-Pacific, for example, that is where its military will head. And Europe can go hang.

So, on the face of it, the problems confronting democratic Europe appear immense. History tells us that global economic disorder, as I have written about before in these pages, does not dovetail well with long-term peace. Rather, it leads to political turmoil and very often war. Europe is already struggling badly economically and the decisions across the Atlantic look set to make that situation even worse. Domestic troubles top the concerns of the voting populace, making mobilization a huge issue; our armed forces in Europe are currently tiny, and not least in Britain, France and Germany. With this in mind, political leaders are wondering how to repair potholes and fund health systems ahead of how to urgently rearm. ‘The coffers are bare,’ comes the cry. Meanwhile, an emboldened Russia, apparently gaining the admiration rather than condemnation from its biggest historic enemy of the past eighty years, continues to fire ever-more missiles at beleaguered Ukraine. And if Putin is allowed to prevail there, where else will his ambition lead him? All in all, the future is troubling, to say the very least.

Yet, the road ahead can and should be far brighter for Western Europe. The population of Russia is shy of 144 million and declining; the USA’s population is 340 million. By contrast, the population of Europe is 744 million and filled with brilliant minds and enough people to achieve all that needs to be achieved. The EU represents the third largest economic bloc in the world.

What’s more, there are ways and means of mobilizing and preparing Europe for any future conflict that can enhance many people’s lives and lead to a dramatic boost in the economy. Ten years ago in Sweden, for example, the government introduced the Total Defence Duty, which made everyone aged 16 to 70 eligible for national service. This was greeted with dismay by some, but actually, the Swedes have discovered that it has instead led to greater political awareness, an increased sense of national cohesion and a less self-centred society. Total Defence Duty might mean military service but it could also be served in a civilian capacity - with rescue services, childcare and healthcare, for example. It also stretches to ‘general national service obligation in activities that must also function in the event of danger of war, or war.’

There is some talk now that all NATO members in Europe should adopt a similar approach. Not everyone is cut out for military service and even within the military there are today many roles that do not involve being in frontline infantry units, for example. The belief is that such an obligatory service can help create a sense of purpos and unity and be used as a means of generating bottom-up human capital. Advocates believe there are huge benefits to society as a whole if structured correctly. I’m not so sure, but we certainly need to increase the size of our armed forces and that applies to both full-time and part-time reservists. Highlighting the broader benefits of service is certainly key to this.

There is also a way of funding dramatically increased defence spending across the board without further bankrupting government coffers. Now being taken very seriously is a plan to create a Defence, Security and Resilience Bank - effectively an allied bank based along much the same lines as the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. This is what is known as a Multilateral Lending Institution - or MLI - and provides concrete plan to finance national security.

The idea is actually pretty straightforward. The DSR Bank would be built around sovereign guarantees provided by its member states — primarily European democracies to begin with, but open to values-based partners further afield, such as Canada, Japan or South Korea. These guarantees are the engine of this proposed new Bank: they don’t involve upfront spending, but rather sit on the Bank’s balance sheet as financial assets. This in turn allows it to raise capital on global bond markets at the cheapest possible rates.

For those in the dark about how this works, bonds are debt securities sold to investors. Bonds are effectively a loan, usually issued by governments. When someone buys a bond, the purchaser is essentially lending money to the issuer in exchange for regular interest payments or a return of the value plus interest at a specified future dates. The larger the economy of a government and the more stable it is, the greater the value of the government bond.

So, alongside raising capital through bonds, member nations would also contribute paid-in subscribed capital. But again, this is not a hard cost — rather, it is an investment. It sits as an asset on national accounts, counts toward a country’s defence investment, and carries a powerful multiplier effect: for every pound or euro subscribed, many more can be mobilised.

The genius lies in the structure. Because the Bank holds these guarantees and subscribed capital as assets, it gives member governments breathing space. They can ramp up rearmament and build long-term resilience without inflating their own national debt or triggering politically toxic cuts elsewhere. Defence, in other words, is no longer being pitted against healthcare or education – or even repairing potholes. Rather, defence investment and spending becomes part of a broader strategy for economic growth as well as national security. The Bank would issue long-term, AAA-rated bonds – ie, with the highest possible guarantees and security - backed by the full faith and credit of its membership, and then channel those funds directly into procurement, vital infrastructure, supply chain strengthening, and technologies that can be then used in both military and civilian day-to-day capacities; as everyone knows, there’s nothing like military advancement in developing future technology as a whole. The Second World War, and the dramatic developments that witnessed, is a case in point.

In other words, the DSR Bank offers a mechanism that turns shared risk into shared strength — a financial architecture for deterrence, built not on fear, but on collective resolve.

And the loans issued by the Bank would allow nations to act immediately, investing at scale in the defence industrial base. This would massively boost economic growth — and, critically, right here in Europe. It would also grow international markets and provide a long-term foundation to sustain Europe’s defence industry well beyond any single crisis. Europe would become not just better defended, but a strategic hub of global security.

In other words, Europe can become the new arsenal of democracy. We have the people, the brains, the scale and the wherewithal. What’s not to like? And, as I write this, the plan already has formal backing from the European Parliament, while John Healey, the UK Defence Secretary, confirmed in the House of Commons on 22 April that the UK government was working on the initiative. Everything is in place for the Bank to be operational by 2026.

The challenge, then, is not one of manpower or possibility - but of political will. The advantages of democracies - that the people regularly get to choose their political leaders - are also their shortcomings: that governments tend to think in short-term cycles and the next election rather than taking a long view. ‘No Russian tanks will be crossing the Pyrenees,’ noted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of Spain, for instance. Maybe not, but Spain is a part of NATO, part of an economic bloc and rearmament can and should be seen as a boost to both economic growth and national cohesion; Sanchez announced on 22 April that it would be increasing defence spending to 2%. It’s not enough, but it is a start and a step in the right direction.

In other words, Europe can turn matters around - if there is the will.

It is most likely Germany, France and Britain that will have to take the reins - their example, their drive, their leadership, will be vital. It is about selling a message: laying out the threats, and explaining what can be done about it and how the solution is one that can actually lead to vastly improved circumstances, both societally and economically. The final point is this: that any talk of mobilisation and rearmament is about creating a credible and viable deterrent. It is about making Putin, for example, think again before potentially invading the Baltic States and in so doing triggering Article 5 of the NATO treaty - which commits all NATO nations to militarily defend its fellow members. It is about preventing war. If Europe can unite, make itself militarily strong and independent of the USA and, at the same time, grow its economy, then we can all look forward to decades more of peace.

With thanks to Robbie Boyd and Rob Murray.

My new book, VICTORY 45, co-written with Al Murray is out now.

www.ww2headquarters.com
