title: One German’s War
html:
The Second World War is slipping from living memory but I was very fortunate to become fascinated by the subject in my early thirties and at a time when there were plenty of veterans still around. When I was researching my first few books on the subject, I made the most of travelling around the world meeting and talking to a large number of people who had lived and fought through the war.

 

Generally speaking, it was fairly easy to track down veterans from the winning side and even comparatively straightforward speaking to Italians too – and perhaps I’ll write about some of those incredible people I met in later posts. German veterans, though, were often understandably much harder to pin down. I did, though, get to talk to a good number and I’m very glad I did. It’s interesting meeting older people. For the most part, I found I warmed to veterans in much the same way one would warm to anyone. With some, the connection was there from the outset; with others it was harder work. Some were incredibly warm and open; others more brittle, more reserved. That’s as one would expect. A lot of veterans, regardless of the side they fought on or what nationality, were simply kindly old men, in their twilight years and happy to chat to a much younger neutral party who was showing obvious interest in their life and stories. 

 

There was one German veteran, however, who has rather haunted me ever since. His wartime experiences were, in the big scheme of things, unremarkable, but his story has stayed with me far more vividly than most. It must be over twenty years since I visited Freidrich Büchner at his family home in Ludwigsstadt, but I can remember it as clear as if it was a week ago, for what he told me had a profound and lasting effect. 

 

I had put an ad in a veterans’ journal and he had written to me, in German, a letter landing on my hall floor in the familiar beautiful hand-writing of people brought up and educated in those pre-war years. He wrote that he would be glad to talk to me and suggested I visit him. Fortunately, I had an English friend, Sarah, who had married a German and was living in Berlin with their young son, who agreed to help out, and so she played go-between, ringing Herr Büchner and arranging a time to visit. It was wintertime and there was snow about, and the days were short. We drove from Berlin to Leipzig and from there, on to Ludwigsstadt, through rolling and largely empty farmland and through dense pines forests thick with snow. It was a monochrome landscape – brooding and slightly foreboding too.

 

Herr Büchner and his wife had invited us to arrive around 11am; the plan was to chat first, then have some lunch, then possibly chat some more. I was always a little nervous about having meals, because of the clatter of cutlery, the clammer of the meal and because back then I was still using a dictaphone to record the conversation. They were far from ideal for the task and couldn’t really cope with ambient noise; but I didn’t want to miss anything. On the other hand, it was obviously kind of them to feed us and neither of us wanted to appear rude. Sarah and I agreed beforehand that we would try hard to keep off the topic of the war during lunch.

 

It was a square house on a slight rise on the left-hand side of the road as it dropped down into the small town. Not a big house, but not small either; a comfortable, middle-class place, and warm and homely. Herr Büchner and his wife would have been in their late seventies; they seemed fit and well and welcomed us warmly. Settling down in the living room, we began our chat. I found that having a translator was actually quite helpful. While Sarah was repeating my questions and Herr Büchner was answering, I had the time to digest his previous answer and prepare for what I would ask next.

 

Anyway, we did what I always did when talking to veterans: we started at the beginning. He told us he was born on 29 April 1926 in Jena, not far from where he now lived.  It was the same house in which he was raised. ‘This house was built in 1927,’ he said, ‘the year after I was born. My father and grandfather had a business making slates - slates for schools, like blackboards, but smaller and which were used by pupils instead of exercise books. But the factory finally closed in 1989.’ He had one younger brother – he had become an art director in a museum. There had been a little sister too, but she had died when Herr Büchner had been very young.

 

Despite this tragedy, his had been a good childhood. Ludwigsstadt was part of Turingen – a largely rural area with its own distinct accent. The old family slate factory was now used for manufacturing hospital equipment, but the town was famous for its slate. The quarries had become exhausted in recent times, but it had been big business before the war - the biggest single employer in town. The only quarry still going was for making roof tiles, he told us.   

 

As a boy, he’d gone to the local school initially then to a secondary school in Saalfeld. To begin with, he took a train each day but then later lodged with another family; this, he told us, was quite common. He had rather enjoyed it. Turingen had a good reputation for schools and his was a Gymnasium, a school that prepared students for university rather than for apprenticeships.

 

I’d not yet asked him at all about the war, or about the Nazis, but as though worrying he was boring us with tales of his childhood, he suddenly announced that he’d gone to war aged eighteen and returned home when he was twenty-one. ‘When I got back,’ he said, ‘my father had become ill and worn out; there weren't many men left, and he’d had to work much harder than he might otherwise have done. It had taken its toll. I was sat down by my mother and told her that I had to help my father and the family business.’ And so, his path had been decided. He worked in the family business for forty years and eventually moved his own family into his parents’ house. He wasn’t complaining; he found the work interesting, and although it had been hard work, he had enjoyed it and had been happy to take on the family business. His had father died back in 1951, aged 72.

 

It felt as though we were galloping forward too fast, so I asked if we could go back a bit to his childhood once more. After all, German childhoods under the Third Reich were very different from those in western democracies. He seemed happy enough to talk about those days. Like everyone else, he had been in the Hitler Youth. He’d enjoyed it – especially all the sports. Ludwigsstadt hadn’t been big enough to have all the specialist branches, although there was one that made model aeroplanes. That wasn’t for him, however. He just enjoyed all the history they were taught and the hiking and camping.    

He pointed out that when Hitler had come to there had been millions of unemployed but in a matter of a few years there had been zero unemployment; this had also been achieved by civil projects rather than just military build-up. He didn’t say it in as many words, but implied that Luwigsstadt was a quiet backwater and that his parents were hardly politically motivated; as a boy he’d clearly been pretty sheltered. Politics wasn’t discussed. Rather, he’d just got on with the business of growing up. ‘I had very little idea that war was coming,’ he told us. ‘Generally, I would say that there was no real concern or awareness of what was going on. Only just before war broke out did we start to realise what was round the corner. Certainly everyone was happy to be working, though. Economic prosperity was what everyone was bothered about.’ Did he remember the 1936 Olympics, I wondered? ‘Only vaguely,’ he replied.

Everyone had been very happy about the Anchluss of Austria, however. After the First World War and the creation of Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Austria, the Allies had forbidden Germans from going to these countries, he said, but these were places where many people had family. So, they had all been happy when these borders had been relaxed in 1938 and 1939.

 

We’d been talking for perhaps an hour or so when his wife called us for lunch. We sat around the dining table in the adjoining room for what felt like a traditional lunch – boiled ham and boiled vegetables. As a Brit having grown up on boiled food, I thought it was delicious, and thankfully we managed to talk widely and generally – polite but genial small-talk. It was after lunch that the mood perceptibly changed, however. ‘We’ll continue talking upstairs,’ Herr Büchner announced. ‘I have a room at the top of the house.’ We followed him up to what was the apex of the roof area. There was a desk and bookshelves as well as armchairs around a coffee table. The shelves were filled with books about the war. His Iron Cross was in a frame on the wall. An inner sanctum at the top of the house.

 

We sat down and began talking again. He had been thirteen when the war had begun. In late August, he’d been on the North Sea coast for a holiday. They’d been staying on an island but on the way back were in a Youth Hostel on a boat in the harbour when there had been a great commotion; this was the announcement of the Ribbentrop-Molotov Pact. Most people, he said, believed Danzig should be linked to East Prussia, as it had been before 1919. ‘When we invaded Poland,’ he said, ‘I don't remember feeling any jubilation but there was a sense that it was an important job that had to be done.’

 

He followed what was happening in the war, just like everyone else. He read newspapers and listened to the news on the radio. The Hitler Youth also kept him and his friends informed. Then a lot of the older boys in the town began heading off to war, so he was very aware of the impact it was having. The war made the family slate business a lot tougher. Not all the slate had come from the local quarries but supplies from elsewhere now dried up, as did labour. There were also severe food shortages. His father had to work all hours to keep things going but managed to get a contract making wooden ammunition boxes; that helped. Everyone who could pitch in did so; Herr Büchner spent the school holidays working in the factory along with lots of other boys. ‘Life was hard,’ he told us, and everyone was worried about the 'children' who'd been called up.’

 

He had volunteered for the armed forces when he was seventeen in the hope it would give him greater choice; in other words, he’d done so for pragmatic reasons rather than for any gang-ho desire to go off and fight. As it turned out, the call-up didn’t come until he turned eighteen, even though that had been in 1944 by which time the German manpower shortage was critical. ‘When you're six,’ he said, ‘you would go off to school and when you were eighteen you would go off and become a soldier.’

 

He had started his training on 31 May 1944 at Würzburg. Three months’ basic infantry training was followed by a special course for reserve officers for a further three months. After this, he became an instructor himself, teaching basic training to the next drafts of young recruits. Eventually, in March 1945, with the end of the war in sight, he was given a Field Post number and finally posted to Verona with two other youngsters, the main first port of call for any German troops arriving in Italy. All three joined the 98. Infanterie Division, although Büchner was sent to the Panzer Jäger Abteilung, which was an anti-tank unit. The 3rd Company had 20mm flak guns, on which he’d trained at Würzburg. He was welcomed in well enough, and couldn’t recall any great sense of doom and gloom. ‘The war was not over yet - so we had to make war,’ he said. ‘That was the attitude. I think, we all felt that we had a job to do and that we were simply getting on with it.’ When he joined, it was at the end of a long winter in which the Italian front had been comparatively quite with no major offensives by the Allies. That, though, was soon to change. They were all waiting for the Allied spring offensive they knew was coming. Their unit was in the plain of the River Po, just to the north of the edge of the mighty Apennines. ‘We were in a village next to a railway,’ he said. ‘We were by a railway embankment in a meadow.’

 

They dug foxholes and scrapes for the guns. There were four cannons per 'zug' - or battery – and four zugs in each of the company, and five men assigned to each cannon. Herr Büchner was an unteroffizier – a corporal - and was commander of one of the cannons. The rest of the 3rd Company was not far away, while the HQ of the 98. Division was also fairly close by. A field telephone was the link between them and the rest of the company and also the division. Each cannon was about 20 metres apart.

 

They lived cheek-by-jowl with the Italians in the village and as far as he was concerned, relations were pretty good. There was no looting or pillaging – about this he was adamant. The Germans were chronically short of food and cigarettes and so bartered with the Italians, and paid – again, he was insistent about this – for extra eggs, wine and other food to bolster the meagre rations. Nor was there any raping of Italian women. ‘If you raped an Italian, you would be sentenced to death,’ he said. ‘But I certainly don't know of anyone raping Italians. No-one did it. It was too dangerous. But there were friendships with Italian women and that was something different - although not in my company. There was neither the time nor opportunity.’

 

At this point, Frau Büchner came up with a tray of coffee, which she placed down on the table, then discreetly slipped out again. Herr Büchner began pouring out the coffee into cups with saucers and teaspoons, which now slightly rattled as his hands had begun to shake a little. It really struck me; I’d not noticed any shakes beforehand, so this was something new. I wondered whether it was because of what we were discussing, but then again, his experiences, as he had been recounting them, had been fairly innocuous up until now.

 

That was not the case for much longer, however. As we sipped our coffee, I realised everything he’d told us so far had been building up to what now followed: his experiences during the final offensive in Italy and the end of the war. The Allies attacked on 9 April. That morning, bombers came over and plastered their positions. He had felt utter terror and he and others had hidden in some wine cellars next to the railway embankment. The Italians began shouting and screaming; the bombs were not very effective but the noise, the trembling of the ground, and the sudden violence had been frightening. And while their guns had escaped, the same could not be said for some of the houses in the village.

 

The 98. Division was behind the River Santerno between Lugo and Sant’Agata, near Imola, and they were attacked by British and Indian troops. The Jäger battalion was a further kilometre back. No sooner had the bombers gone than the ‘Jabos’ came over – what the Germans called fighter-bombers – followed by a heavy artillery barrage. Shells screamed over. All that first day, they were under assault: bombs, cannon fire, shelling. It was relentless. That first night they were ordered to pack up and move back, about 12 kilometres. The next day, they set themselves up and fired back but again, once darkness fell, they retreated again. ‘This went on pretty much every day,’ he said. ‘The front was moving back bit by bit. We were constantly under fire, but we were shooting back. We tried to shoot down fighters as well, but we didn't have the range to hit the bombers. I wasn't aware that we managed to actually shoot down any fighters at all.’

 

On 21 April, they reached the mighty Po, a wide and comparatively fast-flowing river. It was at this this point that he realised it was all over. There were no bridges left and very few boats. Most of the division managed to cross over the course of three nights on a boat bridge that had been hastily built, but each day, such was the preponderance of enemy Jabos, the pontoon boat bridge had to be dismantled, then rebuilt under the cover of darkness. It was bewildering. Herr Büchner’s company arrived in the midst of chaos: a mass of men, vehicles and horses. Thousands of horses. Their own guns were towed by horses but now came the order to abandon everything – all vehicles, all equipment. All horses. ‘And so, we had to shoot them all. We had to destroy them.’ His voice started to quaver and then suddenly he completely broke down. He sat opposite us, his head in his hands unable to prevent his tears or convulsive sobs.

 

‘I’m so sorry,’ I said. ‘Please don’t feel you have to tell us this.’ Sarah put a hand on his shoulder, but he held up a hand. ‘No, no,’ he said, ‘I want to tell you.’ Gradually, he recovered his composure, then, taking a deep breath, continued his tale. They managed to get across the boat bridge. There were long queues, but they made it over one night. Many did not. Lots had tried to swim for it and while some did get across plenty of others were drowned. It was terrible. The scale of destruction, the desolation. The realisation of what he was witnessing: an army imploding. Strangely, though, there was no panic. There wasn’t any feeling at all at the time. Only afterwards.

Once over the other side, it was simply a case of fleeing north. The discipline and operational organisation of the German Army had begun to disintegrate – after all, with almost no weapons, what could they now do but run for the hills? From the Po, the Alps loomed in the distance. In the chaos, Büchner and a few of the men he was with managed to get a ride in a half-track that had somehow made it across. Their aim was to get to the Brenner Pass, the route through the Alps out of Italy into Austria; it was this same route, either by rail or road, that almost all German Army men and materiel had flowed into Italy. Now, they hoped it might be their means of escape too.

On 28 April, they were nearing Belluno, up the River Piave Valley beyond Padova and Rovigo. Just before they reached the town, they stopped at a farmhouse and asked for a room. The Italians offered them beds, which they gratefully took. Büchner slept well, but the following morning there was suddenly pandemonium; the house was full of partisans. ‘I don't know what happened to the two guards we had posted outside the farmhouse,’ he said, ‘but I think they must have been killed.’ The dozen of them were now prisoners of the partisan band and led up into the mountains, where they were corralled around a mountain hut, along with another sixty or so other German prisoners. They weren’t all German, however; a number were conscripted men from conquered territories, including a number of former Soviet soldiers. On 30 April 1945, they were led out of the mountain hut and lined up with the partisans all around them, the Italians clutching a mixture of rifles and sub-machine-guns. A man wearing a red scarf - who Büchner assumed was the partisan leader  - now gave a long speech. Büchner was worried; the partisans seemed twitchy and then suddenly three of the Russians were pulled out and the partisan commander pulled out a pistol and aimed it at the head of the first. But it jammed, so he angrily demanded another pistol, but this jammed too. Finally, he grabbed a sub-machine-gun, but made a terrible job of the execution.

At this point in the telling, Herr Büchner suddenly broke down again. His face dissolved, his hands went to his head and his shoulders shook. It was an awful moment. Again, we tried to reassure him and tell him that he didn’t have to go on. ‘No,’ he said again as he began to recover. ‘I want to tell you.’ We waited a moment while he composed himself. The Russians were on the ground, writhing and screaming, and some of the other Germans were ordered to take them away and finish the job. Büchner didn’t see it but eventually the screaming stopped. It was terrible, he said. Just terrible. And then he looked away a moment, wiped his eyes again. ‘That was the day after my nineteenth birthday,’ he said at length. ‘The day Hitler killed himself.’

The rest of his story seemed to be a lot easier for him to tell after he’d unburdened himself. Two days later, the rest of them were taken back down the mountain to Belluno; it was 2 May and the war in Italy was over. It was the first unconditional surrender signed by the Germans. The Americans arrived soon after and Büchner and the other prisoners were reunited with much of the rest of the company and sent to a school, which acted as a temporary prison camp. ‘Eventually,’ he told us, ‘we were taken to a large British prison camp near Rimini. I stayed at Rimini until August with about 10,000 others.’

 

He eventually got home on 17 March 1947, joined the family business and never really left Ludwigsstadt again.  Married, had kids, and got on with his life. We talked a little more about the crossing of the Po. Some 7,000 bodies were recovered, he told us. It was estimated, he said, that as many as 10,000 German troops lost their lives trying to cross the river; he’d obviously read up about it since. ‘It says something about the German troops that they preferred to risk drowning than surrender even though the war was already lost,’ he said. ‘We didn't want to be prisoners.’ Herr Büchner now sat back in his seat and exhaled – through exhaustion, through relief. He was silent a moment; we all were. Then he said, ‘I’ve never, ever told anyone what I have just told you.’

 

Soon after, we bid him and his wife goodbye. It had been an extraordinary day, and I remember feeling very wistful as Sarah and I drove back towards Berlin. I knew it was extremely unlikely I’d ever see him again, and nor have I. That last line of his had really struck me. Our own veterans here in Britain – or in any other of Allied war-winning nations – might have chosen not to talk of their experiences but at least their sacrifice had been appreciated. They had been victorious, part of a moral crusade and a fight for freedom. At anniversaries and once a year in November, there is a national commemoration. Veterans are venerated and revered, and yet men like Friedrich Büchner, sent off to fight at eighteen, had to feel ashamed of what they had been compelled to do.  They had had to bottle it up, not mention it, part of a national and collective guilt.

 

Arguments still rage over just how much ordinary Germans knew of the terrible crimes in the East and the horrors of the Holocaust yet it was clear to me that day that Herr Büchner had been an innocent, caught up in something over which he had almost no control. He, too, had suffered. The horrors of what he’d seen and experienced had been bottled up inside him all those years. I was a young, thirty-something neutral. My arrival that day, I realised, was like offering him a chance to lie on a psychiatrist’s couch and unburden himself. I hope it helped, because he was a lovely fellow; a kind, old man who had suffered much.

There were many victims in that terrible war.

title: STOPPING THE PANZERS
html:
I was in the Ardennes last week with my great pal and podcasting partner, Al Murray, filming a new series of WW2 Walking the Ground about the Battle of the Bulge.  That battle, begun on 16 December 1944 in the depths of winter, was not Hitler’s last gamble, as it has regularly been called, because that suggests there was a chance of success.  There was not.  Rather, it was another act of gargantuan folly by a man who had lost what very small grip on reality he had ever had.  The battle plan – to burst through American lines in the forested and hilly Ardennes of Belgium and Luxembourg, split the Allies in two, and drive a wedge all the way to Antwerp was dead in the water before it even began.  All the senior German commanders knew this, because no matter how many troops were gathered for such an operation, how many tanks or guns, it was never going to be enough to overcome the immense material might of the Allies by this stage of the war.

 

Of course, a breakthrough American positions was achievable, but the further German strike forces progressed, the longer their own lines would be stretched.  They would also take hits themselves – through being attacked by the American defenders, by mechanical failure, and by the need to peel off men and material to hold the ground already captured.  Even if they did reach Antwerp, then what?  They’d have perhaps half a dozen tanks and a few hundred men left to do what, exactly? It was, the quote General MacAuliffe, totally nuts. Yet despite Hitler’s obvious cognitive decline, he still held an iron grip on Germany and its people, and especially so his military commanders.  And so, Operation HERBSTNEBEL – Autumn Mist – went ahead.

 

Much has been made since the end of the war of the German tactical superiority.  German troops, it has been argued, were more flexible, more agile, and better able to think on their feet that either the western Allies or the Soviet Red Army.  They lost only because they did not have the vast manpower and material might of their enemies.  In recent years, this theory has been largely kicked into the long grass, although admiration of the way in which the Germans organized themselves into kampfgruppen – ad hoc battle groups of tanks, artillery and infantry – remains. 

 

Perhaps the most famous – or rather, infamous – kampfgruppen of the Battle of the Bulge, is that of Kampfgruppe Peiper, named after its charismatic 29 year-old commander, Joachim Peiper, former adjutant to SS Reichsführer Heinrich Himmler and tank commander in the SS. 1. Panzer-Division ‘Liebstandarte Adolf Hitler’.  During the Bulge, he commanded the 1. SS Panzer Regiment along with some additional artillery, anti-aircraft guns and extra infantry, including, for part of the time, some Fallschirmjäger – paratroopers – from the 3. Fallschirmjäger Division.  Peiper was due to reach the mighty River Meuse, some 60 miles from his start, in three days and get across in four, but they started almost a day late because the initial breakthrough had been slow, then found they were being pecked at by American rearguards for the next thirty miles or so.  Having pushed on beyond the town of Stavelot, they then found themselves facing an increasingly more meaningful response from the Americans.  Within a few days, his spearheads were cut off by US reinforcements sweeping in behind him.  Frantically searching for ways across the rivers Peiper’s men continually confronted, from the Ambleve to the Salm and the Lienne, this major attack group became increasingly dissipated, dislocated and discombobulated.  Eventually, Peiper had to abandon all his vehicles and try and break through American positions at night.  Only around 770 men of the 4,800 he’d begun with made it through to German lines on Christmas Eve 1944.  All 800 vehicles and 117 tanks and tracked assault guns were knocked out, broken down or abandoned. All, and would not now be sufficiently replaced.

 

Peiper’s men got substantially further than the neighbouring main thrust to their north, however, which barely advanced ten miles before being stopped dead.  In both cases, whether to the north where the SS 12. Panzer Division ‘Hitler Jugend’ was in the driving seat, or in the centre of the 6. Panzer Armee’s thrust where Peiper and Co had been attacking, it was ad hoc battle groups of Americans that did the halting.

 

Unlike the French in May 1940, the Americans in the Battle of the Bugle were able to hold on to the nodal points – crossroads, villages and towns, railway junctions, bridges – long enough to derail the very tight German timeframe.  Hitler’s plan depended entirely on speed of movement – and with it, surprise.  The aim was to burst through American positions and drive on before the Americans had time to respond.   This meant that snatching back that precious time from the Germans was crucial for US success. A blocking force at a key crossroads that held up the Germans for a day or so, or even half a day, made all the difference, as it allowed the Americans time to bring in reinforcements from elsewhere.  Roads were also vitally important because it was winter, and although cold, it was not freezing when the battle began and huge tanks – let alone vehicles – struggled to cross muddy, wet, open fields.  As a consequence, roads became the arteries of the German advance.  They also became crucial to the American defence.

 

The story of the Battle of the Bulge is one of many comparatively small engagements with hastily formed mixed units of American infantry, engineers, anti-tank gunners and tanks, grimly holding onto crossroads.  Al and I wandered all over the battlefields but one area that made an especially strong impression was in the north, where the main effort of the German 6. Panzer Armee had been thrust.  After walking through the thick pine forest of the Krinkelterwald through which the 12. SS Panzer Division advanced, we then headed to a crossroads just to the east of the Twin Villages of Krinkelt and Rocherath.  Lausdell was more a confluence of roads and tracks than a crossroads but it was here that Lieutenant-Colonel William McKinley’s mixed task force – what the Germans call a kampfgruppe – held up the main German thrust for more than eighteen hours.  By the time the Germans finally pushed past, US reinforcements had arrived and were firmly lodged on a crucial bit of high ground, the Elsenborn Ridge.  And that was that – the Germans could get no further.

 

The battle is littered with similar other stories.  Fuller’s Task Force east of the crucial town of St Vith held up the Germans a day.  At Parker’s Crossroads, the panzers were again held up; and also at Manhay and Longvilly and Noville and at Lanzerath and many other places besides.  These are the stories of desperate stands by Task Force Lovelady, Task Force Cherry, and Task Force Mayes – just to name a handful; all were battle groups, hastily flung together in the very best tradition of German agile and tactical kampfgruppen.    These forces held up the Germans, allowed the reinforcements to be hastily manoeuvred into place – with astonishing operational deftness, incidentally - and, crucially, gave time for the mighty American artillery to move up, dig in and find their range.  Artillery forward observation officers, able to direct fire, were also a key component of these American battle groups.

 

And they proved decisive, blunting the panzers and with it, Hitler’s absurd plans.  The thing about forming such rapidly put-together battle groups is that it required really good training. Because different units were being expected to form themselves quickly into a new combat unit and then immediately co-operate and fight together, and often under an unfamiliar commander, the men involved needed to understand what was expected of them.  That in turn required an understanding of what the different component parts could do – how infantry and armour worked together, or how best to use combat engineers and accompanying artillery, and so on.  Most American troops arriving in the theatre would have had between a year and two before going into action, whereas by this stage of the war, new German soldiers would have been lucky if they’ received six weeks’ training.

 

The Bulge battle was also marked by numerous acts of astonishing bravery by the Americans.  Outlying blocking positions were told to hold on ‘at all costs’ and usually did; and while they held up the panzers all right, they did so at a terrible cost.  This extraordinary self-sacrifice could only come from a very strong sense of duty, combined with incredibly good training and, ultimately, immense materiel strength.  Curiously, though, the narrative of the war has tended to focus more on American muscle than prowess.  Wandering over the snow-covered battlefields of the Ardennes last week, I couldn’t help thinking it was time to change the dial a little.  Sure, the Americans were the arsenal of democracy, but by December 1944 they also had a damn good army too with the kind of tactical flexibility and nous we have traditionally applied to the Germans rather than the Allies.

title: Getting Ready For War
html:
I was recently at a conference in Athens where a former British Chief of the Defence Staff warned us we were now in the foothills of World War Three.  He may well have been right to say this.  On the other hand, he might be entirely wrong, but I’m not sure the UK or any other country in the west should be complacent on this matter.  It’s surely not worth taking the chance; at the very least we know there a number of world leaders out there who think ill of us and our western partners and would happily see us crushed given half the chance.  The key, really, in the short to medium term, is for NATO and the west to show enough unity and military and economic strength to make any potential enemies think again.  Unfortunately, the ultimate deterrent – nuclear weapons – is not really a deterrent any more because a number of countries have them and if one was ever fired in anger, that would very likely be the rapid end of the world.  Or, to put it another way: if a British submarine commander had his finger hovering over the red button, we would have already lost. 

The answer is to have a strong enough conventional deterrent to make our enemies unlikely to want to take the risk or going to war. This is unquestionably the best way to ensure ongoing and lasting peace.  Reading through predictions about Britain’s latest forthcoming strategic defence review, however, it’s clear very little is going to be happening any time soon to rectify the much-reduced scale of the UK’s armed forces.  The Royal Navy is going to continue to shrink, the Army is already below strength, we don’t have enough aircraft, recruitment has been outsourced to private companies, and it seems that almost all our current procurement projects are late and coming in over-budget. It’s reckoned we’d struggle to field a single brigade of a few thousand frontline troops effectively let alone a division.  France has a larger armed forces than Britain but not by a huge amount while Germany’s is even smaller than that of the UK.  So, if we are really in the foothills of World War Three, then this is hardly good news for Britain or for those in the west and NATO looking for greater collective impetus from the largest nations in Europe.

Inevitably, comparisons are being made with the 1930s.  Back then, political upheaval followed financial catastrophe and much of Europe lurched to the right, albeit far further so than today.  The well-trodden narrative is that Britain was late to the rearmament party and still badly playing catch-up when the war broke out in September 1939.  Neville Chamberlain, the Prime Minister, threw the Czechs under the bus, appeasing Hitler in an effort to buy time.  So, too, did the French.  It then took the best part of six years to rid the world of the Nazis and the cruel imperial ambitions of the Japanese, and at the war’s end, tens of millions were dead, even more millions displaced and the world was changed forever. 

 

It's true that Britain was not really ready for war in 1938 at the time of the Munich Crisis and it’s also true that then, as now, the vast majority of the population were not for war mongering or remotely willing to enter another European, let alone, world conflict.  Yet, had Britain been far militarily stronger in 1938, would the war have ever begun in the first place?  Would Hitler have gambled and invaded Poland?  It’s impossible to know but it is worth considering just how Britain was placed in the late 1930s. 

 

It was certainly the case that Britain had a small army. In 1936, it stood at just 192,325, a figure that fell further – slightly – the following year.  There were also 141,000 members of the Territorial Army and a further 57,500 men in the British Indian Army.  All were volunteers. These were comparatively small figures for a leading nation in the 1930s but it must be remembered that Britain’s situation was very different to that of France or Germany, for example.  Britain was an island, not continental, nation, and one that lay at the heart of a huge global trading empire.  Its military strategy was not an aggressive, land-grabbing one, but one designed to defend its sovereignty and global interests. 

 

Nor did the small size of the army mean Britain was behind in terms of an armaments industry.  Rather, in the first part of the decade, Britain had been the leading armaments producer in the world, most of which had been exported, but those factories – and their workers – had not vanished a few years later.  Far from it, and Britain was well-placed for rapid expansion. Firms like Vickers Armstrong and its subsidiary, Vickers Aviation, as well as Hawker Siddeley, Rolls-Royce and de Havilland were among the largest industrial employers in the country and invested huge sums in research and development.

 

And before he was Prime Minister, Chamberlain had been Chancellor of the Exchequer and had instigated a huge upgrade of Britain’s warships and an even larger expansion of the Navy, working on the sound principle that it made good sense to undertake the largest projects – building modern warships – in a time of peace. In 1939, the Royal Navy was comfortably the world’s largest.  Chamberlain had also been a powerful advocate of developing the Royal Air Force.  It was largely down to him that by 1938, the RAF had two modern fighter planes in the Hawker Hurricane and Supermarine Spitfire, and as Chancellor, he had continued to oversee Britain’s further investment in the arms industry.  Just because he had favoured appeasement in 1938, did not mean he was in any way slow to build up Britain’s military strength.  It’s also worth noting that while the current British government says the UK cannot afford to rearm at the moment, Britain could not afford it in the 1930s either.  They still did, however.  By the outbreak of war, Britain also had the world’s first – and at the time only – fully co-ordinated and modern air defence system.  If any government’s first objective is to protect the people it is governing, then the Baldwin and  Chamberlain governments were doing all they could in the late thirties to ensure they were protected from the growing threat of the dictators. 

There were also then, as now, logistical considerations that mitigated against a large army.  If France or Germany wanted to move their millions of troops, they could put them on trains or into vehicles.  If Britain planned to do the same, it had to transport the army by a vast armada of ships.  And once oversees, it then had to be maintained, requiring even more ships.  Nor was there much space to upkeep a large army within Britain itself.  In other words, maintaining a large army in peacetime made little sense.  Far better to focus on air and naval power for Britain’s defence, which was exactly what they did.  In any case, by the outbreak of war, France was a formal ally and had an army capable of rapid expansion into millions of men.

Britain also had the huge advantage of immense global reach.  A map of world shipping from 1937 shows a number of ant lines of ships flowing around much of the globe and in and out of Britain.  One of the strongest links from Britain is to Argentina in South America.  This was not part of the empire, but the UK had considerable extra-imperial assets there; British companies owned much of Argentina’s port facilities, railways and ranches, for example.  Companies with global reach meant a very strong purchasing power, most useful when buying much-needed ores and minerals once war broke out.  I’ll write a bit about this in a later post, but the point is this: Britain might have had a small army in 1939 and an air force that was smaller than that of Nazi Germany’s Luftwaffe, but it had a very strong defensive military capability, and, crucially, the kind of wealth, internal industrial infrastructure and global reach that meant that when it did need to rapidly accelerate its rearming it was incredibly – and decisively - placed to do so.

I’m sure it’s all too obvious that we are not remotely in the same position today.  Nothing can be built on time.  Procurement projects sink under the weight of red tape, regulation, and catastrophic inefficiency.  Joining the armed forces is largely unappealing due to the low wages, low morale, and the paring back of every aspect of military requirements and efficiency; there’s not enough kit, not enough ammunition, not enough aircraft, not enough ships, much of its day-to-day running is in the hands of private companies only interested in a profit. The purchasing of new helicopters two-and-a-half years ago, for example, was halted at the last moment because the MOD suddenly decided some competition was needed. It wasn’t. Two – foreign - firms who subsequently tendered for the contract then pulled out at the last minute, wasting valuable time, money an effort, and presumably had entered the bid in the first place only to undermine that of the original British firm. The RAF still doesn’t have any of these new helicopters. Really, it’s not only depressing but deeply worrying. 

Poland, meanwhile, approaching 5% of GDP on defence, has the fastest growing economy in Europe.  It’s the Keynesian model: rearming and boosting the economy at the same time. The Poles are proving this can still be done. Russia is war weary, no longer has the ballast of the Warsaw Pact countries and currently is not the threat that Nazi Germany was. But is it worth tempting Putin to invade the Baltic states and triggering Article 5? And doesn’t Trump have a point that we’re complacently overly dependent on the United States? World power is rapidly shifting, the US is turning to the Indo- Pacific, and Western Europe is politically weak and militarily vulnerable, even with our new NATO allies.  The British government might argue we cannot afford to significantly rearm, but the cost would be as nothing should those foothills of World War Three develop into mountains.

title: Paddy Mayne and the Victoria Cross That Never Was
html:
Well, hooray for SAS: Rogue Heroes. It’s put the Sicily campaign and Operation HUSKY into the consciousness, it’s made black and white footage of wartime Tommies look cool thanks to the accompaniment of rock music, and those who didn’t know about the tragedy of the glider assault that helped spearhead the Allied invasion, now do. So, what’s not to like? And, more importantly, a lot of people are now talking about Paddy Mayne. These are all very good things, even if, like me, you find Jack O’Connell’s portrayal of a character sharing the same name unspeakably annoying and completely unwatchable.

Subscribe

One of the effects of all this New Year SAS chat is that Ben Wallace, former Defence Secretary and ex-army officer, has publicly called for Paddy Mayne to have one of his medals upgraded to a Victoria Cross, Britain’s highest award for valour. Various others have waded in, and now a motion has been put forward to Parliament formally have a nearly eighty year-old miscarriage of justice amended. Last time I checked, there were forty-four names attached to this motion, one that claims that he ‘won the Victoria Cross at Oldenburg in North West Germany on 9th April 1945.’ This is not strictly speaking true. Rather, he was recommended for a Victoria Cross and while there were a number of high-ranking signatures supporting this, and not least Field Marshal Sir Bernard Montgomery, commander of 21st Army Group, the recommendation was downgraded at its final pass to a DSO, a Distinguished Order. Mayne had already won this particularly gong three times.

I wonder how many of the forty-four current signatures have looked into why Mayne was recommended for a VC that day in April. It’s not written up in every book about the SAS by any means, although Hamish Ross, who wrote Mayne’s authorised biography and had access to a wealth of previously unpublished letters, journals and papers, gives it decent coverage. So, too, does Ben Macintyre in the book that eventually spawned the TV series. Certainly, it was an extraordinary episode in what had already been a truly remarkable wartime career.

The SAS had grown considerably by the time the war was coming to end, so much so that it had been formed into a brigade under Brigadier ‘Mad Mike’ Calvert, a former Chindit who had spent much of the war in Burma and South-East Asia. On 9 April, B and C Squadrons of 1 SAS found themselves in Meppen, in north-west Germany and close to the Dutch border. The River Ems passed southwards through the town and the two SAS squadrons had been seconded to the Canadian Second Army to help spearhead a route for Major-Genera Chris Vokes’s 4th Armoured Division on its drive to the German town of Oldenburg. From here, they were to push on to Wilhelmshaven on the Baltic. Their mission was codenamed Operation HOWARD and the two squadrons were to be accompanied by Lieutenant-Colonel Paddy Mayne, by this time commanding 1 SAS.

The SAS were in their specially adapated jeeps. While these nippy and highly manoeuvrable vehicles had been thier transport of choice since the North African desert days, and while these were equipped with Vickers machine-guns and loaded to the gunwales with ammunition, they were not remotely armoured and anyone riding in them was extremely vulnerable to say the least. That was especially true if in the vanguard of an advance into enemy territory where knowledge of any likely resistance was very limited.

On 10 April - not the 9th - B Squadron was in the lead under the command of Major Dick Bond. He was a former member of the Auxiliary Units, the special highly secret units of the Home Guard trained to create a resistance force had Britain been successfully invaded back in 1940. Bond and his men were approaching the village of Börger from the south, about thirty-five miles south-west of Oldenburg. As they passed a series of farm buildings arranged in an L-shape, they came under attack by panzerfausts and small arms, fired from the buildings but also from a copse that lay by the road just beyond the buildings. Bond and the three others in his jeep swerved off the road, baled out and jumped into a drainage ditch, as did the men in the jeep following behind. Moments later, as Bond poked his head up, he was sniped and killed instantly by a bullet to the head. His driver, a Czech Jew called Michell Levinsolm, did the same a short while later and suffered the same fate.

News of this ambush reached Mayne by radio message and within ten minutes of the attack, he reached the other jeeps now halted a little way to the south, and out of immediate danger. Mayne was upset by these deaths and clearly in one of his silent rages. After being told what had happened and assured no enemy firing had come from the first of the farm buildings, Mayne picked up a Bren gun light machine-gun and some extra magazines, and headed towards the buildings. Opposite these, pinned down in the ditch on the far side of the road by the abandoned jeeps, there were now six men, two of them badly wounded.

Mayne’s driver, a fellow Ulsterman named Billy Hull, followed his boss. Mayne led the way to the first of the farmhouses, which they then entered. Hull was told to head upstairs and to then fire a burst of his Tommy gun from one of the windows. On the ground floor below, Mayne watched, and sure enough, after Hull’s rattle of bullets, there was a ferocious response from the neighbouring farm building. Now he knew where the enemy were. As Hull scuttled back downstairs, Mayne fired the Bren at the house opposite, raking the place, then hurrying over and clearing it off all the enemy inside; presumably he’d killed them all. At any rate, there was no more enemy threat from these buildings.

With the first part of his rescue plan carried out, he hurried back to the rest of the squadron. The farm buildings had been silenced but there was still shooting coming from the copse. He now called for a volunteer to man the Vickers on his jeep. Lieutenant John Scott, who had made the switch to the SAS from the SBS, immediately offered. It had been Scott who had urged Levinsohn to try and reach Bond - an order that had seen the young Czech get himself killed. A sense of guilt seems to have made Scott volunteer to help Mayne now.

Mayne’s plan was really no different from the ‘who dares wins’ approach he had adopted in the desert, when he’d led raiding parties on German and Italian airfields. Driving in jeeps and blasting at everything they saw with machine-guns had been very successful. So, off they went, Mayne driving and Scott manning the twin Vickers. It was a truth of the war that while one machine gun was firing at the enemy, those on the receiving end tended to keep their head down; or, even if they did fire back, they were most likely wild shots, and that was the case now. As Scott hammered away the limited return enemy fire was wayward, then became increasingly sparse, and then stopped altogether. Clearly, the German troops in the copse - all Fallschirmjäger, paratroopers - had either been killed or had scarpered. Mayne’s brazen tactics had once again paid off.

He now turned the jeep around, drove back and with Scott still giving him cover, jumped out, lifted the two wounded men into the vehicles, then headed back to the main party. ‘Throughout the entire action,’ noted Lieutenant Scott afterwards, ‘Colonel Mayne showed a personal courage that it has never before been my privilege to witness.’

Almost the entire SAS squadron had witnessed this action, so vital for any gallantry award, and Mike Calvert had no doubts about recommending Mayne for the highest accolade. This was rubber stamped by General Vokes, General Simonds, the Canadian Second Army commander, and by Monty himself. Certainly, his action fulfilled all the requirements for aVC.

This, however, is no reason to upgrade it now, eighty years on. The truth is that ever since the Victoria Cross came into being there have been those given it who perhaps, on later reflection, should not have been, and many, many more instances of those entirely worthy who did not even get a DSO let alone a VC. And consider why this is being discussed now: because the BBC have released a highly fictionalised drama series in which a character very loosely based on Mayne is the central character. Suddenly, his exploits have been thrust back into the limelight. Mayne himself, who was naturally shy an self-deprecating, would have been mortified to think a bunch of MPs were trying to get such an award upgraded; he’d know it would be for the wrong, not right, reasons.

And what about all those many others who equally risked their lives, performed suicidal feats of bravery and self-sacrifice, but who didn’t even get a single medal? Why single out one man now? If Mayne is upgraded, would that open the floodgates to more? Much of our British democracy is based not on law but precedent and the precedent on the matter of medals is that the final decision is final and remains that way. By upgrading Mayne’s fourth DSO that precedent would be challenged. Furthermore, we would be imposing today’s mores onto an event that happened eighty years ago. It is not up to us now to start altering history.

And spare a thought for John Scott. He had earlier received a Military Medal - below a DSO - before being commissioned, but was merely Mentioned in Dispatches for his manning of the Vickers gun beside Mayne. Had he not also put his life directly on the line? Where are the calls for a medal for him? This entire lack of any gong for Scott makes a nonsense of any upgrade for Mayne.

The 1 SAS commander was unquestionably an extraordinary warrior, great leader of men, hugely charismatic and undeniably an exceptionally brave man. He also remains one of our best-known figures from the Second World War, and feted, honoured, and held in awe by most who know of his exploits. There are statues of him, as well as books and now TV dramas in which his legend continues. And he has four DSOs. Four, of a medal that is incredibly hard to be awarded once. Regardless of whether his astonishing action near Oldenburg back in April 1945 deserved a VC or not, Mayne has way more accolades than many others also deserving of our understanding, knowledge and admiration. We should leave him be.
